title: Debiasing and t -Tests for Synthetic Control Inference on Average Causal Effects
The Unintended Consequences of #MeToo: Evidence from Research Collaborations in Economics and Finance
abstract: ABSTRACT How did #MeToo alter collaboration between women and men? I show junior female researchers start fewer projects after #MeToo. A decrease in collaborations with male coauthors—especially new senior male coauthors at the same institution—largely explains the decline. The decrease is larger at universities with higher perceived harassment accusation risk and smaller where both women and men publicly express greater awareness of gender issues. I find no evidence that reduced collaboration improves research outcomes for junior female researchers. The results suggest that #MeToo led to a breakdown in trust that came at a cost for junior women's career opportunities.

title: Carbon Emissions and the Bank-Lending Channel
abstract: Abstract We study how firm-level carbon emissions affect bank lending and real outcomes in a sample of global firms with syndicated loans. We exploit bank-level climate commitments as firm-level shocks to lending relationships, using firms' prior credit exposures to identify credit supply effects. Firms with higher emissions that previously borrowed from committed banks receive less bank credit. Evidence from lending volumes, prices, and within-firm-time loan-level data indicates a supply-side shift away from high-emission firms, not explained by borrower risk. Affected firms reduce debt, leverage, size, and investment, yet we find no reduction in future emissions, instead documenting evidence consistent with greenwashing. (JEL G21, G23, G30, D62, Q50)

title: Adverse selection with sequential risks
Beyond the “supply chain” framing: Cattle ranching as a vanishing mediator of deforestation and dispossession in the Brazilian and Colombian Amazon
abstract: Unsustainable land-use change has become an increasingly critical social and environmental issue. Over a few decades, vast expanses of land with native vegetation or devoted to mixed-farming systems have given way to large-scale agriculture, incurring considerable biodiversity and livelihood loss. Cattle ranching and the production of a handful of internationally traded commodities such as soy and palm oil play a pivotal role in that expansion. They have led to numerous sustainability initiatives to curb their negative social and environmental impacts, yet a “supply chain” framing poses important limitations, for it typically fails to consider relationships between sectors and broader landscape dynamics. For one, there may be much stronger drivers than food consumption at play. This article draws from the frontier literature and explores the concept of “vanishing mediator” to analyze the role played by cattle ranching in particular. Comparing the Brazilian and Colombian Amazon, we assess how ranching intermediates an ongoing transition between pre-frontier forest areas and capital-intensive monocultures. We draw from land-use data and the scientific literature on each of the two cases as well as on a total of 30 key-informant interviews done in Brazil and Colombia. Our results show that cattle ranching’s role in spearheading deforestation in both countries cannot be understood without reference to its broader context, for it works as a vanishing mediator between pre-frontier settings and industrial agriculture. Ranching occupies frontiers with little infrastructure, paving the way for monocultures; it is instrumental to the land grabbing that makes the endeavor highly profitable; and, crucially, it precariously absorbs and co-opts displaced smallholders. Cattle ranching introduces the latter — as well as incoming settlers — to state institutions that previously neglected them and to a market-driven approach to land use that still preserves the trappings of rural living. Ultimately, however, people migrate to sprawling cities and clear the way for capital-intensive crops such as soy in Brazil and oil palm in Colombia. We conclude that the notion of individualized “supply chains” is shortsighted for dealing with such broader dynamics. Instead, effective sustainability interventions require addressing local vulnerabilities and investing in economic alternatives that can successfully hedge against deforestation drivers.

title: Smartphones, information, and bargaining power: Evidence from pastoral areas in China
Shrinking the Term Structure
Visible from Afar: Remote Employees’ Collaboration Responsiveness to Managerial Requests
The Connectivity Paradox of Flexible Team Arrangements
abstract: Organizations rely on team-based structures to promote connectivity and performance. Yet, recent research suggests that increasingly flexible team arrangements, characterized by multiple team membership (MTM) and fluid team membership (FTM), may simultaneously foster and undermine social capital in organizations. To address this connectivity paradox of flexible team arrangements, we integrate research on MTM and FTM and develop multilevel theory linking these practices to social capital and performance at the firm and individual levels. We test our theory in two complementary studies. Study 1 uses fine-grained data from a knowledge-intensive organization (n = 3,690 employees) to examine our individual-level predictions. Study 2 tests the full model with multi-source data from 106 organizations (n = 15,342 employees). Across both studies, MTM is positively related to individual social capital and indirectly to individual performance, whereas FTM shows negative associations. Study 2 further shows that flexible team arrangements (i.e., firm-level structures based on MTM and FTM) are related positively to organizational social capital and indirectly to firm performance. Our findings contribute to research on teams in general and flexible team arrangements in particular, and hold important implications for social capital theory.

title: Back to the Beginning: Rediscovering a Beginner’s Mind Enhances Advice Provision to Novices
abstract: People often seek advice from those with more expertise. However, expertise can create a barrier to providing useful advice as it limits advisers’ ability to communicate concretely, yielding advice that may fall short of its potential value. In this paper, I examine how rediscovering a beginner’s mind—defined as a process of experiencing one’s former novice state of development in a focal domain—enables advisers to give more useful advice to novices. Because every adviser was once a novice, this former self can be a valuable resource when giving advice. Building on construal theory, I test whether rediscovering a beginner’s mind helps advisers communicate more concretely, generating advice that novices view as more useful and worthy of adoption. Across three main studies featuring managers and musicians, including one correlational study and two experiments (with 656 advisers and 571 advisees, generating 3,762 unique pairs), I find the predicted patterns and demonstrate how rediscovering a beginner’s mind operates beyond recalling past experiences or learning new skills more generally. I discuss how these findings contribute to our understanding of how advisers can be better equipped to provide developmental advice.

title: Beyond Statically Motivated, Rational, and Atomistic Actors: Extending Tabasi-Nejad and Deutsch’s “Effect of Policy Maker Motives on Their Response to Corporate Political Activity”
Countering Organizational Rigidity Through Operational Resource Bundling: Integrating Resource Orchestration and Dynamic Capabilities
abstract: As organizations mature, standardized systems help meet increasing needs for efficiency. However, this often results in resources being used in rigid ways, compromising the flexibility necessary to leverage opportunities, create value, and address customers’ emerging needs. Here we address solutions to this drift to rigidity, focusing on how operational managers bundle resources to create value for the firm. Our qualitative study is based on data collected from an organization with operations across 252 locations. This data consists of 92 interviews with strategic and operational managers, ethnographic observations, and archival records. We uncovered three pathways for resource bundling that are focused on markets, customers, or organizational renewal. In each, senior-level strategic managers initially provided resources, including channels for standardization, information systems, and technical infrastructure that became rigid in their usage. When operational managers sensed this drift to rigidity, they seized flexible resources (connection, solution development, and employee development processes) to combine with the rigid resources. We refer to this as Operational Resource Bundling (ORB). Strategic managers collaborated with the operational managers to adapt how resources were used, helping to ratify, endorse, and mobilize the bundles to achieve value creation and competitive advantage. We extend earlier work by specifying how a particular type of resource orchestration—ORB—constitutes a value-generating micro-mechanism of dynamic capabilities. ORB uncovers the role of operational managers in balancing standardization versus customization through identifying and combining resources.

title: How Followers Respond to Leader Differentiation: The Importance of Considering All Leader Differentiation Properties
abstract: A central tenet of many leadership theories is that leaders treat their followers differently. Although leader differentiation is ubiquitous, its effects on leaders and followers are not well understood and theory and research have not simultaneously considered its three key properties: Leader–member exchange (LMX) differentiation, LMX quality, and LMX social comparison. We developed a theoretical model in which these three properties interact to influence followers’ supervisory interactional justice perceptions and subsequently their supervisor-directed deviance and supervisor-directed organizational citizenship behaviors (OCBs). To test our model, we conducted a pre-registered experiment (Study 1), a single-level, multi-wave study (Study 2), and a multilevel, multi-wave, multisource study (Study 3). Results consistently supported our theoretical model. First, LMX differentiation indirectly influenced supervisor-directed deviance and OCBs via supervisory interactional justice. Second, the three leader differentiation properties interacted to predict supervisory interactional justice. Specifically, when LMX quality and LMX social comparison were both high, the negative impact of LMX differentiation on followers’ supervisory interactional justice perceptions was the weakest and did not reliably differ from zero. Third, when LMX quality and LMX social comparison were both high, LMX differentiation’s positive indirect effect on supervisor-directed deviance, and its negative indirect effect on supervisor-directed OCBs, via supervisory interactional justice perceptions, were the weakest and not reliably different from zero. These are among the first studies to simultaneously theorize and investigate the interactive effects of the three central properties of leader differentiation, and to demonstrate its effects for both followers and leaders.

title: Transgenerational Intentions and the Emergence of Family Firms: Evidence from China’s One-Child Policy Reform
abstract: Are family firms born or made? We argue that firms become family-oriented as transgenerational intentions gain salience and reshape owners’ mindsets. Leveraging China’s one-child policy reform as an exogenous shock to within-family succession feasibility, we conduct a difference-in-differences analysis of 2,837 listed firms. We find that, relative to nonfamily firms, firms for which family succession is feasible increase R&D intensity following the reform, with the effect driven primarily by lone-founder firms. Our findings identify conditions under which founder-led firms transition toward family-oriented behavior, providing new insight into the “ made ” side of the born-or-made debate in family business research.

title: Trust in the Gray: A Qualitative Study of Trust and Repair in Gray Markets
abstract: Although trust is critical for entrepreneurs in all markets, it likely differs in gray markets from that in white or black markets. In this inductive study, we find a coherent configuration of trust mechanisms in a gray market that offers new insights into how entrepreneurs can use their network (i.e., referrals and “lineaging”) and heuristics (i.e., “villageing”) to build trust in new stakeholders when trust formation is challenging and violations are costly. We also offer new insights into the practices for verifying (i.e., impromptu tests and extensive probationary periods) and maintaining (i.e., financial support) trustworthiness, as well as repairing trust.

title: Whom You Pay Matters: How the Payment Path of Shared Expenses Affects Purchase Satisfaction
abstract: Abstract This research investigates how the method of paying a shared expense affects purchase satisfaction. When multiple consumers share an expense (e.g., a meal, Uber ride, or vacation), each consumer can pay their own share directly, or one consumer can pay the total and others can repay them. Eight preregistered studies showed that indirect payment through another consumer led to higher purchase satisfaction versus direct payment to the vendor. This effect emerged regardless of the existing relationship (friend, acquaintance, or disliked person), or whether the consumers spent different amounts. Mediation evidence showed that indirect payment increased purchase satisfaction by providing relief from resolving indebtedness. Moderation evidence further supported our proposed process as this effect disappeared when either a financial obligation was made salient, or the focal consumer initially paid the total. This research highlights the distinction between direct and indirect payment paths in shared expenses, contributing a new construct to the consumer finance area. It also has implications for consumers who should realize the effects of shared expenses on their decision satisfaction and budgeting, and marketers who could encourage shared payments to increase satisfaction at little cost.

title: Media Sentiment on Foreign Countries and International Asset Allocation
abstract: We examine whether U.S. media sentiment on foreign countries influences domestic investors’ international asset allocation. Using flows to country-specific mutual funds as a proxy for investor demand, we find that negative media sentiment, measured by the interaction of negative tone and media attention given to foreign countries, is strongly associated with reduced investor flows into funds targeting those countries. This relationship is driven, at least in part, by media sentiment that is unrelated to the economic fundamentals of the targeted countries. We employ The Wall Street Journal’s acquisition by News Corp to support the causal interpretation of our findings. Our results highlight the perception-shaping role of media narratives in driving global investment decisions. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: L. Ma acknowledges funding support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72103008]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05504 .

title: A Nonparametric Framework for Online Stochastic Matching with Correlated Arrivals
abstract: The design of online algorithms for matching markets and revenue management settings is usually bound by the assumption that the demand process is formed by a fixed-length sequence of queries with unknown types, each drawn independently. This notion of serial independence implies that the demand of each type, that is, the number of queries of a given type, has low variance and is approximately Poisson distributed. This paper proposes a nonparametric framework for modeling arrival sequences in online stochastic matching that departs from the serial independent assumption. We propose two models, Indep and Correl, that capture different forms of serial correlations by combining a nonparametric distribution for the demand with standard assumptions on the arrival patterns: adversarial or random order. The Indep model can capture arbitrary serial correlations within each customer type but assumes cross-sectional independence across types, whereas the Correl model captures common shocks across customer types. We demonstrate that fluid relaxations, which rely solely on demand expectations, have arbitrarily bad performance guarantees. In contrast, we develop new algorithms that achieve optimal (constant factor) performance guarantees in each model. Our mathematical analysis includes tighter linear programming (LP) relaxations that leverage distribution knowledge and a new lossless randomized LP rounding scheme for Indep. We test our new LP relaxations and rounding scheme in simulations on real and synthetic data and find that they consistently outperform well-established matching algorithms, especially on real data sequences that exhibit greater demand variance. This paper was accepted by Itai Ashlagi, revenue management and market analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05424 .

title: An Analysis of Heritability in Preferences Using Behavioral Models of Decision Making
abstract: We investigate the heritability of risk, uncertainty, and time preferences using a large-scale field experiment with adult twins, complemented by a comprehensive meta-analysis of prior studies. Our research introduces a novel empirical approach that integrates behavioral genetics with structural econometrics, enabling us to directly quantify the heritability of latent preference parameters in behavioral models of decision making, without relying on observed proxies. Our incentive-compatible experiment is the first to simultaneously elicit all three types of preferences within the same individuals in a twin study. Our findings reveal a stronger genetic influence on risk and uncertainty preferences than previously reported. We demonstrate that conventional proxy measures for preferences and simplified structural models tend to overstate the influence of unique environmental factors. These results help contextualize preference heterogeneity as a driver of persistent differences in decision making across individuals, leaders, and organizations. This paper was accepted by Aurélien Baillon, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: Support from the University of Technology Sydney and from the Australian Government through the Australian Research Council’s Centre of Excellence for Children and Families over the Life Course [Project IDs CE140100027 and CE200100025] is gratefully acknowledged. This research was facilitated through access to Twins Research Australia, a national resource supported by the National Health & Medical Research Council since 1981, administered by the University of Melbourne. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00669 .

title: Entrepreneurial Teams: Prior Industry Experience and Early-Stage Growth
abstract: We use career backgrounds of initial employees from a full cohort of U.S. startups to measure founding teams’ skillsets. Startups with more diverse prior industry experience grow faster than same-industry local peers. One-standard-deviation-higher diversity is associated with 16% (10%) higher five-year employment (sales) growth, controlling for demographic diversity, prestartup wages, and other observables. Startups in innovative industries and facing lower coordination costs among team members drive the results. To address endogeneity, we exploit shocks in which teams suddenly lose members with unduplicated skills. Overall, combining individual specialization with team-level diversification allows teams to act as “jacks of all trades and masters of each.” This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: This research uses data from the Census Bureau’s Longitudinal Employer Household Dynamics Program, which was partially supported by the National Science Foundation [Grants SES-9978093, SES-0339191 and ITR-0427889], the National Institute on Aging [Grant AG018854], and grants from the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation. Supplemental Material: The internet appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.00773 .

title: Can Task Motivation Backfire? The Roles of Perceived Task Interdependence and Interaction Avoidance
abstract: The extant literature on task motivation has generally demonstrated its beneficial effects on workplace outcomes. Although some evidence has raised concerns about the potential link between task motivation and maladaptive behaviors, this line of work has been grounded in an intrapersonal perspective that focuses on employees’ internal regulation. Guided by motivated information processing theory, we adopt an interpersonal perspective to examine how task motivation may, under certain conditions, lead to interaction avoidance, a maladaptive workplace behavior with downstream implications for job performance. We theorize that, when perceiving a lower level of task interdependence, employees with higher task motivation are more likely to engage in interaction avoidance. This avoidance, in turn, is negatively related to job performance. Across an online experiment with a U.S. sample, a field experiment with a Chinese sample, and a survey with a Chinese sample, our hypotheses are supported. This research builds a more balanced understanding of how task motivation influences employee behavior and performance. In practice, managers should actively channel the effort of highly task-motivated employees to ensure their motivation translates into effectiveness rather than counterproductive avoidance.

title: Dominant Deceptions: How Future-Oriented Narratives Transform into Deception
abstract: Drawing on a multi-year, qualitative study of a promising venture in a nascent industry, we develop a process model tracing how future-oriented narratives can transform into deception. In the venture we studied, the founder’s future-oriented narratives were initially viewed as evidence of his visionary foresight. As these narratives traveled downward through the organization, employees responsible for operations translated the founder’s broad vision into specific targets and metrics. Some details described an attainable future; others reached so far beyond the attainable that they became liminal, occupying a grey zone between right and wrong. Over time, growing internal and external demands for tangible progress created an expectations-reality gap, prompting employees to engage in temporal reorientation, shifting statements from “we will” to “we have.” Their statements crossed from liminal to deceptive, now asserting as fact something that did not exist. Once formalized in presentations, websites, and other artefacts, the claims became dominant deceptions: codified, specific, past- or present-tense deceptions deliberately reproduced across the organization. In this codified form, the deceptions became misconduct that, if detected, could have been acted on by social control agents. We propose that three enabling conditions sustained this transformation: visionary attribution (belief in the founder’s unique foresight), interpretive flexibility (the ambiguity of new technologies that allows multiple plausible meanings), and moral justification (the framing of deception as serving a higher mission). Because the process unfolded diffusely and incrementally, the transformation could only be observed retrospectively, in the accumulation of actions across individuals, artefacts, and time. By tracing this process, we extend research in narratives and in organizational misconduct.

title: Social Performance Feedback and Managerial Moral Self-Regulation: The Microfoundations of Corporate Social (Ir)Responsibility
abstract: Despite growing interest in the microfoundations of corporate social activities, prior research has not articulated the full chain connecting firm-level conditions to managers' psychological processes (a topdown pathway) and back to firm-level corporate social behavior (a bottom-up pathway), leaving existing microfoundational accounts incomplete. Drawing on the behavioral theory of the firm (BTOF) and moral self-regulation theory, we develop a cross-level moral feedback model that integrates both pathways by linking firm-level social performance feedback, individual-level managerial cognition, and firm-level corporate social responsibility (CSR) and corporate social irresponsibility (CSI). We argue that social performance feedback activates managers' moral self-regulation. When a firm falls below its social performance aspiration, its managers perceive a diminished firm image, which undermines their moral self-image and triggers moral cleansing behaviors-manifested as increased CSR and/or reduced CSI. Conversely, when a firm exceeds its social performance aspiration, its managers perceive an enhanced firm image, which elevates their moral self-image and activates moral licensing behaviors-manifested as reduced CSR and/or increased CSI. Study 1, using archival data, examines the main effects of firms' social performance feedback on CSR and CSI. Study 2 uses a series of experiments to examine the proposed micro-level mechanisms, demonstrating how managers' perceived firm image and moral selfimage sequentially mediate the effects of social performance feedback on CSR and CSI. These studies provide complementary evidence for our multilevel behavioral model. Our study contributes to research on the microfoundations of corporate social activities, behavioral strategy, and moral self-regulation.

title: Survival of the Flattest: Teams with Low (But Not High) Status Differentiation Turn Failure into Success by Adding High-Status Members
abstract: Most prior research on teams’ responses to failure treats teams as closed systems. However, after failures, teams may seek to improve performance by bringing in new members. Adopting a teams-as-open-systems perspective, we test which teams are more willing to add high-status members following failures and whether doing so improves team performance. Drawing on status hierarchy research, we posit that after a team failure, members will feel uncertain about their own status (particularly those with high status). More importantly, we predict that the impact of this status uncertainty on members’ willingness to add high-status new members depends on teams’ pre-existing status differentiation. Specifically, status uncertainty leads members in low-status-differentiation teams to perceive adding a high-status new member as a potential benefit to collective performance, whereas it leads members in high-status-differentiation teams to perceive the addition as a potential threat to their own status. We theorize that these individual perceptions shape teams’ collective decisions through an emergent process. Taken together, we predict that, at the team level, failure will increase the willingness to add high-status members in teams with low, but not high, status differentiation, and such addition improves subsequent team performance. Using longitudinal archival data on product development teams (Study 1, N = 4,811 teams) and two pre-registered experiments at the individual (Study 2, N = 783 participants) and team levels (Study 3, N = 222 teams), we found support for these predictions. This research advances the literature on team failure and illuminates dynamics between membership change and social hierarchy.

title: Diversity and/or Inclusion? Evidence from Disability Quota and Inclusion Laws in Brazil
Repatterning Interactions in Remote Work Environments: Bolstering Psychological Safety Through Mutually Humanizing Self-Disclosure
abstract: Existing research on psychological safety suggests that remote work might make it more challenging for workers to engage in the sorts of interactions that promote psychological safety. This raises the question: How is psychological safety bolstered when groups work remotely? Drawing on data from a 7-year longitudinal qualitative study—including 275 interviews and approximately 330 hours of observations—of a professional services organization that shifted from an in-person to a remote work environment, I present a process model of how psychological safety can be strengthened among workers interacting virtually. I find that remote work supports interactional patterns that facilitate self-disclosure among group members. Learning more about one another, workers become mutually humanized, and psychological safety is bolstered. This psychological safety is accompanied by a set of associated practices that help people coordinate on work tasks while also sustaining flexibility in where and when they work. Reflecting improved psychological safety and associated practices, group members attend to and accomplish both work tasks and nonwork activities. This study contributes to the psychological safety literature by identifying a distinct process through which psychological safety can be promoted in remote work environments: mutual humanization via self-disclosure, which is supported through interactional patterns facilitated by remote work. Importantly, this distinct group-initiated process expands theorization beyond its current focus on leader-initiated social learning. This study also identifies how psychological safety supports role management, integrating theories of psychological safety and work-nonwork roles to expand understanding of psychological safety’s positive consequences.

title: The information content of private information acquisition: evidence from FOIA requests to the SEC
abstract: Abstract This study examines whether Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests to the Securities and Exchange Commission convey value-relevant information about publicly traded firms and whether sophisticated investors trade on that information. Our empirical analysis reveals heterogeneous value relevance associated with different types of requests. Specifically, requests submitted by proxy agents to probe for ongoing investigations as well as anonymous requests are negatively correlated with future returns, while requests from institutional investors and intellectual property entities are associated with positive future returns. Our results also support the direct-trading hypothesis, showing institutional investors and short sellers trade on FOIA-obtained information. Our findings add to the information-acquisition literature by highlighting the heterogeneous value signals in FOIA requests, particularly the negative value signals.

title: Firm Investments in Employee‐Led Entrepreneurial Ventures
abstract: ABSTRACT Firms increasingly support employee‐led startups by providing funding in exchange for equity. These investments create a dual role for employees, who pursue their entrepreneurial ventures as shared residual claimants while continuing to work on core tasks under incomplete fixed‐pay contracts. Although the investments align incentives within the startup, their effects on employees' effort in their core roles remain unclear. Using an experimental economics approach, I examine how a firm's investment decision affects employees' effort on core tasks. To isolate what is unique about equity investments, I use a non‐equity gift of equal monetary value as the baseline. The results show that employees reduce effort more when the firm denies a non‐equity gift than when it denies an equity investment. This difference arises because employees view a denied equity investment as the firm's business judgment based on risk and expected return, rather than as a failure to act generously. When funding in either form is provided, employees reciprocate positively, resulting in similarly high effort. Overall, the findings suggest that equity‐based entrepreneurship programs can help motivate effort on both startups and core tasks while mitigating the harm of rejecting employees' proposals.

title: Media Review: What is Justice when All is Water?
abstract: Philippopoulos-Mihalopoulos' book, Hydrojustice is a dense immersion into the watery world of post-Anthropocene, post-2.0˚C warming; a world where water is no longer something humans' control, harness, surf, or build stable empires on, but something which engulfs much of what we take for granted today.The book allows us a glimpse into a world where comforts of today are history, visible only though an opaque watery pool vividly reminiscent of injustices endured.As organization scholars, we read the book in search of understanding the relationship between humans and water to shed light on challenges to upgrade current practices of organizing and managing life; and this takes us to thoughts about ways we rely on water(s) today.Not only is water a life-sustaining force organic beings need to stay alive, we humans also use water to help us flush away unwanted excrement, including faeces and urine, dirt in our clothes, as well as diverse industrial effluents from the dense city centres.

title: Review of Invisible Barriers: Understanding and Overcoming Discrimination in the Workplace
Breaking the Silenced Legitimacy: Multi‐source Environmental Legitimacy Evaluations and Firm Green Innovation
abstract: Abstract This study explores how multi‐source environmental legitimacy evaluations influence corporate green innovation. Building on the multilevel theory of the legitimacy process, we argue that multi‐source legitimacy evaluations—encompassing evaluations from environmental organizations, industry associations, banks and other stakeholders—enhance the validity of environmental legitimacy evaluations and encourage more substantive environmental practices, that is, green innovation. Using longitudinal panel data from Chinese listed firms from 2014 to 2021, this study uses the Corporate Information Transparency Index project in China as a carrier for multi‐source environmental evaluations to examine its impact on green innovation. Our empirical results show that such evaluations significantly promote corporate green innovation. This positive effect is stronger for firms with greater media coverage and for those operating in regions with more developed institutional intermediaries.

title: Linguistic Markers of Destructive Leadership: An Exploratory Cross‐domain Study
abstract: Abstract This article examines how destructive leadership in politics and business is reflected in distinctive patterns of language use. Drawing on Pennebaker's psycholinguistic theory and his Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) analytical framework, we report two studies. Study 1 (politics) compares campaign speeches by an acknowledged destructive leader (Donald Trump) and a non‐destructive leader (Kamala Harris) during the 2024 US presidential election campaign. Study 2 extends the analysis to business leadership in the medical technology sector by comparing speeches by an acknowledged destructive leader (Elizabeth Holmes, Theranos) and a non‐destructive leader (Omar Ishrak, Medtronic). Consistent linguistic markers across both studies were pronoun usage and negative emotional tone: destructive leaders displayed more self‐reference (‘I‐talk’) than collective reference (‘We‐talk’) and greater third‐person plural reference (‘They‐talk’) relative to other personal pronouns, along with a more negatively valenced emotional tone. By contrast, clout, analytical thinking and surface‐form indicators of linguistic simplicity were less consistent, while authenticity appeared context dependent. These findings contribute to destructive leadership theory and suggest that ‘at‐a‐distance’ linguistic analysis which entails the systematic examination of leaders’ natural language use without direct access or interaction has practical value for diagnosing destructive leadership in hard‐to‐reach populations and may also have a role to play in intervening to prevent harmful outcomes taking hold.

title: Principal Workers: Orchestrating AI Agents Improves Productivity
abstract: For the artificial intelligence (AI) economy, we propose a principal worker model where each knowledge worker is both a task architect and an AI agent orchestrator. As task architect, the worker divides each task into subtasks and delegates some to AI agents. As agent orchestrator, the worker optimizes outputs from AI agents and synthesizes all outputs into a coherent deliverable. Workers who augment themselves with AI agents produce more and earn more. To reap productivity gains, organizations must implement policy changes on how they develop workers and incentivize them to use AI effectively.

title: Compliance Without Transformation: A Systematic Review of Means‐Ends Decoupling in EPR and Implications for UK Packaging Reform
abstract: ABSTRACT Extended producer responsibility (EPR) has been widely adopted across European circular economy governance yet three decades of implementation reveal a persistent and underexplained gap between formal compliance and upstream environmental outcomes. This systematic review of 45 studies spanning packaging and Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment schemes asks why producers comply with EPR obligations without undertaking substantive ecodesign change. Applying means‐ends decoupling theory to mandatory regulatory contexts, the review identifies the following three interacting mechanism layers: behavioural mechanisms including cost pass‐through, satisficing and status quo bias; organisational mechanisms including principal‐agent fragmentation and collective cost averaging; and structural opacity conditions that prevent effective monitoring and correction. Together these mechanisms produce compliance without transformation as a stable organisational equilibrium rather than an isolated implementation failure. The review extends decoupling theory beyond voluntary sustainability standards into binding regulatory regimes and generates practical implications for UK packaging EPR, showing that fee modulation alone is insufficient and must be reinforced by complementary measures targeting transparency, organisational capability and supply chain incentives.

title: Circular Economy Readiness and Maturity: What Are We Poking and Prodding?
abstract: ABSTRACT As interest in transitioning to a circular economy ( CE ) is growing, CE readiness and maturity are becoming key topics. CE readiness reflects the preconditions to adopt CE practices, while CE maturity indicates the level of advancement in their implementation. Therefore, identifying, examining, and assessing the elements that shape CE readiness and maturity is essential to move toward a CE . This study leverages a systematic literature review to provide a critical overview of how CE readiness and CE maturity are assessed. In particular, the article first clarifies the difference between CE readiness and maturity, noting that these concepts are often used interchangeably despite their distinct meanings. Second, it critically summarizes approaches, frameworks, and tools for assessing CE readiness and maturity. Last, leveraging a thematic analysis, this study categorizes the 1003 items measuring CE readiness and maturity in 12 dimensions: organizational governance, human capital, product and business model innovation, technology and data, financing and economics, interorganizational relationships, production and distribution, product use, end‐of‐life, market and power dynamics, social indicators, and government policy and regulations. The 12 dimensions are grouped into three analytical clusters: firm‐level capabilities and organizational conditions, inter‐firm and value‐chain dynamics, and institutional and contextual conditions. The study links these clusters to different theoretical perspectives, arguing that no single theory sufficiently explains CE readiness and maturity and that a systems perspective is needed to integrate these complementary viewpoints. The study paves the way for more rigorous and epistemologically valid tools and highlights relevant gaps in the literature.

title: Managers' Values and the Adoption of Environmentally Sustainable Practices Among Small and Medium‐Sized Enterprises: A Configurational Approach
abstract: ABSTRACT Small and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs) play a critical role in sustainability transitions, yet the mechanisms through which managers' values shape environmentally sustainable practices (ESP) remain insufficiently understood. Existing research often treats managerial values as independent predictors and pays limited attention to their interaction with organizational and contextual conditions. Drawing on values theory, paradox theory, institutional theory, and a configurational perspective, this study examines how combinations of managerial values, organizational capabilities, and organizational field conditions influence the adoption of ESP among SMEs. Using data from 409 Canadian SMEs and Qualitative Comparative Analysis (QCA), the study investigates the interplay between self‐transcendence values (STV), self‐enhancement values (SEV), entrepreneurial orientation, firm size, network participation, sector membership, and export activity. The findings identify four configurations associated with the adoption of ESP and four configurations linked to their absence, highlighting both equifinality and causal asymmetry. While STV frequently support environmental engagement, they are not necessary across all sustainability pathways. Likewise, SEV appear in both sustainability and non‐sustainability configurations, indicating that their influence depends on broader organizational and contextual conditions. Notably, one sustainability pathway combines STV and SEV, suggesting that environmental responsibility and performance‐oriented aspirations can be mutually reinforcing rather than contradictory. By uncovering multiple pathways to environmental sustainability, the study advances configurational understandings of SME sustainability and offers implications for managers and policymakers.

Can digital twins redefine destination management? A socio-technical framework from a machine learning driven systematic review
abstract: Purpose This study aims to systematically map and synthesise the fragmented knowledge on digital twins (DTs) within tourism destination management. It also highlights how DTs can transform destination governance, sustainability practices, crisis management and visitor engagement through real-time simulation and data-driven insights. Design/methodology/approach Following the PRISMA protocol, peer-reviewed studies were systematically collected from three databases (Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect) and analysed using BERTopic, a BERT-based machine learning algorithm for topic modelling. This machine learning based computational literature review approach enabled the identification of hidden thematic patterns across interdisciplinary sources. Findings The analysis revealed four dominant themes: digital transformation and heritage management, crisis management and adaptive resilience, data-driven visitor engagement and sentiment analysis and immersive futures with the metaverse. These themes were synthesised into a novel socio-technical maturity framework that positions DT adoption along two continua: technical complexity (static representation to dynamic simulation) and social integration (centralised control to collaborative governance), thus revealing four developmental levels and their inherent tensions: ownership versus access, automation versus human judgment, personalisation versus surveillance and virtual versus authentic. Practical implications The framework provides DMOs and policymakers with a diagnostic tool to assess their DT maturity, anticipate socio-technical challenges at each level, and strategically guide digital transformation, crisis resilience and visitor engagement. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study pioneers machine learning-driven topic modelling in tourism DT research, offering the first socio-technical framework that conceptualises DTs not merely as technological artefacts but as socio-technical systems, reframing destination management from reactive administration to predictive governance, from physical places to phygital ecosystems and from technology adoption to socio-technical orchestration.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: How could corporate social responsibility alleviate social occupational stigma consciousness?
abstract: Purpose Although social occupational stigma consciousness reduces individuals’ well-being and work outcomes, research on strategies to mitigate social occupational stigma consciousness remains limited. Based on social identity theory, this study aims to systematically examine the mechanisms through which corporate social responsibility (CSR) influences hotel employees’ social occupational stigma consciousness. Design/methodology/approach Study 1 conducted a content analysis of hotel employee reviews posted on Glassdoor. Study 2 collected data from 372 hotel employees via the online survey platform Credamo. Study 3 extended the investigation by surveying 295 Chinese hotel employees to evaluate the proposed model in greater detail. Findings Social dirtiness was identified as the most prevalent form of occupational taint, highlighting the significance of social occupational stigma consciousness among hotel employees. CSR was found to reduce social occupational stigma consciousness mainly by increasing employees’ perceived respect, rather than by enhancing organizational identification. Moreover, responsible leadership moderated the relationship between perceived respect and social occupational stigma consciousness. Research limitations/implications Because this study relied on cross-sectional data, it could not fully identify or examine the dynamic causal relationships among the variables. Moreover, the model included only the social dimension of occupational stigma consciousness. Although Study 1 drew on online reviews from a broad range of sources, additional empirical samples from a wider range of hotels and geographic regions would further enhance the generalizability of the findings. Practical implications Hotel employees constitute an important occupational group for examining occupational stigma consciousness, which may undermine both employee well-being and job performance. By highlighting the role of organizational-level initiatives, particularly CSR, this study provides managers with practical strategies to help reduce employees’ occupational stigma consciousness. Originality/value The findings enrich the literature on occupational stigma and offer evidence-based strategies for hotel management to improve employee morale, motivation and engagement.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Novel net zero policy for small and medium sized enterprises: Introducing relationship-to-carbon and policy congregations
abstract: We are failing to make sufficient progress to reduce carbon emissions by business. The progress of small and medium sized enterprises (SMEs) to reach net zero is particularly slow, despite them being responsible for half of non-household emissions; as such, climate change policy is failing to reach most SMEs. We present a new typology based on relationship-to-carbon, which overcomes the challenge of SME heterogeneity to enable meaningful engagement with carbon reduction. Building on this, we conceptualise a novel approach to climate policy beyond metaphorical carrots, sticks and sermons , to add congregations , a relational approach to policy. We argue that firms entrained in the carbon economy (rather than intrinsic or extrinsic ) can be engaged in carbon reduction through collaborative, dialogic and relational instruments drawn from feminist policy. We use the example of the UK construction sector to illustrate how the conceptual typology, and the extension of policy approaches, might operate in practice.
journal_name: International Small Business Journal: Researching Entrepreneurship

title: How Firms Combine Sustainability-Oriented Partnerships to Improve Environmental, Social, and Governance Performance: A Qualitative Comparative Analysis Study
abstract: A partnership portfolio for sustainability (PPS) is the set of partnerships a firm uses to pursue sustainability goals. Although sustainability-oriented partnerships can improve environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance, we know less about how a firm’s full partnership portfolio shapes these outcomes. Drawing on modern portfolio theory and alliance portfolio research, we examine how PPS configurations influence ESG performance. Using qualitative comparative analysis of 979 sustainability partnerships across 35 global fashion firms, we identify multiple pathways to high ESG performance. Firms achieve strong ESG outcomes through either large, issue-diverse portfolios or smaller, focused portfolios that combine geographical reach with interventions across multiple levels of change. Neither portfolio size nor partner diversity is universally beneficial; rather, ESG performance depends on configurational fit among portfolio characteristics. These findings challenge assumptions that more partnerships or greater diversity automatically improve ESG outcomes and advance a portfolio perspective of sustainability-oriented partnerships.

title: Not just invited to the party, but also asked to dance: how inclusive work practices foster organizational commitment over time
abstract: Building on optimal distinctiveness theory and workplace inclusion literature, the present two-year prospective study investigated whether, why, and for whom inclusive work practices can enhance employees’ affective organizational commitment. Specifically, we hypothesized that inclusive leadership and opportunity-enhancing human resources practices (OHRP) help individuals to experience meaningfulness, and, directly and indirectly, foster affective commitment. Additionally, we hypothesized that the relationship between inclusive leadership and OHRP, on the one hand, and meaningfulness, on the other hand, is more pronounced for proactive individuals. To empirically test our research model, we collected data in two waves, with a two-year temporal gap, from a representative sample of 251 Dutch employees. The results of path analyses indicated that both inclusive leadership and OHRP were positively related to meaningfulness. The link between inclusive leadership and meaningfulness was significantly positive for individuals who scored average or high on proactive personality, yet it was non-significant for less proactive individuals. Additionally, both inclusive leadership and OHRP contributed to long-term affective commitment through meaningfulness. We show how and for whom inclusive work practices foster meaningfulness and long-term affective commitment, thereby both integrating and challenging existing assumptions in the inclusion literature.

title: Who, how, and where: navigating towards a micro-foundations perspective on university technology transfer ecosystems

The Effect of Peer Firm Restructuring on Corporate Investment Decisions
abstract: This study examines whether companies’ investment decisions are influenced by their industry peers’ restructuring activities. We expect that peer firm restructuring leads to a reduction in a company’s investment levels through two economic channels: (1) signaling deteriorating industry conditions during negative shocks, and (2) signaling efficiency-enhancing restructuring that increases competitive pressure during positive shocks. Consistent with our expectations, we find that same-industry peer firms’ restructuring is negatively associated with a company’s capital expenditures, after controlling for industry sales growth and other industry-level attributes. Our results hold both in industries experiencing negative shocks and in industries experiencing positive shocks. Additional analyses show that in highly competitive, growing industries, the negative effect of peer restructuring on investment is driven by restructuring peers whose efficiency improves post-restructuring. This effect is also stronger in capital-intensive and high-volatility industries, where firms face higher adjustment costs and greater uncertainty. Consistent with our investment findings, stock option-based evidence shows that firms facing high levels of peer restructuring exhibit significantly greater implied volatility skewness, a market-based measure of downside risk. Taken together, our findings highlight the informational value of peer firms’ restructuring activities in corporate investment decisions, offering insights into how firms adapt resource allocation strategies in dynamic economic environments.

Backcasting: An innovative approach to conflict management for transformative innovation projects
abstract: Environmental issues and sustainability transition are nowadays among the most contentious arenas, as they entail complexity, uncertainty and a multiplicity of different interests and visions. Transformative innovation projects, that attempt to address the key challenges that our society is currently facing, have increased rapidly over the last decade as a solution to wicked problems, including sustainability. Yet, the development of these projects does not occur without difficulties. Transitioning to a more sustainable system is a significantly controversial and conflictual issue, as different actors have diverse perspectives on what sustainability means and how to achieve it. Studies on how to manage conflict in innovative and transformative contexts are scarce and methodologically limited. This paper conceptualises participatory backcasting as a conflict management approach for transformative innovation projects and investigates the key mechanisms through which backcasting supports the management of stakeholder conflicts. The article draws on an intervention research aiming at co-experimenting participatory backcasting with 24 transformative innovation projects engaged in fostering agroecological transition in France. This approach engages project participants in a collective visioning exercise to define the desired future to which the project aims to contribute. The case studies show how backcasting can contribute to 1. underlying conflicts to emerge in a constructive setting, 2. to overcome the stall caused by conflicts in project management, and 3. to create a collaborative plan to reach the desired transformations. This process underlines the value of letting conflict emerge in order to foster a better problematisation and a more cohesive participation. Yet, to achieve such result, backcasting should be supported by a critical approach to facilitation in order to address power asymmetries.

title: Should production experience or enjoyment experience be used? The impact of virtual influencers’ persuasion strategy on purchase intention
abstract: Purpose Although virtual influencers (VIs) have emerged as a critical tool for brand promotion, the differential effects of two persuasive strategies, production experience and enjoyment experience, on consumers’ purchase intentions remain underexplored. By integrating signaling theory with mind perception theory, this study aims to address this gap, examining how and when VI persuasive strategy influence purchase intentions through the lens of sender–signal congruence. Design/methodology/approach Three experiments were conducted to investigate the impact of VI persuasive strategy (production experience vs enjoyment experience) on purchase intentions. Furthermore, the mediating roles of perceived quality and authenticity were examined, alongside the moderating effects of platform type (utilitarian vs hedonic) and controller type (artificial intelligence [AI] vs human). Findings The production experience strategy was found to significantly enhance purchase intentions compared to the enjoyment experience strategy, a relationship mediated by perceived quality and authenticity. In addition, platform type was identified as a significant moderator: the production experience strategy proved more effective on utilitarian platforms, whereas the enjoyment experience strategy was better suited for hedonic platforms. Controller type was also found to moderate these effects. Specifically, for AI-controlled VIs, the production experience strategy elicited higher purchase intentions, whereas for human-controlled VIs, the differential effectiveness between the two strategies was mitigated. Research limitations/implications By systematically comparing these two persuasive strategies, the current literature on VI marketing is advanced. Moreover, by unpacking the dual-mediation pathways, this study successfully integrates mind perception theory with signaling theory, thereby profoundly expanding the theoretical and application boundaries of both frameworks within AI marketing contexts. Practical implications Actionable guidance is provided for brands seeking to optimize the linguistic design of VIs. Specifically, the latent potential of the production experience strategy is highlighted, and practical recommendations are offered for aligning persuasive strategies with specific platform types and VI controller configurations. Originality/value Novel theoretical insights are contributed by conceptualizing sender–signal congruence as a fundamental prerequisite for signal effectiveness in AI communication. Consequently, the underlying pathways and boundary conditions governing VI persuasion are comprehensively clarified.

title: Sponsorship outcomes in sports rivalries: the moderating role of gender and team identification
abstract: Purpose While previous research predominantly portrayed sporting rivalry as a threat to sport sponsorship outcomes, this study aims to examine its potential benefits and the impact of gender on sponsorship outcomes in a sporting rivalry research context. Design/methodology/approach The study combines social identity theory and sponsorship research to explore (rival) sport consumers’ responses to a sponsorship leveraging strategy involving sporting rivalry in two experiments (Study 1 n = 406, Study 2 n = 327), depending on their gender and level of team identification. Findings The data revealed that female sports consumers with medium to strong team identification tend to respond positively to the rivalry reference of the team sponsor, while the opposite is true when the sponsor of the rival team references the rivalry in its sponsorship leveraging, and vice versa for male sport consumers. Leveraging sponsorships with a rivalry reference created ambivalent sponsorship outcomes among sports consumers, depending on gender and the level of team identification. Consequently, rivalry marketing contexts must be considered as a double-edged sword with ambivalent consequences on consumers’ behavior. Research limitations/implications This research focused on one sponsorship case and one country, and data were gathered in a region where the rivalry between two cities does not affect only sporting spheres. Practical implications Before integrating sporting rivalry into sponsorship-leveraging measures, sponsors should carefully consider potential negative responses from some sports consumer groups. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first study to consider both rival sport consumer groups and to focus on the impact of gender on sports consumers’ responses to leveraging sponsorship with rivalry references. It advances the literature regarding the effects of rival sponsorship as an identity threat to the rival team’s sponsor and supporters and considers how this affects sponsorship outcomes, further providing valuable knowledge about gender dynamics in a competitive marketing or rivalry research context.

title: Performative narratives and destination image in cross-cultural tourism livestreaming
The Process Model of Anxiety: A Framework and Review of Anxiety in the Workplace
abstract: Anxiety is an extremely common and consequential affective experience in organizational life, yet workplace anxiety research remains fragmented across theories, methods, and domains. In this review, we argue that anxiety is best understood not as a static or uniformly maladaptive state but as a dynamic process with identifiable stages. To organize research on workplace anxiety, we introduce the process model of anxiety (PMA), which specifies appraisal, activation, processing, fatigue, and behavior stages, while emphasizing feedback, regulation, recovery, and the role of contextual factors in modulating the process. We integrate research from organizational psychology, affective science, stress, cognition, and health to explain when anxiety undermines performance, well-being, and relationships, and when it may support vigilance, preparation, safety, or compensatory action. We conclude by identifying future directions for dynamic, multilevel, and intervention-oriented research on anxiety in organizations.

title: Global market integration, national security salience, and new product development alliances in aircraft manufacturing
What Jobs Do Workers Want? Worker Preferences in Global Value Chains
abstract: ABSTRACT What do workers in global value chains (GVCs) consider a good job? Research on work in GVCs largely studies compliance with standards set from the top‐down rather than worker preferences. Understanding worker preferences is crucial because workers are the intended beneficiaries of governance institutions; policies better aligned to their preferences could enjoy greater legitimacy and effectiveness. To explore what GVC workers want, we embedded an experiment in an original survey of 2500 workers in 50 formal Moroccan apparel factories integrated into GVCs. These workers highly valued jobs with characteristics that reduced their exposure to physical risks and provided job stability. They also had strong preferences for jobs with supervisors that treated workers respectfully. By contrast, worker preferences for wage increases available in the Moroccan context were weak, especially when compared with non‐wage features. Our results suggests that when wages are compressed and extended working hours is the main way to increase earnings, preferences for non‐wage attributes may dominate. We also find more similarities than differences between men and women workers; although women place greater value on respectful supervision, safety and childcare benefits, their overall preferences closely track those of men. These findings provide novel evidence to inform efforts to improve jobs in GVCs.

title: Diagnosing Institutional Design‐Implementation Gaps: A Dual‐Layer Systems Modeling Language Protocol for Visualizing Institutional Change Mechanisms
Towards inclusive prosperity: comparative analysis of Indigenous procurement policies in Canada, Australia, and New Zealand
abstract: Indigenous procurement is widely promoted as an instrument of economic reconciliation, yet headline gains often mask limited transformational impact. Applying McCrudden’s social procurement framework, we conduct a systematic cross-national comparison of identity-specific procurement architectures across Canada, Australia, and Aotearoa New Zealand. We show that contract values cluster heavily within major metropolitan hubs and narrow industry sectors, leaving remote and early-stage community enterprises marginalized. Furthermore, persistent cross-national data gaps and aggregated reporting conceal these structural inequities while enabling policy distortions like fronting. We recommend structural reforms including regional benchmarks and independent auditing to align procurement with genuine Indigenous economic sovereignty.

title: Why Street-Level Bureaucrats Leave: The Effects of Organizational Transparency and Role Conflict
abstract: Street-level bureaucrats often lack workplace clarity, which contributes to higher turnover. Drawing on street-level bureaucracy theory and the Job Demands–Resources model, this study examines how organizational transparency and role conflict, two dimensions of workplace clarity, shape turnover intentions among social workers in Chinese nonprofit organizations. Using multilevel data from the China Social Work Longitudinal Study, we find that organizational transparency reduces and role conflict increases turnover intentions. Value fit mediates both relationships, and job autonomy moderates them by enhancing the benefits of organizational transparency and buffering the harms of role conflict. Findings validate the extension of street-level bureaucracy theory to the nonprofit context and offer actionable insights for improving workforce stability in a complex governance environment.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: A population-based study of obstructive sleep apnea: using probabilistic case ascertainment through health administrative databases
Face‐to‐Face With Administrative Burdens: Design Simplification, Emotional Costs, and Procedural Outcomes in Digital Welfare Applications
abstract: ABSTRACT Recent scholarship on administrative burden has increasingly focused on psychological costs, design interventions, and digital burdens. This study combines these interests and examines the psychological costs of negative emotions during administrative encounters at varying levels of digital maturity. Building on affective events theory and employing facial coding in a controlled experiment, the study demonstrates that negative emotions rise during bureaucratic encounters, with frustration resulting in more errors made by applicants. Simplifying the procedure through pre‐filled forms does not reduce negative emotional arousal; however, it enhances satisfaction with the procedure. Vulnerable citizens, as indicated by low education and foreign citizenship, benefit more from this informational integration than other groups, suggesting that procedural redesign can enhance the inclusiveness of public service delivery. Overall, the research advances both scholarly and practical understanding of the emotional dimension of administrative burdens from a process‐oriented perspective, highlighting the persistent challenge of reducing emotional costs to enhance citizen experiences.

title: Calibration labour: making careers machine-legible under algorithmic hiring
abstract: This article reconceptualises algorithmic hiring as a transformation in the communicative conditions of recruitment rather than primarily as a problem of decision-making. Drawing on two years of ethnographic fieldwork at a London-based employment agency and training programme, it examines how employability is produced when recruitment is mediated by AI-enhanced applicant tracking systems (ATS). The article introduces algorithmic legibility as a communicative regime through which candidates encounter evaluation via asymmetrical proxy signals – such as metrics, thresholds, and prolonged silence – rather than through dialogic explanation. It demonstrates how this shift transforms job seeking from an interpersonal imitation game rooted in socialised modelling into a rationalised calibration game that demands calibration labour: the iterative, individualised restructuring of CVs, timelines, and narratives to align with opaque infrastructural criteria. The article argues that this infrastructure reconfigures recruitment into a restrictive recognition game in which visibility is increasingly reserved for biographies that can be readily rendered machine-legible. Under these conditions, interpretive labour is redistributed downwards, institutions are relieved of explanatory accountability, and marginalised jobseekers are compelled to become technicians of their own datafied subjectivities. Beyond corporate selection, this shift erodes the status of employment as a locus of social recognition and civic participation, contributing to the production of the algorithmic citizen – a subject whose socio-political inclusion becomes increasingly contingent upon continuous machine legibility. Algorithmic hiring, the article argues, governs access to work not through selection alone, but by reshaping whose lives can be rendered recognisable, on what terms, and through what forms of labour.

title: Influence operations 2.0: the evolution of social media manipulation in Southeast Asia
abstract: Given the dynamic and constantly evolving character of domestic online influence operations (IO), more knowledge of how these operations are changing is critical for efforts to counter the corrosive effects of IO on democracy and public debate. This article analyses the evolution of IO in Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines, using interviews with individuals involved in executing such operations. We identify a five-fold transformation. First, we trace a shift from state-dominated influence campaigns to a broader spectrum of clients. Second, we observe increased outsourcing of the operational work to private companies and freelancers. Third, we find a shift from quantity to quality in social media accounts, with IO workers operating fewer, more carefully crafted and influential profiles, alongside more limited use of automated bots. Fourth, content strategies have matured: instead of simply echoing state narratives, contemporary IO use data analytics to craft content tailored to specific audiences, often through subtle reframing of news rather than blatant disinformation. Fifth, dissemination methods have similarly shifted – from overwhelming social platforms with content to a more responsive, targeted, and data-informed approach. These changes signal a move toward more refined and strategic influence tactics. We conclude by highlighting likely causes of these transformations, and discuss implications for efforts to counter IO.

title: Interpretable modelling of pedestrian crashes at crosswalks considering holistic visual road environment characteristics

Not Just What Happened, But How it Felt: Subjective Distress and its Role in Adolescent Health After Childhood Physical Abuse
abstract: The role of subjective experience in understanding the links between childhood physical abuse and mental and somatic outcomes is gaining recognition but remains underexplored. Using data from a large population-based sample of youth (12–16 years) and generalized linear models, we examined whether current and past peak subjective distress following physical abuse were associated with symptoms, measured by the Hopkins Symptom Checklist (HSCL-10) and the Children’s Somatic Symptoms Inventory (CSSI-8). Causal mediation analyses were conducted to investigate whether subjective distress mediated the relationship between physical abuse and health outcomes. Subjective distress accounted for variation in symptoms, above and beyond severity and frequency of physical abuse. The impact of physical abuse on health was largely transmitted through subjective distress. While severity and frequency of maltreatment remain independent predictors of health outcomes, this study underscores the necessity of incorporating measures of subjective experience to understand the pathways linking childhood physical abuse to later health outcomes.

title: The battle of the brides: Co-wife competition and aggression across 19 cultures
abstract: The dominant account of women's intrasexual competition holds that women prefer indirect over direct aggression, a prediction supported by experimental studies drawn largely from young women in WEIRD settings competing over low or hypothetical stakes. The present analysis examines co-wife competition as a theoretically motivated high-stakes test case, using systematic analysis of the eHRAF World Cultures database. Ethnographic records from 19 cultures spanning five world regions were coded using a four-domain scheme covering causes, modes, resolution strategies, and prevention strategies, developed inductively and refined. Competition for the husband's sexual attention and general preference was the dominant cause (73.7%), followed by material resource competition (36.8%). Physical aggression between co-wives was the most frequently documented competitive mode, confirmed in 63.2% of cultures. Resolutions varied, with the most frequent being the husband's intervention or relationship dissolution (both 47.4%). The prevention domain revealed that spatial separation of wives was the most common structural response to co-wife hostility (57.9%), indicating that polygynous households are routinely organized to deter anticipated conflict. These findings support the conclusion that direct female aggression is a common, and often the dominant mode of co-wife competition under high-stakes conditions, occurring in addition to indirect strategies rather than replacing them, and running counter to the prevailing view that women rarely aggress directly.

title: It’s hard enough having cancer as an adolescent or young adult, but what about its financial impact?

Multi-objective optimisation of hydrogen and methanol-based hybrid power systems for service operation vessels: A techno-economic and environmental analysis
abstract: Decarbonising offshore-wind service operation vessels (SOVs) requires fuel-pathway choices that balance cost, emissions, and onboard integration. This study develops a bi-level techno-economic and environmental optimisation framework for a 5 000 GT offshore wind farm SOV, coupling NSGA-II architecture sizing with second-by-second rule-based energy management. The three alternative pathways compared are dual-fuel methanol engines (DFME), liquid-hydrogen proton-exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFC), and methanol-reforming fuel cells (MRFC). The framework minimises capital expenditure, lifecycle operating expenditure, and well-to-wake carbon intensity over a representative 14-day mission profile, with TOPSIS used to select one balanced decision case from each Pareto front. A unified β ∗ / Γ ∗ metric is introduced to quantify the weight reallocation or deck-volume expansion associated with each pathway. Relative to the diesel baseline, the TOPSIS designs reduce well-to-wake carbon intensity by 68.7% for DFME, 83.3% for MRFC, and 93.6% for PEMFC, while increasing lifecycle cost from 29.14 MUSD to 96.89–110.72 MUSD. No pathway is universally dominant across cost, emissions, and integration-related indicators. DFME provides the lowest lifecycle cost and highest technology readiness. MRFC offers the most favourable weight-and-volume fit among the deep-decarbonisation options. PEMFC achieves the largest carbon reduction only when the green-hydrogen production emission factor remains below approximately 2.1 kgCO 2 e/kgH 2 .

title: Multi-dimensional weighted adaptive consensus control for resilient operation of a multi-microgrid system with HESS
A stabilized equivalent LCOE framework for assessing the economic potential of stable wind and solar power in China
Obstacles to Sub-Saharan Africa’s clean energy transition: the ‘tyranny of sovereign ratings’
abstract: Sub-Saharan Africa’s clean energy transition is constrained by a financial architecture shaped by persistent perceptions of high risk. Sovereign credit ratings (SCRs) play a central role in determining borrowing costs and access to capital, yet in sub-Saharan Africa they appear misaligned with observed default and recovery outcomes, particularly in infrastructure finance, where default rates are low and loan recovery is high. While high borrowing costs also reflect structural economic, institutional, and political challenges, we argue that prevailing credit rating methodologies and regulatory frameworks amplify these constraints by transmitting sovereign risk mechanically to long-term, asset-backed clean energy investments. Drawing on evidence from multilateral development banks and private infrastructure finance, we show how this misalignment contributes to elevated costs of capital, reinforcing procyclical investment dynamics, and slowing clean energy deployment. We situate this argument within broader debates on climate finance and just transitions, highlighting how distorted risk assessments disproportionately affect the deployment of capital-intensive clean energy in low-income contexts. We conclude by outlining policy-relevant reforms – including adjustments to credit rating practices, recognition of infrastructure as a distinct asset class in financial regulation, and the development of credible Africa-based rating institutions – that could help align financing costs more closely with underlying risks and support a more equitable global energy transition.

title: From waste to resilience: A circular biochar framework for climate-smart agriculture in Africa
Land-use policy architectures for brownfield regeneration: A comparative analysis of Spain and the Netherlands
Multidimensional efficiency and institutional scale heterogeneity in protected areas: Evidence from Italy
abstract: Protected areas play a central role in territorial governance and the provision of environmental public goods, yet their performance is typically evaluated through effectiveness-based frameworks rather than through efficiency analysis. This study provides a multidimensional assessment of 27 Italian National Parks, conceptualized as multi-mission public organizations operating within complex territorial and institutional contexts. Four mission-specific domains - ecological performance, tourism valorization, managerial administration, and governance capacity - are evaluated using Data Envelopment Analysis within a non-radial framework that captures asymmetric inefficiencies across functions. The analysis explicitly examines the role of institutional scale, distinguishing between pure technical inefficiency and structural scale effects. Results reveal differentiated performance regimes: ecological outcomes are largely anchored in territorial endowment, whereas tourism and managerial domains exhibit both slack-driven and scale-related inefficiencies. Governance performance appears strongly conditioned by the configuration of institutional scales. These findings highlight the importance of scale alignment and mission-specific benchmarking for improving the design and coordination of protected-area governance systems.

title: Does energy infrastructure modernization drive manufacturing quality? Micro-evidence from China's ultra-high voltage projects
