Affective Polarization, Media Outlets, and Opinion Dynamics
abstract: Abstract We study opinion dynamics in a social network consisting of two groups. Agents update their opinions by conforming to members of their own group while rejecting the views of the opposing group (affective polarization), and by listening to a media outlet that may provide biased information. We characterize the long-run opinions and identify when affective polarization and media bias lead to ideological polarization, persistent disagreement, or failures of learning. We also derive when information interventions or censorship improve the accuracy of average opinions} and reduce disagreement, and when they backfire: better information helps only under specific media bias configurations and when directed to the agents we identify as most effective at propagating it through the network.

title: Local Shocks and Regional Dynamics in an Aging Economy
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies how population aging shapes regional adjustment to local shocks. I develop a dynamic spatial general equilibrium model that incorporates aggregate demographic change, life‐cycle variation in migration and employment choices, and forward‐looking investment in local capital. Applying the model to Japan, I find that aging can mitigate welfare losses from a negative local shock. Although older populations are less mobile, reduced outmigration sustains local capital demand and slows capital disinvestment, limiting declines in labor productivity. An extension illustrates the model's use for post‐disaster policy evaluation, highlighting a potential tradeoff between spatial equity and aggregate welfare.

title: Does Digitalization Widen Labor Income Inequality?
abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a growth model that endogenizes the occupational choice of workers with different ability levels to study how digitalization affects labor income inequality. The framework incorporates digitalization's multifaceted effects on the economy: (i) it influences economic growth through automation, and (ii) it affects labor income inequality through labor productivity (demand side) and labor time modulation (supply side). We examine how these channels influence wage inequality between skilled and unskilled workers, within each skill group, and economy‐wide. The analysis reveals that digitalization's impact on labor income inequality—whether exacerbating or mitigating disparities—depends on the inequality metric employed.

title: Assessing the Environmental, Economic and Social Impacts of a Greenhouse Gas Emission Tax in Swiss Agriculture
abstract: ABSTRACT Agriculture accounts for about one fifth of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, making mitigation a key policy priority. Although policymakers are increasingly considering market‐based approaches such as taxes, their broader impacts remain insufficiently assessed. This study examines the environmental, economic and social impacts of a GHG tax on Swiss agriculture. Using the agent‐based sector model SWISSland, representing 3077 farms and capturing heterogeneous responses to taxation and structural change, we simulate tax levels of 100, 200 and 300 CHF/tCO 2 eq for 2024–2030. We consider three mitigation pathways: technical measures, structural changes in land use and livestock numbers, and farm exits. We assess their impacts on GHG emissions, nitrogen surpluses, biodiversity, farm income, food production and food security. A GHG tax activates abatement mechanisms and induces dairy herd reductions, grassland extensification, shifts towards crop production for direct human consumption, and livestock farm exits. At 100 and 200 CHF/tCO 2 eq, emission reductions are mainly driven by technical measures, whereas at 300 CHF/tCO 2 eq they increasingly result from structural adjustment, including livestock farm exits and land reallocation to less emissions‐intensive production. A tax of 100 CHF/tCO 2 eq reduces emissions by 5%, while higher tax rates achieve greater reductions but increase sectoral income losses from 13% to 25%. Food self‐sufficiency and calorie production remain stable. The model also shows environmental co‐benefits, including lower nitrogen surpluses and increased biodiversity areas. These findings highlight synergies and trade‐offs across sustainability dimensions and suggest that redistributing tax revenues could mitigate adverse effects and improve policy outcomes, while enhancing the policy's social acceptability.

title: Immigration and crimes against natives: the 2015 refugee crisis in Germany
Culture Promotion, Information Disclosure, and Firm Value: Evidence From Confucius Institutes
abstract: ABSTRACT Using the staggered establishment of Confucius Institutes in the United States, which promote underrepresented Chinese culture in local communities, we examine the nexus among culture promotion, information disclosure, and firm value. We find that the value of treatment firms (i.e., firms headquartered near a Confucius Institute) decreases significantly after the establishment. Our results are consistent with the argument that culture promotion in local communities impedes firm value by eroding local social capital. Moreover, firms with better information disclosure are resilient to the decline of firm value. We also observe a significant increase in nonmandatory disclosures, while mandatory disclosures remain unchanged. Our results are not likely driven by the change in local economic conditions.

title: Choosing Startup Investors: Does Gender Matter?
abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate whether startups respond differently to male and female investors during outbound origination, a setting where female investors often report being marginalized by male founders. Using a randomized field experiment, we examine gender differences in startups' responses to investor outreach. Leveraging the rapid increase in outbound origination, our field experiment involves 40,572 startups sending identical unsolicited emails from fictitious male and female investors. Startups are substantially more likely to read emails from male investors, visit their websites, and attempt to make contact. This pattern is stronger for angel investors than for VC investors. Disclosing professional certifications increases a male investor's email's likelihood of being read but reduces the corresponding female investor's chances. A second experiment with 4836 recently incorporated startups reveals similar gender‐based choices. The findings provide large‐scale field evidence suggesting that gender‐based frictions in entrepreneurial finance may extend beyond founders' access to capital to investors' access to deal flow.

title: Weathering hard times with bushmeat: rural household coping under rainfall shocks
abstract: While bushmeat can be a crucial protein source for food insecure households, its consumption and trade raise significant concerns for both human health and wildlife conservation. Here we investigate how rainfall shocks influence rural households’ income from and reliance on bushmeat hunting. Drawing on data from nearly 8,000 rural households across 24 low- and middle-income countries, matched to gridded rainfall records and detailed agricultural season calendars, our study distinguishes between the effects of shocks depending on their type, intensity and timing of occurrence within the agricultural cycle. We mitigate endogeneity concerns faced in prior studies relying on self-reported shocks and cross-sectional data, by constructing a quarterly household panel survey integrated with objective, high-resolution data on climatic moisture stress. We find that dry conditions increase both bushmeat income and its share in total household income, particularly during critical agricultural periods. Conversely, wet conditions have the opposite effect, often decreasing hunting due to improved agricultural yields. However, these effects vary depending on the intensity of wet conditions. Additionally, we find heterogeneity in responses across socio-economic strata, as wealthier households tend to have higher bushmeat income during dry periods, likely due to better access to resources. The study increases our understanding of when and by whom climate stressors induce greater wildlife offtake, providing important insight for targeted development and conservation policy.

title: The Effectiveness of Carbon Pricing: A Global Evaluation
abstract: Abstract We estimate the effect of the staggered adoption of carbon pricing policies across the globe between 1990 and 2017 on per capita $$\text{CO}_2$$ emissions from fossil fuel combustion. We use recent econometric techniques robust to treatment effect heterogeneity. Our dynamic treatment effect estimations indicate gradual adjustments after implementation, resulting in a 19 to 23 percent decrease in $$\text{CO}_2$$ emissions after 10 years. These effects were primarily driven by resource substitution rather than improvements in energy efficiency and were not driven by short-term responses to carbon prices. Our results are robust to controlling for the potential effects of renewable energy policies. These results highlight the role of carbon pricing policies in steering medium-term expectations and complementing the climate policy mix.

title: Effects of the New Revenue Recognition Standard (ASC 606) on the Informativeness of Earnings and Revenues
abstract: ABSTRACT We show that earnings announcements are accompanied by larger decreases in the bid–ask spread and the price impact of trades and a larger increase in price efficiency following the implementation of the new revenue recognition standard (Accounting Standards Codification 606 [ASC 606]). The implementation of ASC 606 is associated with a significant increase in the accuracy of analysts’ revenue and earnings forecasts and a decrease in the post‐earnings announcement drift (PEAD). These results indicate that ASC 606 has improved the informativeness of earnings and altered the effect of earnings announcements on the firm's information and trading environments.

title: Medical Brain Drain: The Role of Job Attributes and Individual Traits
abstract: Medical brain drain poses a major challenge for health systems, reducing physician supply and undermining public investment in medical training. Prior work examined migration flows and their macroeconomic determinants. This study uses a discrete choice experiment to assess how individual background and personality traits shape medical student intentions to migrate and whether job attributes are valued differently at home and abroad. We surveyed 527 senior medical students from 12 Italian universities between November 2020 and July 2021, using Italy as a pertinent case given high physician emigration and limited inflow of foreign-trained doctors. We find that students require compensation of around 30% of physicians' average starting salary to accept a job abroad rather than at home. Those from higher-quality schools or medical families, and those who are more altruistic, competitive, and risk-tolerant, require less compensation to migrate. Valuations of several job attributes also differ by location: at home, students value permanent contracts and professional development; abroad, they are willing to accept temporary contracts but reject under-skilling. These findings suggest that emigration may disproportionately involve the best-trained students. Policy simulations show that improving working conditions, job security, or professional development opportunities each substantially increases the predicted probability of choosing a domestic job, with salary increases having the largest effects.

title: The promise and limits of industrial statecraft: the US response to China’s EV battery dominance
abstract: In the literature on US-China techno-strategic rivalry, the semiconductor sector has received particular attention – a sector where the US is the incumbent leader. This paper shifts the focus to the EV battery sector to examine the rivalry when China is the emerging leader. In responding to China’s leapfrogging in EV batteries, the Biden administration pursued a strong industrial policy to build domestic capacity. While the US ‘industrial statecraft’ in the Biden era catalysed significant investment in battery cell production, project initiations in upstream segments, particularly in battery mineral processing, remained very limited. The relative success in cell production reflects an alignment between policy goals and corporate interests: subsidies make onshoring competitive and returns predictable. In upstream segments, by contrast, US policy largely remained ineffective at mitigating entry barriers and de-risking uncertain returns. In conceptualising the promise and limits of industrial statecraft, the paper argues that outcomes are mediated by a state-capital bargain, conditioned by macro-structural context and underlying sectoral dynamics.

title: The language of leaving: Decoding defection via B2B customer language features
abstract: Abstract Customer language data (e.g., online reviews, call transcripts) is widely available. Yet, research in B2B contexts is still in its early stages of analyzing a full range of customer language features to derive insight. Using an empirics-first approach, this research sequentially identifies robust and parsimonious language features in B2B customer data that are diagnostic of customer experiences and predictive of forthcoming purchasing decisions. The authors examine five categories of how business customers speak: sentiment, temporality, certainty, concreteness, and personal pronouns. Results reveal that sentiment and temporality consistently reflect customer experience and provide incremental predictive value of customer defections within request-for-proposal (RFP) decisions. The authors demonstrate this pattern across customers’ written (Study 1), spoken (Study 2), and pre-RFP (Study 3) language. These studies leverage empirical regularities to advance early-stage theorizing around psychological distance and language-based models of customer defection. Illustrating the managerial relevance of customer language features, findings show that in a customer’s collective communication prior to an RFP decision, a 1% increase in past focus raises the odds of a multimillion-dollar RFP defection by 8.4%. The research also equips practitioners to compute sentiment and temporality in customer language via large-language-model prompts and statistical code, facilitating resource allocation and prioritization of customer accounts.
journal_name: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: Leveling the Playing Field? Generative AI and Entrepreneurial Storytelling
abstract: Cultural entrepreneurship research emphasizes the importance of storytelling and other cultural skills, yet recent work suggests that generative artificial intelligence (AI) levels the playing field for entrepreneurs lacking such skills. In this conceptual article, we challenge this view by outlining how the widespread use of AI tools likely leads to systematic changes in the institutional norms and expectations that shape entrepreneurial storytelling. Anchored in evidence-informed assumptions about average entrepreneurs’ use of AI, our theorization suggests that widespread AI adoption will lead to a homogenization in entrepreneurial storytelling—creating an evaluative environment that may require even greater cultural skills to navigate.

title: The Benefits of Bundling Material Goods with Moderate Usage Complementarity
abstract: Abstract Firms can bundle material goods together in various ways, including based on their usage complementarity (i.e., the likelihood that the goods are used together). While prior research has investigated the consequences of bundling products that are high (vs. low) in usage complementarity, the current research uncovers the benefits of bundling products that are moderate in usage complementarity (e.g., a coffee mug and a folding chair). Thirteen pre-registered experiments show that bundling products that are moderate in usage complementarity offers companies a unique advantage: Bundling these products prompts consumers to view them as relatively more experiential compared to bundling products that are low or high in usage complementarity and compared to their non-bundled components. This perceptual shift occurs because bundling products with moderate usage complementarity increases contextualization—the degree to which consumers consider the setting in which the products could be used rather than the use of the products themselves. It also changes consumer behavior in ways that can benefit firms (e.g., increasing purchase likelihood when seeking an experience). This research offers theoretical contributions to the bundling and material-experiential literatures and practical implications for companies interested in different bundling approaches and obtaining the advantages of heightened experiential perceptions for material goods.

title: Media Review: Painted horses and floating signifiers: How China talked its way into capitalism
Integrated intelligence, autonomous operations, and trusted autonomy: AI-driven SCM performance in 2040
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI)-driven advancements may enhance supply chain management (SCM) performance across SCOR-DS processes by 2040, addressing the lack of systematic, long-horizon, cross-process evidence on AI-related performance effects. Design/methodology/approach A foresight-oriented real-time Delphi study assessed 13 projections developed from desk research and 12 semi-structured expert interviews, then refined in internal and expert workshops. Seventy experts rated each projection’s expected probability, impact and desirability, providing qualitative rationales. Results were analyzed using descriptive and consensus statistics, stakeholder comparisons, dissent diagnostics, qualitative coding and fuzzy c-means clustering, discussed through a complex adaptive systems lens. Findings Experts expect substantial AI-enabled SCM performance gains by 2040. Results indicate layered AI integration. Integrated intelligence emerges as the most plausible and impactful pathway, reflecting deeply embedded, predominantly assistive AI across planning, sourcing, fulfillment and returns. The autonomous operations pathway captures more selective, contested moves toward AI-led training, shared AI infrastructures, unmanned production and autonomous mass customization. Trusted autonomy is less directly impactful yet enables adoption by stabilizing data protection, contractual delegation and safety-related AI use. Assessments vary across SCOR-DS stakeholder groups, while country-based differences are negligible. Originality/value This study offers a SCOR-DS-wide, Delphi-based analysis of how AI-driven SCM performance enhancement is expected to unfold by 2040 as a layered, process-uneven configuration rather than a single linear trend. Through a complex adaptive systems lens, it shows that these trajectories operate through distinct mechanisms: schema and network-connectivity changes, shifts in agent composition and self-organization and governance-based boundary setting, thereby advancing theorizing on AI as an adaptive agent in supply networks.
journal_name: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

title: Knowledge governance in internationalized business groups: Ownership ties, structural holes, and headquarters innovation in Taiwan
Navigating Consumer Emotional Vulnerability in Services
abstract: The growing awareness that consumer vulnerability extends beyond a person’s fixed status or identity is prompting concern to better understand the overlooked lived experiences of vulnerability that are under-theorized, poorly accommodated, and potentially harmful. We take the cascading mental health crises around the world as a critical impetus to conceptualize consumer emotional vulnerability (CEV) in service ecosystems and define it as psychological fragility that increases a person’s susceptibility to emotional harm in service exchange. We identify four dynamic tensions of CEV—invisibility, inescapability, uncertainty, and hypersensitivity that clarify its meaning and two dimensions (velocity and duration) that describe how it is organized. Our conceptual analysis embeds CEV within a network of antecedents, moderators, mediators, and consequences; derives a framework for service providers to implement CEV interventions; and synthesizes key theories related to intervention design. We propose new interventions grounded in the defining tensions of CEV and offer guidance for future service research seeking to promote consumer agency and reduce psychological strain. We contribute to service research by theorizing a pervasive yet overlooked form of vulnerability and offering actionable strategies to effectively support emotionally vulnerable consumers in service interactions and ecosystems.

title: Managing Critical Frontline Agent–Customer Interactions: The Role of Service Recovery Explanations Across Artificial Intelligence and Human Agents
abstract: Responding to service failures represents an acid test at organizational frontlines, where human service agents, alongside a growing share of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered service agents, engage in service recovery. Particularly when recovery outcomes are only partially favorable, customers may perceive these decisions as unclear or difficult to understand, potentially impairing their evaluation of the service encounter. This raises the question of whether explanations of service recovery decisions should be provided and, if so, how and by whom. Addressing this practical need and the related research gap, the article examines the effects of service recovery explanations on customers’ post-recovery reactions. Across three main studies and three supplementary studies spanning multiple service industries, the authors demonstrate that service recovery explanations can enhance customer satisfaction and choice by fostering perceptions of agent competence and warmth. These beneficial effects, however, depend on key contingencies: rationales outperform excuses and justifications, specific explanations tend to be more effective than general ones, and explanations provided by AI service agents can be more impactful than those delivered by human service agents. Overall, the article advances understanding of service recovery communication and offers actionable guidance for managing both AI- and human-mediated service recovery.

title: Credit or Constraint: Postcolonial Feminist Ethics of Empowerment in Microfinance
abstract: Abstract The microfinance industry has long been promoted as a “win-win” intervention in the Global South, producing both economic returns and social benefits. The industry disproportionately targets women as borrowers. In this paper, we argue that the ethical narrative of microfinance can fail to deliver—or actively obstruct—social gains for women by conflating the provision of credit with empowerment. Empowerment, we explain, cannot be reliably proxied via financialized metrics such as loan disbursement or repayment. Instead, it requires a connection between capital and agency that depends on women’s legitimacy as economic agents—a legitimacy shaped by cultural gender norms and, in postcolonial economies, by colonial legacies. By using a postcolonial feminist lens to critically analyze the contexts in which microfinance initiatives are enacted, scholars and practitioners can make visible the structural barriers which constrain women’s empowerment. We present a case study set in Ghana to demonstrate how capital, agency, and legitimacy can decouple. This project contributes to feminist business ethics by theorizing how structural and historical conditions mediate the relationship between credit and empowerment.

title: Islamic Business Ethics, Muslim Feminism, and the Rhetorical Construction of Entrepreneurial Legitimacy: Evidence from Emirati Women
abstract: Abstract Despite the United Arab Emirates’ state-led promotion of women’s entrepreneurship as central to national transformation, Emirati women entrepreneurs continue to face patriarchal norms that frame entrepreneurship as a masculine domain, rendering their entrepreneurial legitimacy both precarious and contested. Based on in-depth interviews, this study examines how women entrepreneurs construct entrepreneurial legitimacy within a patriarchal Muslim context, marked by a tension between empowerment rhetoric and gendered constraints. Drawing on Suddaby and Greenwood’s (2005) framework of rhetorical legitimation together with Islamic business ethics and Muslim feminism, we demonstrate how Emirati women entrepreneurs mobilise state-led empowerment and national transformation discourses to construct entrepreneurial legitimacy. We show how they align their entrepreneurship with national development goals through teleological strategies and with globalisation through cosmological strategies. We also reveal how they employ historical strategies that draw on both Emirati and Islamic history to legitimate their entrepreneurial pursuits. The analysis further reveals how Emirati, Muslim women entrepreneurs employ a Muslim feminist perspective, reinterpreting Islamic principles and business ethics to affirm their agency and inform their ontological and value-based strategies, thereby positioning their entrepreneurship as morally grounded and socially responsible. At the intersection of Islamic business ethics, Muslim feminism, and rhetorical legitimation, our analysis reveals how rhetorical legitimacy in patriarchal religious contexts depends on prior, often invisible, feminist ethical interpretation of religious texts, thereby positioning interpretative agency as a precondition for rhetorical legitimation. This study advances scholarship on women’s entrepreneurship, business ethics, and religion by demonstrating how legitimacy is constructed through interpretative work that reconciles ethical principles with rhetorical legitimation.

title: Pricing on Carbon Transition Risks: Carbon Emission Trading and Stock Returns
abstract: ABSTRACT Relying on the phased rollout of the carbon emission trading (CET) pilot policy, we estimate a staggered difference‐in‐differences (DID) model to identify how transition risks induced by carbon pricing policies are priced in stock returns. Our results show that after CET implementation, stocks of CET‐covered firms command a significant carbon risk premium, providing empirical support for the carbon risk premium hypothesis. The premium arises from the market pricing of three distinct cash‐flow risks triggered by CET: operational uncertainty, credit deterioration, and information asymmetry. Meanwhile, divestment by rational investors serves as a key transmission channel for the premium. Dynamic analysis reveals pronounced time variation in the premium: it is significant during the initial period, persists for two years after implementation, then gradually attenuates, and reappears after the national CET launch. We further find that exposure to these risks is partially captured by established market factors (size/ SMB , value/ HML , profitability/ RMW ), indicating that carbon risk itself does not constitute a standalone pricing factor. Third‐party verified environmental ratings account for a substantial fraction of the cross‐sectional variation, whereas self‐disclosed environmental information by firms has limited explanatory power, indicating that information asymmetry constrains the market's ability to price carbon transition risks. This study provides microlevel evidence on how carbon policies are transmitted through capital markets.

title: Cultural Theory, Political Ideology, and Burden Tolerance: The Role of Core Beliefs in Shaping Support for Administrative Burdens
abstract: Administrative burdens embedded within many public policies are often politically contentious, such that core values and belief systems can drive either support or opposition. In this paper, we use survey data from US respondents to replicate and extend previous research on the public acceptance of administrative burdens in general. First, we confirm the measure's validity by examining its effects on beliefs across policies that range from highly polarized to less politically contentious. Second, we test the relationship between tolerance of administrative burden and cultural theory (CT) variables that tap into worldview orientations related to hierarchy, egalitarianism, individualism, and fatalism, which previous research has found predictive of policy preferences across a wide range of domains, even after accounting for political ideology and partisanship. We hypothesize that egalitarians and individualists will generally be less tolerant of burdens, while hierarchs will be more accepting of burdensome requirements. However, this effect varies depending on the nature of the burdens and how they relate to perceived threats for each worldview.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Does Gender Budgeting Improve Women's Well‐Being, Equality, and Empowerment?
abstract: ABSTRACT The United Nations' fifth Sustainable Development Goal calls for gender equality and empowerment. Gender budgeting (GB) has been proposed as a potential mechanism to reduce gender disparities. This is a novel approach to budgeting that considers the impact of public spending on women and other underrepresented groups. Despite its growing popularity, spreading to over 80 countries since its launch in the 1980s, the effectiveness of GB remains less understood. This study tests whether GB has led to tangible improvements in women's well‐being, equality, and empowerment. We use an event study research design with staggered adoption to analyze data across 47 countries from 2000 to 2023. Our analyses of average and heterogeneous treatment effects reveal short‐ and long‐term impacts; notably, we find significant reductions in maternal mortality ratios and adolescent birth rates, as well as improvements in women's political empowerment.

title: Improving Dietary Data Quality in Nutrition Studies: Development and Validation of an Explainable, Reproducible, Open Machine Learning-Assisted Framework for Outlier Detection in 24-Hour Recalls
abstract: Twenty-four-hour dietary recalls (24HRs) are widely used in nutritional epidemiology, but repeated administration is required to capture within-person variability, introducing temporal dependence and challenges for data cleaning. Existing outlier detection approaches are largely static, manual, and based on adult-centric thresholds, limiting reproducibility and scalability. We developed and validated an explainable, reproducible machine learning (ML)-assisted framework to detect and evaluate implausible intake values in cross-sectional and longitudinal 24HRs and to generate AI-ready dietary datasets. The open pipeline integrates automated statistical detection using digitized National Cancer Institute 5th-95th percentile intake ranges, longitudinal interquartile range-based flagging, and ML-based rule explainability for outlier detection. Validation was conducted using the Microbiota, Growth, and Diet (MiGrowD) study in Ontario, Canada (126 children aged 8-12 years), and data from the 2015 Canadian Community Health Survey-Nutrition, a nationally representative sample of Canadian children and adults with repeated 24HRs (n = 15 216). Across energy intake and seven nutrients, 75 recalls containing at least one potentially implausible value were identified. In longitudinal data, the framework achieved > 77% sensitivity, 97% specificity, and 88% precision, outperforming the static method. This explainable data-driven framework improves data quality, transparency, and reproducibility, supporting scalable epidemiologic analyses using AI-ready dietary data.

title: Early-life and Adulthood Eviction and Risk of Depressive Symptoms in Black Reproductive Age Women: Social Epidemiology to Combat Unjust Residential Evictions (SECURE) Study
abstract: Residential evictions and chronic depression are worsening public health issues that disproportionately affect Black communities, though few studies have examined their association. Using qualitative and quantitative data from the (ANONYMIZED FOR REVIEW); 2021-2024; n = 1428). We used Poisson regression to estimate risk of high depressive symptoms (Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression (CESD) score 16+; Cronbach's alpha: 0.91) associated with 5 measures of eviction, by type, recency, and life-stage. We also used a content analysis methodology to mix responses to an open-ended survey question about the impact of childhood eviction (n = 349) with quantitative data to provide a deeper contextual understanding of the findings. Fifty-four percent (n = 775) of participants had CESD scores indicating they were at risk for clinical depression. We observed between 14-17% higher risk of high depressive symptoms among those who reported childhood eviction and recent and lifetime court-ordered eviction, compared to those who did not, in adjusted models (95% confidence interval range: 1.01-1.28). Qualitative data suggests that childhood eviction may be associated with risk of clinical depression through 5 novel potential mechanisms. The 20-item depressive symptom scale completely aligned with the qualitative themes. Future research, mental health interventions and policy solutions are warranted to achieve health equity goals.

Who Pays the Piper Calls the Tune: Funding Sources and Earnings Management in Charities
abstract: This study examines how funding structures shape earnings management behaviour in charities and, in doing so, contributes to the nonprofit accountability literature. Drawing on resource dependence theory, we argue that funding sources create distinct accountability environments that influence managers’ incentives and opportunities to manage reported financial performance. Using a large panel of U.K. charities from 2007 to 2023, we investigate both accrual-based and real earnings management around a zero-surplus benchmark. The findings indicate that charities employ discretionary accruals as well as adjustments to fundraising and support costs to influence reported outcomes. However, these behaviours vary systematically across funding structures. Charities funded by sophisticated funders and those more reliant on donations exhibit lower levels of accrual-based earnings management, whereas service-oriented charities exhibit higher levels. The findings suggest that donor monitoring, fund restrictions, and accountability pressures play an important role in constraining financial reporting discretion and strengthening financial integrity within charitable organisations. title: Pulse-based state-of-charge and state-of-health estimation of randomly retired lithium-ion batteries for second-life applications
abstract: Retired lithium-ion batteries are an important resource for second-life energy storage, but their practical reuse requires rapid and efficient state assessment under unknown usage histories. To address this problem, we develop a pulse-based framework for joint state-of-health (SOH) and state-of-charge (SOC) estimation of randomly retired lithium-ion battery cells. A set of voltage-response features is extracted from short bipolar pulse tests and used as diagnostic descriptors. Based on these features, two machine learning models, extremely randomized trees (ExtraTrees) and a tabular prior-data fitted network (TabPFN), are employed for battery state estimation and evaluated using data from 270 retired cells that cover three chemistry types and four capacity classes. The results show that TabPFN clearly outperforms ExtraTrees and achieves mean absolute errors ranging from 0.0076 to 0.0306 for SOH estimation and below 0.01 for SOC estimation across all cell groups. To reduce the testing burden, a subset of SOC-dependent pulse tests is removed, and the missing feature points are reconstructed using interpolation methods. The reduced-test results show that near-baseline estimation accuracy can be retained even after removing 40%–70% of SOC-dependent pulse tests, depending on the target state and accuracy requirements. These results demonstrate a practical route toward faster, lower-cost, and scalable state assessment for second-life battery applications.

title: Why Japan’s sovereign climate finance took a transition-bond form: bureaucratic mediation in an eco-developmental state
abstract: This article explains why Japan organized its Green Transformation (GX) sovereign borrowing programme around a transition-labelled use-of-proceeds instrument despite its prior green-finance infrastructure and the international prevalence of sovereign green bonds. It develops a political economy account of instrument choice within an eco-developmental state. The article introduces accommodative instrument design as a process through which bureaucratic actors translate incumbent sectors’ conditional support for decarbonization into an instrument that combines a formal climate objective with gradual adjustment. The analysis draws on documentary evidence and process tracing of policy developments from 2017 through February 2024, including 21 semi-structured interview sessions with 18 participants. It finds that an alignment between the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry and transition-exposed industries helped shape eligible sectors and transition pathways. Environmental actors exerted less influence in the venues where the GX programme and its eligible uses were designed. The article contributes to distributive climate politics and policy-instrument scholarship by showing how mandate-differentiated agencies convert sectoral bargains into the rules of sovereign finance.

abstract: This paper describes the development of novel bio-composite mortars made by reusing waste from the fish canning industry, namely mussel, clam, and oyster shells, as recycled aggregates to achieve a complete (100%) replacement of conventional sand. For each shell type, different granulometric fractions (0.00–1.00 mm, 1.00–2.00 mm, 2.00–4.00 mm, and a calibrated 0.00–4.00 mm blend) were investigated. Several waste-based cement mixes were tested and compared with conventional OPC mortar. Chemical-physical properties and the functional and engineering performance of the new bio-composite mortars were evaluated to explore their potential for construction applications. Main results indicated a strong dependence of mortar performance on both shell type and particle size distribution. In particular, oyster- and clam-shell mortars significantly improved the mechanical properties, achieving increases of up to 120% in flexural strength and 60% in compressive strength compared with the reference mortar, whereas mussel-shell formulations generally exhibited lower mechanical performance; opposite behaviours were observed for the mussel shell. Nevertheless, developed mixes were analysed in light of EN 998-1 and EN 998-2, for plastering and masonry application respectively, demonstrating potentials for uses in construction, including ordinary and lightweight structures and plasters. In addition, with an average 30% reduction in bulk density and a 40% increase in energy behaviour, the bio-composite mortars resulted particularly suitable for improved energy-saving applications. Finally, accelerated aging tests based on salt (4% NaCl) crystallization and exposure to high thermal loads (up to 800 °C), permitted to simulate exposure to prolonged stress and preliminary investigate the evolution of degradation phenomena, suggesting long life span. In conclusion, the use of sole bio-waste aggregate offers a sustainable alternative to conventional landfill disposal of the waste and makes these mortars promising candidates for Minimum Environmental Criteria certification, in line with the European Green Deal and Circular Economy principles.

title: Identification of a polyethene-interacting gut-associated bacterium from microplastic-exposed freshwater Labeo rohita
Land Degradation, Cultural Ecosystem Services, and Ecosystem Disservices in the Sumapaz Páramo, Colombia: An Integrated Socioecological Assessment
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding the relationships among land degradation, ecosystem functioning and human well‐being is essential for conserving tropical high‐mountain ecosystems. This study examined the relationships among land degradation, Cultural Ecosystem Services (CES), ecosystem disservices (EDS) and visitor perceptions at Laguna Colorados in the Sumapaz Páramo, Colombia, by integrating visitor‐perception data with complementary ecological evidence derived from multitemporal remote sensing. Perceptions were assessed through structured questionnaires administered to 92 adult visitors selected using simple random sampling. Responses were analysed in relation to sociodemographic characteristics using Spearman's rank correlations, hierarchical cluster analysis and principal component analysis. Knowledge of Nature and Landscape Appreciation were the most highly valued CES, whereas Religion and Spirituality received comparatively lower ratings and emerged as a distinct perceptual dimension. Tourism, Knowledge of Nature, Recreation and Sports, and Landscape Appreciation were positively associated and were perceived as an interconnected CES bundle. Soil contamination and insufficient surveillance and control were the most frequently reported EDS, each identified by 32% of respondents. These perceptions were broadly consistent with multitemporal remote‐sensing evidence, suggesting increasing vegetation heterogeneity, localised declines in vegetation vigour, moisture loss and greater soil exposure between 2003 and 2025. Integrating social‐perception data with complementary ecological evidence provides a more comprehensive understanding of land degradation as a socioecological process and can inform ecological restoration, adaptive visitor management and evidence‐based conservation planning in tropical high‐mountain ecosystems.

title: The Effect of Nitrogen and Phosphorus Fertilization on Plant Community Along Chronosequences of Reclaimed and Unreclaimed Postmining Soils After Coal Mining
abstract: ABSTRACT Nitrogen and phosphorus availability drive plant community composition, productivity, and ecosystem functioning. During succession, nutrient availability typically changes as organic matter accumulates in the soil, influencing both nitrogen and phosphorus pools. We assessed nutrient limitation along postmining chronosequences (10–50 years old), including sites reclaimed with alder ( Alnus ) plantations and unreclaimed sites undergoing spontaneous succession. Plots received N (50 kg ha −1 year −1 ) or P (5 kg ha −1 year −1 ) fertilization or served as controls, applied over 3 years. Vegetation surveys were conducted in the first and third years, and aboveground biomass of Calamagrostis epigejos was collected in the third year for chemical analysis. Redundancy analysis revealed a significant effect of fertilization on community composition at unreclaimed sites, explaining 7% of the variance, whereas the effect was not significant at reclaimed sites and explained only 2% of the variance. On unreclaimed sites, N fertilization increased herb‐layer cover, reduced species evenness and turnover, but did not accelerate vegetation change. Although the effects of N fertilization are significant in some cases, they are relatively small. Phosphorus fertilization had negligible effects on vegetation in both site types. Nutrient content analysis of C. epigejos biomass indicated that the plant community was more limited by P than by N. However, P fertilization had limited potential to alleviate this limitation. This effect likely results from alkaline soils, in which phosphorus is bound in insoluble compounds that are unavailable to plants. Moreover, the effects of both fertilizers do not appear to be clearly positive in terms of ecosystem restoration.

title: Trade‐Offs and Synergies in Cultivated Land Multifunctionality and Zoning Management in the Dongting Lake Region: A Multiscale Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding the multiscale patterns and interactions of cultivated land multifunctionality is important for conservation, governance, and agricultural spatial optimization in the Dongting Lake region. Using 2020 data, we evaluated economic production (EPF), social security (SSF), landscape‐based recreation (LRF), and ecological maintenance (EMF) functions at the 1‐km, 3‐km, and township scales. The Simpson reciprocal index, Spearman correlation, geographically weighted regression (GWR), and self‐organizing feature map (SOFM) were integrated to assess functional patterns, local relationships, and coupled zoning. The results showed that: (1) EPF and SSF were highest across the plains surrounding Dongting Lake, whereas LRF was highest around urban nodes and landscape‐resource clusters. EMF was highest in the western hills and mountains and the densely connected waterways of western and southern Dongting Lake. With increasing scale, the proportion of high‐value EPF areas declined from 29.25% to 13.22%; SSF and LRF also decreased markedly, whereas EMF remained relatively stable. (2) Functional provision and structural balance were spatially mismatched: the lake plain had stronger provision but lower balance, whereas peripheral hills and uplands showed the opposite pattern. (3) EPF and SSF maintained strong synergies across scales, with Spearman coefficients of 0.88, 0.93, and 0.86. GWR identified EPF–SSF synergies in 97.2%, 95.8%, and 98.6% of units, respectively, while many EMF‐related local relationships became non‐significant at the township scale. (4) SOFM separately identified two functional structures and three relationship structures. Coupling the two clustering results produced six management zones, of which the low‐function, trade‐off‐dominated zone (Z1) and high‐function, synergy‐dominated zone (Z6) accounted for 17.04% and 20.01%, respectively. These findings support differentiated cultivated land management. These findings support zone‐specific management based jointly on functional levels, structural balance, and relationship types.

title: Background complexity affects landscape aesthetic quality: Evidence from subject evaluations and fractal dimension analysis
abstract: Small green spaces on campus (SGSc) possess irreplaceable aesthetic and ecological values. However, studies combining both qualitative and quantitative approaches to improve landscape aesthetic quality remain unexplored. Both subjective questionnaires and fractal dimension values using the box-counting method were used to evaluate SGSc under four background types: buildings, sky, evergreen conifers, and broadleaf foliage. Results showed that: (1) The sky background exhibited the highest fractal dimension value in summer (1.332 ± 0.024), while the value of coniferous background peaked in winter (1.199 ± 0.014). The building background had the lowest fractal dimension values in both summer and winter (1.057 ± 0.002 and 1.053 ± 0.005, respectively). (2) The broadleaf background received the highest subjective evaluation scores in both summer (5.444 ± 0.182) and winter (5.526 ± 0.158), while the building background scored the lowest scores in the two seasons (3.433 ± 0.110 and 2.811 ± 0.113). (3) A significant correlation was observed between fractal dimension values and subjective evaluation scores, which increased significantly as fractal dimension values rose to 1.225 but declined significantly beyond this threshold. Effects of fractal dimension on scenic beauty appeared to have an optimal threshold. This study provided foundational data for intelligent SGS C design and renewal, as well as offered scientific support for the quantitative and qualitative evaluation of scenic beauty.
journal_name: Environment and Planning B: Urban Analytics and City Science

title: A multi-dimensional framework for measuring urban inclusiveness and crime using mobility traces: A socio-spatial study of Lisbon
abstract: Urban inclusiveness and safety are shaped by daily interactions between residents, visitors, and the built environment. Capturing these socio-spatial dynamics requires fine-grained data beyond traditional census or survey-based approaches. This study proposes an analytical framework to measure inclusiveness based on the spatial mixing of residents and visitors, combining anonymized mobile phone data with crime records, Points of Interest (POIs), and socioeconomic indicators. The approach integrates spatial statistics, regression models, and association rule mining to explore relationships between inclusiveness, socioeconomic structure, urban functionality, and crime patterns. Results indicate that non-inclusive areas are more prevalent in higher socioeconomic zones and are associated with higher levels of opportunity crimes. In contrast, inclusive areas exhibit greater functional diversity and visitor presence. Locations identified as problematic by official sources also tend to coincide with higher crime counts and lower inclusiveness, suggesting a spatial correspondence between perceived and observed insecurity. Overall, the findings highlight the role of urban functionality and mobility flows in shaping patterns of exposure to crime. By combining mobility data with multi-source urban indicators, the study provides a data-driven framework to explore socio-spatial segregation and its relationship with urban safety.

title: City distributions across elevation: A maximum-entropy approach
abstract: Most of the world’s cities are concentrated near sea level, far more than low-lying land availability alone would predict. This study quantifies that relationship by combining the elevations of 47,916 individual cities worldwide, each represented by a single point location, with matched national hypsography and modelling elevation intensity within a maximum-entropy framework. Across six candidate intensity models, the data strongly favour concave-cost specifications over the linear-cost exponential. The best AIC fit is a piecewise exponential with a steep low-elevation regime and a shallow higher-elevation regime, while the preferred smooth mechanistic model is a power-law decay, implying a concave effective cost function C(h) ∝ ln(1 + h/h 0 ). Here h denotes elevation above sea level (in metres) and h 0 is a fitted scale parameter that sets where the curvature of the cost function is concentrated. Zipfian rank-frequency scaling (the inverse rank–size power law familiar from city-size distributions) is rejected for city elevations, and the main inference is robust to data perturbations and country stratification. Transport evidence is retained as physical context rather than the central empirical test: scale economies and maritime access provide a plausible mechanism for the steep near-coastal penalty and flatter higher-elevation gradient, but do not identify the statistical pattern.

The Power of Diversity and Inclusion: Impact on Credit Default Swap Spreads
abstract: ABSTRACT In the evolving business landscape, diversity and inclusion (D&I) practices have gained increasing prominence, particularly as societal movements highlight the importance of creating diverse and inclusive workplaces. This study explores how a firm's D&I engagement affects its credit default swap (CDS) spreads, providing new insights into the financial benefits of robust D&I performance. Our empirical analysis shows that firms with higher D&I ratings tend to enjoy lower CDS spreads, a benefit that is particularly significant for highly leveraged firms. We also identify three key mechanisms through which D&I practices help reduce credit risk: enhanced financial health, increased transparency, and reduced agency costs. As such, a firm's commitment to D&I can serve as a strategic tool for enhancing a firm's credit profile, offering a compelling rationale for incorporating D&I initiatives into managerial strategies, regulatory frameworks, and investment choices.

title: Correction to ‘Keeping Up With the Times? Rethinking Social Evaluations Research Under Contemporary Technological and Sociopolitical Forces’
Consumers with Weaker Applications Are Less Receptive to Algorithmic Evaluation
abstract: Abstract Many organizations are adopting algorithms for evaluating various consumer applications (e.g., loans, insurance). This research explores how consumers react to this practice, with the goal of understanding what leads some consumers to react more positively or negatively to being evaluated by an algorithm than others. In the context of consumers applying for access to valued services, opportunities, or benefits, applicant strength (i.e., how strong an applicant believes their case is based on the information they have about their standing) influences their reactions toward algorithmic versus human evaluation. Algorithmic evaluation will have a greater deterrent effect on weaker than on stronger applicants. This asymmetry is explained by weaker applicants’ stronger preference for characteristics of human evaluators, such as flexibility and leniency, that they believe may improve their chances of receiving a favorable outcome. Consumers’ preferences ultimately impact willingness to apply, such that using algorithmic evaluations disproportionally discourages weaker applicants from applying. This research contributes to the literature on consumer responses to algorithms by identifying applicant strength as a novel determinant and by extending the focus from algorithms as advisors to algorithms as evaluators of consumers.

title: The Desire for Perfect Products
abstract: Abstract Some consumers evaluate products against demanding, ever-rising ideals of perfection. We introduce the desire for perfect products (DPP), a novel consumer trait capturing the extent to which consumers desire flawless products. Drawing on four qualitative studies, we identify three characteristics that distinguish high (vs. low) DPP consumers: (1) richer and more demanding ideal points, (2) greater susceptibility to upwardly revising those ideals when exposed to superior products, and (3) heightened sensitivity to even minor negative deviations from the ideal. Across scale-development studies reported in the web appendix, we develop an eight-item measure of DPP, establish its discriminant validity, and validate these characteristics. Across eight experiments, we show that DPP systematically shapes consumer behavior across acquisition and disposal. High-DPP consumers employ more numerous and stringent search filters, exhibit stronger preferences for newer products even when objective quality is unchanged, and are less willing to retain, repair, or donate flawed but usable products. Finally, we identify a managerially relevant intervention: reframing flaws as a source of uniqueness attenuates high-DPP consumers’ negative reactions to imperfect products.

title: Goals, Expectations, and Performance
abstract: People and organizations often set goals to self-motivate and achieve better outcomes in challenging tasks. But goals, and their effectiveness, might depend on what people expect to happen. Do goals reflect expectations or do goals set expectations? How do goals and expectations affect performance? These distinctions are important for motivation and intervention design. We run an online real-effort task to answer these two questions by introducing exogenous variation in goals and expectations. First, we find that goals mostly reflect existing expectations rather than set expectations. Second, practicing an easier version of a task leads to higher expectations and higher performance. Eliciting a goal leads to higher performance as well. However, controlling for expectations, changing the difficulty of the goal has no discernible effect. These results suggest that people benefit from being optimistic and setting a goal, but they cannot fool themselves into expecting and doing more simply by choosing a higher goal.

title: Training Frontline Health Workers in Low- and Middle-Income Countries to Reduce Contraceptive Stock-Outs: Evidence from Indonesia
abstract: Frontline health workers are an indispensable asset in the healthcare ecosystem of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). They not only provide clinical care to patients but also frequently shoulder nonclinical responsibilities such as inventory management. However, many lack the necessary skills to effectively manage inventories, leading to the pervasive problem of health commodity stock-outs. To address this problem, several LMICs have launched training programs aimed at enhancing the inventory management skills and capabilities of frontline health workers. Leveraging fine-grained data over a five-year period (2015–2019) from approximately 17,000 health facilities across Indonesia—where the public health supply chain operates as a hybrid push–pull model—we evaluate the impact of a large-scale inventory management training program on contraceptive stock-outs. Applying difference-in-differences estimations, we find that the training program is associated with a significant reduction in stock-outs (i.e., 6.52 percentage points, or approximately 30%). Our numerical calculations suggest that the training program prevents, on average, more than 800 unintended pregnancies and saves 4.25 maternal and newborn lives per 100,000 women of reproductive age within the catchment area of a treated health facility. A counterfactual benefit–cost analysis shows that on-site delivery of the training program (i.e., on the job within a health facility) yields operational and public health benefits that significantly exceed those achieved through off-site delivery (i.e., outside the health facility in a classroom). Our research highlights the practicality and scalability of human-capital-focused interventions in improving health commodity availability and public health outcomes in LMICs. This paper was accepted by Stefan Scholtes, healthcare management. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03696 .

title: Evolution of Discrimination on Online Platforms
abstract: Research on discrimination has predominantly relied on audit studies, which provide clean causal estimates through randomized profile testing but offer only static snapshots of bias. We adopt a dynamic perspective to examine how racial discrimination evolves over time. Using observational panel data from an online educational platform, we first find that African-American teachers receive 30.2% fewer bookings, and their opened classes are 3.3% less likely to be booked compared with their White counterparts during their first week on the platform, a gap that may indicate initial discrimination. Employing individual fixed effects models, we estimate how this gap evolves over time. The results show a striking 1,007% widening of the initial gap over the 12-week period. Our mechanism analysis shows that new students are significantly less likely to book classes with African-American teachers than with White teachers, even when African-American and White teachers have minimal or comparable reputation metrics. As a result, African-American teachers accumulate reputation metrics and customers more slowly than White teachers. Over time, the growing gaps in reputation and customer base further exacerbate the booking gap, driven by both new and repeat students. Our findings suggest that traditional audit studies may significantly underestimate the long-term consequences of early-stage discrimination and highlight how reputation and repeat customer accumulation serve as bias amplifiers on online platforms. We also show that this amplification mechanism operates regardless of whether the initial gap stems from racial discrimination and thus generalizes to other contexts. This paper was accepted by Srikanth Jagabathula, market design, platform, and demand analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02111 .

title: Leveraging Collective Advice-Taking Behavior to Infer Accuracy and Improve the Wisdom of Crowds
abstract: Wisdom of crowds estimates can be compromised when some agents’ predictions are systematically biased. A natural remedy is to aggregate predictions from a subset of more accurate agents rather than the entire crowd. I propose cluster weight on advice (CWOA), a novel “two-shot” algorithm to identify a more accurate subgroup in a single-prediction-problem context. CWOA first applies kernel density estimation to identify clusters of similar initial predictions. If multiple clusters emerge—indicating potential heterogeneity in agents’ information—the algorithm proceeds to present a piece of numerical advice (e.g., the group mean) and elicit updated predictions. This enables the calculation of the weight on advice (WOA)—the scaled magnitude of each agent’s belief revision. CWOA then averages the updated predictions within the cluster with the lowest mean WOA. A behavioral model and simulations explain both why and when cluster-level WOA signals accuracy. Better-informed agents—having already incorporated higher-quality information—perceive less corrective value in the advice and therefore, exhibit lower WOA. CWOA does not require agents to know the true biases or the composition of the crowd; a modest relative advantage in perceived estimation bias by better-informed agents may be sufficient, even under misperceptions of variance, advice quality, and psychological biases in advice taking. Empirically, I first test and confirm the model’s key insight in a controlled experimental setting. I then validate CWOA’s performance across multiple preregistered and archival data sets, including a study in which numerical advice comes from artificial intelligence. CWOA consistently outperforms benchmarks, including the state-of-the-art metaprediction-based methods. This paper was accepted by Jack Soll, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04499 .

title: The Salience of Entrepreneurship: Evidence from Online Business
abstract: We examine the decision to become an entrepreneur in the context of online business. Using data on entrepreneurs from a large e-commerce marketplace in China, we find that individuals are more likely to start online businesses after observing the salient success of nearby stores. Leveraging the platform’s store rating system and detailed geographic information in rural China, we show that an upgrade in a local store’s rating leads to a significant increase in new store entries nearby. This effect diminishes with physical distance and intensifies with the salience of the upgrade. However, these entry decisions appear to be suboptimal; entrants driven by local upgrade events underperform in sales and are more likely to exit, especially during downturns in overall market conditions. Our findings are consistent with salience-based theories of decision making, in which individuals overweight highly visible local information. This paper was accepted by Lin William Cong, finance. Funding: C. Liu acknowledges financial support from the Research Grant Council of the Hong Kong SAR, China [Project 12503324]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04409 .

title: Develop Your Team’s Social Capital, Not Just Their Skills
abstract: High-performing employees who are tapped as potential leaders often don’t get the help they need building social capital in an organization. Although social capital is key to developing the influence future leaders will need to be effective, managers often prioritize providing experiences that build skills and job performance rather than making assignments that help individuals broaden their networks. Recent research offers lessons on how social capital is built and tends to operate in practice.

title: Impact Risk in Impact Investing: A Systematic Review of Impact Risk Drivers and Governance Responses and an Integrative Framework
abstract: ABSTRACT This study systematically reviews impact risk in impact investing to identify its dimensions, drivers, governance responses, and interrelationships. Drawing on a qualitative thematic analysis of 56 articles published between 2011 and 2025, the review integrates previously fragmented research on impact‐related risks. We define impact risk as risks arising from the pursuit, governance, measurement, and public claims about impact that threaten the realization, credibility, or social license of impact‐oriented investments. The findings identify five interrelated dimensions: positive impact risk, negative impact risk, impact evidence risk, impact accountability risk, and impact legitimacy risk. For each dimension, the review synthesizes its principal drivers and governance responses. The findings further show that these risks form an interdependent system characterized by risk amplification, risk conversion, and risk mutual reinforcement. The study contributes a five‐dimensional classification of impact risk and an integrative framework explaining how these risks interact, providing a foundation for examining impact risk as an interdependent governance problem.

title: Dynamic Capabilities, Digitalisation and Supply Chain Resilience for Sustainability: Evidence From Organisational Actors in an African Cotton Value Chain
abstract: ABSTRACT Supply chain resilience has become increasingly critical in turbulent environments, yet limited evidence exists on how dynamic capabilities and digitalisation jointly shape rlesilience and sustainability in resource‐constrained agricultural systems. This study addresses this gap by integrating Dynamic Capability Theory and Resilience Theory into a unified capability–resilience–sustainability framework and examining these relationships within Benin's cotton sector. Using survey data from 464 organisational actors operating across Benin's cotton value chain and a hybrid analytical approach combining PLS‐SEM, Random Forest, XGBoost and Monte Carlo simulation, the findings indicate that sensing, seizing and transforming capabilities significantly strengthen supply chain resilience, with transforming capability exerting the strongest influence. Supply chain resilience mediates the relationship between dynamic capabilities and economic, environmental and social performance, while the structural model explains 54% of the variance in resilience. Digital technology adoption strengthens the effects of sensing and transforming capabilities on resilience, whereas institutional support reinforces the contribution of seizing capability to sustainability performance. Machine‐learning analyses complement the structural model by identifying nonlinear and threshold‐based relationships that extend the SEM findings. The study contributes to the literature by providing evidence that resilience serves as the principal behavioural pathway through which dynamic capabilities support triple‐bottom‐line performance.

title: Game On or Game Over? The Influence of In-Game Advertising on Consumer Engagement
Relative Valuation, Risk Factors and Investment Strategies: An Empirical Study of Real Estate Industry in China
How Does the Global Financial Cycle Affect the Systemic Risk of Non-Financial Firms? Evidence from China
Civil Servants' Compliance with Conflict‐of‐Interest Regulation: Evidence from a List Experiment
abstract: ABSTRACT While regulatory governance scholarship has paid significant attention to the normative importance of ethics reform in government, empirical evidence on compliance remains scant. Drawing on insights from the social value activation model and behavioral ethics, this study examines civil servants' compliance propensity under conflict‐of‐interest regulation. Specifically, we examine how a legitimate ethics reform is associated with the voluntary compliance of two legally treated groups: those with policy implementation duties and those with frequent stakeholder engagement. The results of our list experiment with a representative sample of South Korean civil servants ( n = 1977) show that both target groups exhibit higher estimated compliance propensity with the second provision of the Act, restricted and prohibited actions, but that only policy implementation duties are associated with higher compliance propensity with the first provision, reporting and disclosure obligations. Our findings suggest that ethics reform compliance is shaped not only by formal rules and deterrence, but also by administrative role exposure, perceived legitimacy, and the value‐based dimension of civil servants.

title: The Rational Design of Space Agreements: How Bilateralism Shapes Powerful States' Design Preferences
abstract: ABSTRACT The global governance of outer space relies heavily on international agreements, yet the institutional forms of these agreements remain underexplored. This article introduces a new dataset on various design features of 952 space agreements, offering the first large‐N overview of institutional design in space governance. Building on rational design theory, this article analyzes how these design features interact with one another and with negotiation structures. Our results reveal systematic trade‐offs and suggest that power asymmetry has contrasting effects depending on the context: Powerful states tend to favor greater delegation, precision, and enforcement in bilateral agreements, while often resisting them in multilateral settings. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for both power dynamics and bilateralism, two contextual factors often overlooked in rational design theory. By making the dataset publicly available, the article seeks to foster further research on the causes and consequences of institutional variation in space governance and to advance comparative institutionalist scholarship across issue‐areas of global governance.

Restoration of Gut Microbiota Vertical Transmission by Bifidobacterium Mitigates Pollutant-Induced Intergenerational Obesity
abstract: Abstract Mass production and widespread distribution of environmental pollutants enhance human susceptibility to disease, which may be related to gut microbial communities. However, the link between the transgenerational toxic effects of environmental pollutants and animal gut microbial communities remains obscure. Here, we show that environmental dose p,p’-DDE (a typical environmental pollutant) exposure prepregnancy reshapes offspring metabolic homeostasis through vertical transmission of the maternal gut microbiota, inducing the development of obesity. In addition, by taking cross-sectional temporal sampling strategy, we show that Bifidobacterium, whose metabolic production of acetate can interfere with obesity by activating Gpr41 and Gpr43, is the key species responsible for this outcome. Supplementation of Bifidobacterium or acetate in dams or offspring reversed the obesity phenotype in offspring mice. Finally, we confirmed the mechanism by which p,p’-DDE induces oxidative stress to inhibit the growth of Bifidobacteriumin vitro, and this phenomenon was found to be mechanically applicable to a wider range of organochlorine pesticides. In conclusion, our study shows that p,p’-DDE can reshape offspring metabolic phenotype through selective vertical transmission of maternal gut microbiota, and maternal or offspring supplementation with Bifidobacterium may be a promising intervention.

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in Portuguese primary schools: Occurrence in air and implications for children's inhalation exposure
abstract: Background Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent environmental pollutants increasingly detected in indoor environments, yet information on PFAS in school settings remains scarce. Objective We characterized PFAS levels in primary school indoor air and estimated inhalation exposure among children and school staff. Methods We collected 36 indoor and 8 outdoor air samples from 8 primary schools in Porto (the second-largest city in Portugal) and analyzed them for 64 PFAS, including perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAAs) and PFAA precursors. Results PFAA precursors predominated over terminal PFAAs, accounting for 66.5% and 64.6% of total PFAS in indoor and outdoor air, respectively. Among PFAAs, perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCAs) were the dominant class in both indoor and outdoor air (median: 3822.3 and 495.1 pg/m 3 , respectively), whereas polyfluoroalkyl phosphate esters (PAPs; median: 2811.6 and 732.0 pg/m 3 ) and fluorotelomer alcohols (FTOHs; median: 1436.6 and 313.5 pg/m 3 ) were the predominant PFAA precursors. Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS), nonafluoro-3,6-dioxaheptanoic acid (NFDHA), di-sulfonamido polyfluoroalkyl phosphate (diSAmPAP), and 8:2 fluorotelomer alcohol (8:2 FTOH) were the major individual PFAS detected indoors. All PFAS classes showed indoor enrichment relative to outdoor air. Children had higher body-weight-normalized inhalation exposure than adults. Under the low-exposure scenario, FTOHs contributed most to total EDI, whereas PFCAs predominated under the high-exposure scenario. Conclusion Primary schools constitute important indoor microenvironments for PFAS exposure. Although PFAA precursors predominated in indoor air, PFAAs accounted for the largest share of estimated inhalation exposure under the high-exposure scenario, highlighting the importance of considering both PFAA precursors and PFAS in comprehensive exposure assessments.

title: Low-salt closed-loop management of secondary gallium resources: From selective recovery to high-purity upgrading
Microalgae-based bioremediation of heavy metals: Mechanisms, optimization, and environmental applications
abstract: Heavy metal (HM) contamination in aquatic environments remains a persistent global challenge driven by industrialization, mining activities, and agricultural runoff. Microalgae-based remediation has emerged as a sustainable and cost-effective technology, utilizing both passive surface biosorption and active intracellular bioaccumulation mechanisms. This review comprehensively synthesizes recent advances in microalgae-mediated HM removal by integrating mechanistic insights at molecular, cellular, and process aspects. The performance of dried, living, and chemically modified biomass is comparatively evaluated across major HMs, including Cd, Pb, Cr, Cu, Hg, Ni, Zn, and As, under varying operational conditions. Microalgae are categorized into four major phyla to comparatively evaluate their HM adsorption capacities. Quantitatively analysis indicates that biosorption onto cell surfaces is the predominant mechanism while bioaccumulation, i.e., the uptake of HM into cells, is in general secondary but in some cases substantial. Transporter-regulated uptake and intracellular detoxification mechanisms are also discussed. Kinetic, isotherm, and thermodynamic modeling approaches are examined comprehensively, despite recurring inconsistencies in model selection, parameter interpretation, and reporting practices in the literature. Adsorption enhancement strategies, including physical and physiological conditioning, chemical modification, immobilization, biofilm cultivation, and multi-species co-cultivation, are assessed for their roles in improving HM removal efficiency, regeneration stability, and system robustness. By bridging mechanistic understanding with engineering implementation, this review provides a comprehensive framework to advance microalgae-based HM remediation.

title: Membrane-covered composting systems with microbial inoculation enhance humification by shifting regulation toward microbially mediated transformation
Reevaluating the role of woody plants in rangelands: Implications for soil carbon and hydrological dynamics in rangelands
Green space exposure, mediators, and health in older adults: A systematic review
abstract: Rapid population ageing and increasing chronic disease burdens highlight the need to better integrate older adults' green space exposure into environmental and health impact assessment. However, current evidence is fragmented by inconsistent age definitions, reliance on static availability-based greenness metrics, and limited attention to mechanisms, vulnerability, and bias. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we systematically searched Web of Science and Scopus and included 117 studies on green-space exposure and health among older adults. Exposure metrics were grouped within an accessibility–availability–visibility (A–A–V) framework and examined together with environmental modifying factors, behavioral pathways, and health outcomes; keyword co-occurrence and clustering were used to map research foci. NDVI-based availability indicators dominate, while accessibility (e.g. distance, network/time-based access, public transport, street connectivity) and visibility (e.g. street-level greenness, Green View Index) measures are inconsistently defined and applied. Near-home green space and tree canopy are linked to light-to-moderate physical activity and reduced heat, air pollution, and noise exposure, with reported benefits across multiple health domains. We identify major gaps, including scarce dynamic exposure assessment, limited distributional and age-specific equity analyses, and inconsistent risk-of-bias evaluation. We propose an A–A–V indicator framework that links measurable exposure metrics, pathways, and age-relevant health endpoints, offering a practical basis for integrating older adults’ green space-related health into impact assessment and age-friendly urban planning.
