Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03801 .

title: Centralization vs. Decentralization: First Evidence from the Laboratory
abstract: The future architecture of financial systems is a subject of contention, with centralized and decentralized governance proponents. Here, we ask the following question. Would the architecture affect the quality of decision making? We propose a game where financial network participants demarcate the ownership of claims to income. This governance task can be decentralized (shared authority), centralized (single authority), or hybrid (alternating authority). Without communication, all architectures supported poor outcomes. With communication, decentralization ensured good governance and maximum profits, whereas centralization did not—lowering communication’s potency in promoting socially optimal decisions. This indicates that there is scope for decentralization in innovating financial institutions. This paper has been accepted by Camelia Kuhnen for the Virtual Special Issue on Digital Finance. Funding: N. Chemaya acknowledges partial financial support from the NET Institute. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02314 .

title: Rejected Applicant Reactions to Artificial Intelligence/Human Manager‐Based Recruitment
abstract: ABSTRACT The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in job recruitment has transformed recruitment practices. Little is known, however, about how applicants react to AI‐based rejection. Drawing on appraisal theory, we propose that applicants rejected by AI tend to appraise the rejection as others' responsibility, leading to negative emotions and adverse reactions against the organization. Using a person‐centered approach and mixed‐methods design in two studies, we identify four distinct profiles based on the combination of outward‐focused negative emotions (OFNE) and inward‐focused negative emotions (IFNE). Specifically, we argue and test that introducing a human manager to review AI‐based rejection can soothe rejected applicants. Our findings show that involving human touch can shift applicants' profiles, leading to better reactions toward the organization. Theoretical and practical implications for rejected applicant reactions in the context of AI‐based recruitment processes are discussed.

title: Green Innovation and the Nonlinear Productivity Value of Supply Chain Finance
abstract: ABSTRACT Although supply chain finance is often presented as a productivity‐enhancing financial arrangement, limited evidence examines whether its benefits persist as supply chain finance increases and whether green innovation transmits them. This study examines the nonlinear relationship between supply chain finance and total factor productivity using 34,785 firm‐year observations from 3386 Chinese A‐share‐listed firms from 2009 to 2024. Two‐way fixed‐effects estimations reveal an inverted U‐shaped relationship between supply chain finance and total factor productivity, with an inflection point at 0.296. A similar inverted U‐shaped relationship governs the relationship between supply chain finance and green innovation, peaking at 0.249. Green innovation is positively associated with total factor productivity and partially mediates the indirect effects of supply chain finance. The findings persist across alternative measures, 1‐ and 2‐year lags, additional fixed effects, placebo analysis and instrumental‐variable sensitivity tests. The productivity curve differs significantly between heavy‐polluting and nonheavy‐polluting industries.

title: Green Organizational System and Organizational Identification: The Roles of Career Ecological Fit and Environmental Concern
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how a green organizational system (GOS) shapes employees' organizational identification. Drawing on person‐environment fit theory and organizational identification research, we conceptualize GOS as a distinct system‐level construct comprising aligned green leadership, culture, and HRM practices. We argue that GOS provides coherent environmental cues that make sustainability commitments visible, credible, and relevant to employees' longer‐term career judgments. Accordingly, career ecological fit is the key psychological mechanism linking GOS to identification, and employees' environmental concern weakens this relationship because highly concerned employees rely more on internalized standards than organizational cues. Using a two‐wave, multi‐source survey of 366 matched employee–supervisor dyads across 55 subsidiaries of multinational enterprises in China, we find support for the hypothesized mediation and moderated effects. The study contributes by introducing GOS as a system‐level green management construct, identifying career ecological fit as its key mechanism, and specifying when these effects weaken.

title: Cultural Drivers of Circular Economy Performance: Examining When Green Supply Chain Integration and Organizational Culture Become Necessary
abstract: ABSTRACT Achieving circular economy performance (CEP) in resource‐constrained economies depends on the combined influence of organisational culture and green supply chain integration (GSCI). Although both have received increasing attention in the sustainability literature, little is known about how different organisational culture types interact with GSCI to enhance CEP. This study addresses this gap using the competing values framework (CVF) and analysing survey data collected from 311 managers of manufacturing SMEs. Partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS‐SEM) was used to examine the hypothesized relationships; necessary condition analysis (NCA) was employed to identify conditions that are essential for achieving CEP; and importance‐performance map analysis (IPMA) was conducted to identify improvement priorities. The findings reveal that apart from rational culture, the three cultural dimensions (developmental, group and hierarchical) significantly enhance CEP, with the model explaining 54.7% of CEP variance. Green internal integration and green customer integration also have significant positive effects on CEP, whereas green supplier integration does not. Furthermore, green internal integration significantly mediates the relationships between all four organisational culture types and CEP. The NCA results further identify developmental culture (d = 0.275), rational culture (d = 0.191), hierarchical culture (d = 0.160) and green internal integration (d = 0.146) as necessary conditions for achieving CEP. This study extends the application of the CVF to CE contexts in Sub‐Saharan Africa where empirical evidence is scarce. The study provides both theoretical understanding and practical guidance for improving circular economy performance among manufacturing SMEs.

title: Environmental Management System (ISO 14001) and Total‐Factor Carbon Emission Performance: A Two‐Stage Malmquist Data Envelopment Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT As global decarbonization goals become more urgent, it is vital to understand that decoupling carbon from growth is not a purely mechanical process of adopting green machines; it is a socio‐technical transition. Understanding carbon productivity requires analyzing the synergy between voluntary standards and strict regulation, demonstrating that technology only drives societal change when embedded in a robust institutional framework that prevents mere compliance. Therefore, this cross‐country panel study examines whether the diffusion of Environmental Management System (EMS) ISO 14001 is associated with improvements in total‐factor carbon emission performance in 15 countries with the highest ISO 14001 adoption intensity over 2010–2024, yielding a balanced panel of 210 country‐year observations. Using a two‐stage Malmquist Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) model, we decompose change in carbon performance into two critical vectors: change in efficiency (catch‐up effect) and technological change (frontier shift). The decomposition results indicate that, for most countries, 24% in carbon performance observed gains were more closely associated with efficiency catch‐up than with frontier‐shifting technological change. Meanwhile, Germany shows consistently shifted the carbon‐efficiency frontier during the study period. Moreover, panel regression analysis indicates that ISO 14001 adoption intensity remains conditionally associated with these improvements after controlling for energy intensity and industrial structure. This study contributes to the literature by demonstrating that management systems act as technology absorption mechanisms, enabling lagging nations to reach the frontier of existing best practices. Finally, the findings provide a forward‐looking basis suggesting that, without an acceleration in radical technological innovation (frontier‐shift), current efficiency efforts based on voluntary standards will be insufficient to achieve net‐zero emissions goals.

title: Environmental Regulation, Green Innovation, and Firm Competitiveness: A Conditional Innovation Pathway From Selected MENA Manufacturing
abstract: ABSTRACT Environmental regulation is increasingly viewed as a catalyst for innovation and strategic upgrading, yet its effectiveness in emerging economies remains uncertain. This study examines the association between environmental regulation, green innovation, and firm competitiveness in the manufacturing sectors of five selected Middle East and North Africa (MENA) economies between 2010 and 2023. Building on the Porter hypothesis, institutional theory, and the resource‐based view, the analysis develops an integrated conditional innovation framework linking environmental regulation, green innovation, and firm competitiveness under varying levels of institutional quality and firm‐level innovation capability. Using fixed‐effects and dynamic common correlated effects mean group (DCCE–MG) estimators, the results indicate that environmental regulation is positively associated with green innovation, while green innovation is positively associated with firm competitiveness. Mediation analysis suggests that green innovation represents the principal pathway linking environmental regulation and firm performance, while firm‐level innovation capability and institutional quality strengthen this relationship. Quantile estimates further reveal that these associations are more pronounced among innovation‐intensive firms, suggesting heterogeneous and capability‐dependent responses across the firm distribution. Overall, the findings suggest that well‐designed and credibly enforced environmental regulation is associated with stronger innovation and competitiveness outcomes within supportive institutional environments. Given the observational nature of the data, these findings should be interpreted as conditional empirical associations rather than conclusive evidence of causal effects. The study contributes to the literature by extending the Porter mechanism to resource‐dependent and institutionally diverse settings and offers policy‐relevant insights that may inform low‐carbon industrial transformation strategies in selected MENA economies.

title: Strategic Silence? Mandatory Sustainability Disclosure and the Discipline of Corporate Over‐Claiming Under the European Union Non‐Financial Reporting Directive
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether mandatory sustainability disclosure under the European Union Non‐Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD) reduces corporate greenwashing among listed European firms, with a focus on the 500‐employee compliance threshold. We conceptualise greenwashing as strategic decoupling between sustainability communication (talk) and environmental performance (walk). Using merged LSEG Workspace and Orbis data, we estimate a local sharp regression discontinuity design around a predetermined 2016 employment baseline, focusing on 2019–2025 when the key variables are sufficiently observed. Crossing the threshold is associated with a robust decline in a residual‐based excess‐talk measure. Evidence for a standardised talk–walk gap is directionally similar but less precise. Decomposition tests show that the discontinuity sits on the communication side: firms above the threshold reduce sustainability claims, while emissions‐related performance does not exhibit a comparable short‐run shift. We do not detect significant local moderation by external monitoring or organisational complexity, nor statistically significant short‐horizon discontinuities in ESG controversies, valuation, or cost of capital. The evidence is consistent with a sequencing effect in which disclosure pressure disciplines over‐claiming before it produces observable operational change or downstream market consequences.

title: Resolving the Carbon—Performance Paradox: Global Evidence on Stakeholder Engagement, Risk and Institutions
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how greenhouse gas emissions influence corporate performance and explains why prior evidence on the carbon–performance relationship has remained inconsistent. Drawing on institutional, stakeholder and slack resource perspectives, the study investigates the direct effects of carbon intensity and emissions reduction (efficiency) on return on capital employed, return on assets and Tobin's Q, while assessing the moderating roles of stakeholder engagement and idiosyncratic risk. Using a global panel of 3070 publicly listed firms from Europe, North America, Asia‐Pacific and Africa between 2014 and 2023, the analysis employs dynamic System GMM to address endogeneity, persistence and firm‐level heterogeneity. The findings show that carbon intensity is positively associated with market valuation and capital efficiency in capital‐intensive contexts, whereas emissions reduction tends to generate short‐term performance costs. Stakeholder engagement and firm‐specific risk significantly shape these relationships, revealing that the financial consequences of decarbonisation depend on credibility, risk exposure and institutional context. Cross‐regional analyses confirm that the valuation of carbon performance varies systematically across regulatory and market environments. The study contributes to the literature by identifying boundary conditions that explain divergent findings on carbon performance and offers practical implications for managers, investors and policymakers seeking to align decarbonisation strategies with long‐term value creation.

title: Does ESG reduce hospitality firms’ cost of debt? Roles of information asymmetric and internal control quality
How digital human capital investment drives AI innovation in tourism and hospitality firms: The roles of data assets and TMT stability
From benevolent leadership to environmental citizenship in the hospitality sector: an affective commitment mediated pathway
abstract: Purpose This paper aimed to propose and test a research model that investigated the nexus between benevolent leadership (BL), affective commitment (AC) and organizational citizenship behavior for the environment (OCBE) in the hospitality sector. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 372 hotel employees in Poland via a computer-assisted Web interview technique. The hypothesized relationships were gauged using the partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings BL boosted AC, which subsequently predicted OCBE. BL affected OCBE via affective internalization of employees’ emotional attachment to the organization instead of through direct behavioral modeling. Originality/value This study adds to the leadership–sustainability research by demonstrating that BL, a non-environmental leadership style, relates to OCBE through employees’ AC, rather than through a direct link. The results underscore AC as a significant internalization mechanism that connects moral leadership with context-specific environmental citizenship rather than direct behavioral relationship.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: The Influence of Brand–Game Congruity in the Promotional Phase of Advergames: The Role of Perceived Legitimacy
abstract: Advergames—video games created by brands to convey their message—are continuously used in advertising. As voluntary entertainment experiences, their success depends on both in-game engagement and pre-play promotion. This research examines how brand–game congruity influences consumer responses in the promotional phase. Three experimental studies explore the role of three types of brand–game congruity: advertising, image, and lifestyle congruity. The combined findings establish that high congruity strengthens perceived legitimacy, leading to more favorable attitudes and behavioral responses to both the brand and the game, prior to the game experience. These insights offer relevant managerial implications for optimizing both advergame promotions and advertising effectiveness.

title: Moonlighting and the transition to full-time entrepreneurship
abstract: Abstract This paper examines the transition from moonlighting to full-time self-employment using panel data from the Survey of Income and Program Participation. Motivations for moonlighting vary—from financial necessity to entrepreneurial experimentation—and these motivations shape the likelihood of transitioning. The paper finds moonlighters with higher moonlighting income and weaker attachment to their primary job are more likely to become self-employed. Access to employer-provided health insurance inhibits transition, and marriage allows for risk-sharing which promotes entry. Understanding the nuanced pathways from moonlighting to self-employment offers critical insight for designing policies that lower barriers and support entrepreneurial growth.

title: Boredom and psychological well-being among the self-employed
abstract: Abstract Individuals not only seek a happy and meaningful life, but an interesting rather than a boring one. In this paper, we analyze data from 19,000 individuals across 25 European countries to demonstrate that self-employment is associated with modestly lower boredom on average—a relationship that is not captured by traditional measures of hedonic or eudaimonic well-being. The negative association between self-employment and boredom is small but robust across broad sectors, significantly stronger among those with ten or more employees, and similar in size to the associations between self-employment and life satisfaction or meaning in life. While this association is not restricted to low-income individuals, the data do not allow strong conclusions about whether this association generalizes to high-income employees. We replicate our main findings in a separate sample of 1000 US participants. Using this sample, we also show that our main results are not driven by individuals with lower boredom proneness self-selecting into self-employment. Taken together, our results suggest that prior research has overlooked an important dimension of the relationship between self-employment and well-being.

title: Adolescents’ entrepreneurial or employment intention for individualistic and communal business purposes
abstract: Abstract Adolescents today are increasingly more agentic and more communal than prior cohorts and want social and environmental change. When contemplating an occupation to provide them with income and self-actualization, they face a concurrent choice between employment and self-employed entrepreneurship and between individualistic (profit and work satisfaction) and communalistic (social impact and environmental restoration) business purposes. Employment choices may be restricted by high local unemployment, automation, and artificial intelligence. Noting that entrepreneurial behavior can be pursued independently or as an employee, their occupational choices include starting a firm or joining a firm as an employee (and acting entrepreneurially or not). We study the determinants of their occupational intentions and find bespoke configurations of their personal and parental characteristics that culminate in their occupational intention and their preferred combination of business purposes. Interestingly, most of the sampled adolescents did not exhibit traditional gender role expectations, males were mostly communalistic in their preferred business purposes, and no group of females sought profit as their primary business purpose. This paper contributes to the literatures on entrepreneurial intention, adolescent development, and parental influence on adolescent choice with implications for policy, education, and research.

title: Subsidy for the first hires and firm performance
From approval to routine use: the two-stage technology transfer of new drugs in U.S. clinical practice
Fostering managers’ trust in performance measurement systems through business intelligence: a longitudinal case study
abstract: This paper explores whether and how the adoption of business intelligence solutions promotes managers’ trust in performance measurement systems by enhancing the use of the information these systems provide. The analysis was conducted through a longitudinal case study of an Italian company, using empirical material collected via non-participant observation, document analysis, and interviews with managers. The findings were interpreted using a theoretical framework that combines three studies on organisational trust. This approach enabled a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between business intelligence solutions and managers’ trust in performance measurement systems, focusing not only on outcomes but also on antecedents and the processes through which trust develops. The results show that business intelligence solutions can play a pivotal role in structuring and mobilising trust relationships between managers and performance measurement systems. However, such relationships do not emerge automatically as a result of adopting more advanced technological tools. The technical advancements associated with business intelligence solutions are not, in themselves, sufficient to stimulate the degree of perceived ability, benevolence, and integrity that is essential for structuring a trust relationship between managers and performance measurement systems. Rather, the case study shows that trust unfolds as the outcome of a multidimensional, gradual, and dynamic process in which technical advancements must be combined with organisational and individual factors. These factors collectively encourage managers to accept vulnerability and engage in risk-taking behaviours, such as relying on information provided by systems they previously did not trust.

title: Signal or Solution? Unlocking the Power of Dividends in Mitigating Corporate Default Risk in China
abstract: The relationship between dividend policy and corporate risk has attracted significant attention. We extend this literature by examining how cash dividend distribution affects debt default risk through its role in mitigating agency conflicts. We find that both the presence of cash dividends and higher payout ratios significantly reduce corporate debt default risk, with signalling and internal governance serving as the key mediating mechanisms. Further analyses reveal that this risk‐reduction effect strengthens with macroeconomic uncertainty, operational risk, weak managerial incentives, a high interest‐bearing debt ratio, and among non‐mature firms. Moreover, the interaction between cash dividend distribution and debt default risk significantly promotes a shift toward a longer‐term debt maturity structure. We further demonstrate that the strategic choice of dividend policy has significant implications for corporate risk management and firm value.

title: Do auditors care about firms’ engagement in blockchain? Evidence from auditors’ responses
abstract: Purpose This study examines how auditors respond to firms' disclosed blockchain engagement. While the technology offers potential efficiency gains, it also introduces new risks and complexity. We investigate whether and how auditors use audit pricing and auditor resignation as their strategies to manage blockchain-related risks. Design/methodology/approach This study uses a large sample of Chinese A-share listed companies spanning 2016 to 2022. We extract data regarding corporate blockchain engagement by conducting textual analysis on firms’ publicly disclosed reports. Regression analysis is applied to verify the research hypotheses, followed by a series of robustness tests. In addition, we carry out cross-sectional tests and examine auditors’ responses to distinct categories of blockchain-related activities. We further investigate the relative priority of auditors’ risk management strategies and identify potential channels. Findings There is a positive relation between firms’ disclosed blockchain engagement and audit fees. This relation is more pronounced among larger audit firms, auditors without an information technology (IT) background and those with shorter tenures. Both audit effort and audit risk serve as two plausible channels linking companies’ engagement in blockchain to increased audit fees. Firms engaging in blockchain to facilitate management processes, rather than provide blockchain-related products or services, are associated with elevated audit fees. Although blockchain engagement is also related to a higher likelihood of auditor resignation, we observe a hierarchical pattern in auditor responses, with fee adjustments being the more prevalent initial reaction relative to resignation. Research limitations/implications Our disclosure-based measure may not fully distinguish the depth of adoption, investor-facing signaling or strategic narrative because doing so would require obtaining in-depth blockchain data from the sample firms. This is highly challenging as such data are not subject to mandatory disclosure by regulators and may constitute corporate confidential information. Our findings should be interpreted as auditors’ responses to “perceived blockchain-related risks” rather than a direct response to “the adoption of blockchain technology.” Practical implications First, for audit firms, our results underscore the importance of investing in technological training and developing firm-level expertise in emerging technologies such as blockchain. The finding that the fee premium is concentrated among auditors without IT backgrounds suggests that audit firms that proactively build technological competence may be better positioned to serve clients engaging with new technologies while managing their own costs. Second, for corporate managers, our findings alert them that public blockchain engagement, even when disclosed for strategic signaling purposes, may carry tangible costs in the form of higher audit fees, particularly when blockchain is deployed for internal management processes. This cost should be factored into firms’ cost–benefit analyses when making blockchain investment decisions. Third, for regulators and standard-setters, the heterogeneity in auditor responses documented in our study highlights the need for clearer accounting and auditing guidance for blockchain-based transactions, which would reduce the uncertainty that currently drives elevated audit pricing. Originality/value This study provides evidence consistent with auditors strategically adapting to technological disruptions in their risk management practices. The study offers timely and practical insights for auditors, regulators and corporate managers as blockchain applications continue to proliferate.

title: Understanding cross-platform dynamics in digital music consumption: A panel VAR approach
The social cost of free: service robots, anticipatory indebtedness, and free-trial acceptance
Building brand awareness or driving sales? How influencers’ campaign intent shapes consumer engagement with sponsored posts
Driverless, not thoughtless? Automated vehicle regulation, the dilemma of control, and the prospect of dual corrigibility
abstract: When regulating emerging technologies, authorities must balance available knowledge, means for control, and desirable directions of development. The article asks which normative orientation guides Norway's automated vehicle regulation, how the regulation is configured, and whether this regulatory strategy aligns with the underpinning normative orientation. To answer these questions, the article analyses the policy-making process preceding Norway's Act Relating to Testing of Self-Driving Vehicles, the content of the finalised Act, and interview data from the first automated vehicle trial conducted after the Act's effectuation. The article shows that Norway pursues a two-stage regulatory strategy. During the first stage, interested parties may organise automated vehicle trials; during the second stage, the state will establish a permanent regulation for automated vehicles. This two-stage strategy builds upon the untenable assumption that practical concerns regarding a technology's functioning can be addressed separately from normative concerns. Drawing upon David Collingridge's writings on the dilemma of control, the article argues that practical and normative concerns must be processed in parallel and suggests dual corrigibility – corrigibility of decisions and corrigibility of orientation – as a guiding principle for regulating emerging technologies.

title: Campaign success and activity-system contradictions in livestream influencer marketing
abstract: Purpose Livestream influencer marketing (LSIM) differs from traditional influencer marketing in its real-time selling format, team-based operations and sales-driven integration with e-commerce. Despite LSIM’s rapid growth and importance for e-commerce, emerging research has generally favoured consumer perspectives. The purpose of this paper is to respond to calls for supply-side research by examining the LSIM operational environment, campaign success factors as perceived by livestream influencers (LSIs) and multi-channel network (MCN) team members, and contradictions within LSI–MCN collaborative operations. Design/methodology/approach This mixed-method study draws on activity theory. Sixty-five in-depth interviews were conducted primarily with LSIs and MCN team members; supplementary interviews with five brand sponsors, three platform providers and five viewers enabled triangulation. Survey responses from 112 LSIs and 100 MCN team members engaged with China’s four leading LSIM platforms were also analysed. Findings Results reveal a dynamic LSIM activity system involving interactions among LSIs, MCN team members, tools, culture and policies. Prominent factors in LSIM campaign success, from LSIs’ and MCN team members’ perspectives, include influencer capabilities, LSI–MCN coordination and platform strategies. A two-phase design (2021 and 2024) shows how LSIs and MCN team members respond to activity-system contradictions through adaptive strategies. Research limitations/implications Future research should confirm this study’s results across diverse contexts (e.g. platforms, brand categories and countries). Practical implications Findings offer strategic recommendations for LSIs and MCN teams with respect to capability development, collaboration models and policy implementation. These recommendations can promote sustainable industry performance while addressing inherent contradictions. Originality/value Addressing limited supply-side LSIM research, this study explores LSIs’ and MCN team members’ perspectives on LSIM campaign success factors and how contradictions are managed through adaptive strategies.

title: When Managing Time Comes at a Cost: A Cross‐Role Resource Tradeoff Perspective on Team Temporal Leadership
abstract: ABSTRACT While team temporal leadership (TL) has been widely regarded as beneficial for team functioning, existing research has largely overlooked the potential resource costs underlying these benefits. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, we conceptualize TL as a form of leader resource investment that may create a cross‐role resource tradeoff between leader costs and follower benefits. Using two multiwave, multisource field studies, we examine how TL shapes resource dynamics that ultimately influence the task performance of both leaders and followers. Study 1 indicates that TL increases leaders' emotional exhaustion while reducing followers' emotional exhaustion, thereby shaping their respective task performance. Moreover, the beneficial effects of TL on follower outcomes are stronger under higher team task complexity. To unpack this tradeoff, we further theorize mental effort and process clarity as two micromechanisms. Study 2 shows that team task complexity does not moderate the effect of TL on leaders' mental effort but strengthens the effect of TL on leaders' process clarity, with downstream implications for their emotional exhaustion and performance. Team task complexity also strengthens TL's effects in reducing followers' mental effort and enhancing their process clarity. Overall, these findings suggest that team task complexity primarily amplifies the benefits rather than the costs of TL, making TL a more favorable resource investment when team tasks are more complex. This study advances TL research by uncovering its underlying resource tradeoff and clarifying how it is shaped by cognitive processes and contextual demands.

title: Rules in the light, voices in the dark: exploring pressures and exploitation disclosure behaviour in ready-made garment suppliers
abstract: Purpose The study aims to examine how macro-level pressures drive the adoption of modern slavery prevention mechanisms (MSPMs), how meso-level organisational contextual factors shape their effectiveness, and how MSPMs, in turn, influence micro-level (non)disclosure behaviour of workers at ready-made garment suppliers in Bangladesh. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative research design and an abductive approach were employed in this study. Data were collected through 45 semi-structured interviews with workers, managers, trade union representatives, lawyers, and non-governmental organisation officers, and were complemented by secondary sources. The analysis drew on institutional theory and the theory of planned behaviour to explore macro-level pressures, meso-level organisational contextual factors, and micro-level workers' exploitation (non)disclosure behaviour. Findings The study shows that macro-level pressures such as market access, professional legitimacy, and competitiveness drive suppliers to adopt MSPMs, including grievance and preventive policies, digitalised systems, and training programmes. However, meso-level organisational contextual factors (weak management commitment, cost and time pressures, and fragmented control across supply chains) undermine their effectiveness, resulting in symbolic implementation of MSPMs. At the micro-level, these symbolic MSPMs shape workers' socio-psychological conditions, manifested in negative attitudes, unsupportive social norms, and low perceived behavioural control, leading to non-disclosure behaviour of exploitation. Originality/value This study develops a multi-level framework and empirical explanation of MSPMs by demonstrating how symbolic implementation at the meso-level translates macro-level pressures into micro-level non-disclosure behaviour through workers' socio-psychological conditions. In doing so, it extends the focus of both research and practice from the adoption of MSPMs to their effectiveness in supply chains.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: The Passenger’s Dilemma: Rethinking Consumer Responsibility for Autonomous Machine Behavior
From Symbolic Compliance to Green Transition: The Green Shield Program and Corporate Green Fraud
abstract: This study analyzes the effect of environmental regulation on corporate green fraud using China’s Green Shield Program as a quasi-natural experiment. Adopting a staggered difference-in-differences (DID) approach, we find that the Green Shield Program is positively associated with green fraud of firms in nature reserves. Further analyses of economic consequences reveal that green fraud is correlated with short-term reputation improvement and alleviated financing constraints, as well as long-term corporate green innovation. Heterogeneity analyses indicate that the positive relationship between the Green Shield Program and green fraud is more pronounced for firms with higher executive green cognition, greater analyst coverage, and stricter environmental supervision.

title: Digital Trade Rule Network Status and Energy Resilience: Evidence from 110 Economies
abstract: Global digital trade rules are evolving from fragmented treaty provisions into networked governance arrangements with potential implications for energy security and sustainable transitions. Using panel data for 110 economies from 2000 to 2023, this study estimates the effect of digital trade rule network status on energy resilience with two-way fixed-effects, robustness checks, instrumental‑variable estimations, mechanism, heterogeneity, and regional-competition analyses. Higher network status significantly improves energy resilience. The effect operates through stronger cross-border information flows, institutional coordination, and international technology absorption, and varies across provision types, income levels, digital infrastructure, and energy poverty. Regional competition also matters: a “shielding effect” can strengthen network benefits, whereas a “dilution effect” can weaken them, depending on rule compatibility and agreement timing. These findings highlight digital trade rule networks as institutional channels for strengthening energy resilience. Developing and emerging economies should coordinate gradual rule integration with domestic capacity building, while those facing severe energy poverty should prioritize basic energy access and essential digital infrastructure.

title: Can Digital Financial Inclusion Reduce Child Mortality? A Cross-Country Analysis
Firm Size and Momentum Returns: The Roles of Analyst Coverage and Herding Behavior
abstract: ABSTRACT Momentum strategies have historically generated excess returns, but their effectiveness noticeably deteriorated in the post‐pandemic period, especially in 2022–23. In this paper, we explore how changes in investor attention during and after the COVID‐19 pandemic may have altered the performance of momentum strategies. Specifically, we investigate the relationship between firm size and momentum returns, focusing on two behavioural channels through which attention shifts might operate: Analyst coverage and herding behaviour. We apply a 6‐month ranking and holding momentum strategy across ten groups of firms (based on market capitalization). The portfolios are further segmented by three analyst coverage classes (measured by the number of covering analysts) and five herding quintiles (measured by trading volume and turnover ratio). We find that momentum strategies are more effective in smaller stocks and insignificantly negative in larger stocks. Lower analyst coverage in smaller firms is associated with higher momentum returns. Stocks with a low level of herding tend to generate higher momentum returns compared to those with a medium or higher level of herding.

title: Monetary Policy and Banking Operations: Does Ownership Matter?
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines how monetary‐policy deviations from country‐specific Taylor‐rule benchmarks are associated with bank insolvency risk and profitability, and how ownership and liability‐side funding conditions shape these responses. Using a large cross‐country panel of commercial banks, we show that tighter‐than‐expected monetary policy is related to lower bank insolvency risk. The profitability response is positive on average, but smaller and more sensitive to specification and shock measurement. Monetary tightening also increases banks’ cost of funds, providing evidence of a liability‐side funding‐price channel. Ownership shapes monetary‐policy transmission at both the bank and system levels: the marginal risk response becomes weaker as foreign ownership increases, while a greater system‐wide prevalence of state‐controlled banks reduces the risk‐reducing effect of monetary tightening. Decomposition results indicate that the risk response operates primarily through lower earnings volatility rather than changes in capitalization. These findings remain broadly robust across alternative shock measures, alternative bank outcomes, macroprudential and crisis controls and country‐balanced weighted regressions.

title: Legal Corruption in the Government: An Experimental Study on the Role of Civil Servants' Political Ideology
abstract: ABSTRACT Legal corruption, also known as institutional corruption, has become prevalent in the public sector, but empirical research on this subject is still at a nascent stage. Given its potentially detrimental impact on the perceived level of organizational capacity among internal members, understanding civil servants' views of legal corruption is essential. We contribute to this literature a discussion of civil servants' assessment of legal corruption in the government and evidence from a survey experiment with more than 2000 South Korean civil servants. The results of our analysis suggest that civil servants evaluate the degree of legal corruption in the government through their political lens, that is, their political ideology. Specifically, they tend to be more critical when the government is ruled by a chief executive and party that have different political views from their own, compared to when it is governed by those with the same political views. The implications of this study are clear: the central role of political views and policy preferences in understanding perceptions of legal corruption in the public sector.

title: Contract, Labour Law and the Realities of Working Life
Beyond monolithic state logic: how top-down accountability shapes policy implementation
abstract: How does top-down accountability shape policy implementation? Drawing on institutional logics, this paper distinguishes two state sub-logics: ‘high-stakes context logic’ emphasizing centralized control during crises, and ‘routine governance logic’ allowing discretion during day-to-day administration. These sub-logics condition the perceived legitimacy of accountability demands, felt accountability, and behavioural responses. A survey experiment with over 800 public service respondents shows that, under high-stakes logic, intensified accountability progressively improve compliance, whereas under routine logic, moderate accountability produces optimal compliance, with high-intensity accountability yielding diminishing returns. These findings challenge binary views of accountability and reveal how within-logic variations may alter governance mechanisms.

title: Gender inequality at the street level explained: redoing gender through informal practices
abstract: This study examines whether gendered differences in discretion shape inequality among street-level bureaucrats (SLBs). Focusing on the provision of informal personal resources (IFRs) to clients, we analyzed 59 in-depth interviews with social workers in Israel. While both women and men engage in extensive informal practices, their scope and form differ. Two mechanisms drive the reproduction of inequality: invisibility versus visibility of IFRs, and boundary setting between personal and professional spheres. These findings reveal that discretion in implementation not only is gendered but also reproduces conventional hierarchies, intensifying gender inequality at the street level of public administration.

title: Contingent capacity: navigating organizational dependency in Dutch municipal energy transitions
abstract: Municipalities implementing energy transition mandates rely on contingent workers to fill capacity and expertise gaps, raising concerns about dependency and knowledge loss. Drawing on Resource Dependence Theory and client–consultant literature, this study develops a framework capturing the feedback loop between external reliance and internal capacity development. Fifteen interviews across six Dutch municipalities show that labour shortages and temporary subsidies drive contingent hiring, while short contracts and limited knowledge transfer heighten dependency. Municipalities facing similar constraints diverge through knowledge integration, governance arrangements, and relational dynamics. It advances public administration scholarship by conceptualising dependency as a process rather than structural outcome.

title: Digital resilience in delivering public services. A conceptual model
Government institutions and data custodianship over personal information: Comparing citizen preferences in Hong Kong and South Korea
abstract: Public administration researchers traditionally approach the use of personal information in public service through the lens of direct user control, but a combination of cognitive constraints and rapid digitization has made privacy-preserving choices exceedingly difficult for citizens to manage independently. Recent research has shifted toward the notion of “data custodianship”, where public institutions serve as custodians of personal information. In a survey experiment conducted in Hong Kong ( n = 1031) and South Korea ( n = 1040), citizens evaluated their trust in various institutions serving as custodians tasked with managing biometric information for facial recognition. The findings suggest that while institutional trust can be influenced by accountability mechanisms, it is also shaped by individuals' experiences with public institutions, as well as their political orientation, social trust, and privacy preferences. Trust in one functional domain of data custodianship—such as data collection—may not carry over to others, like storage or management. Custodianship is only viable as a policy alternative to user control in data-intensive solutions if its design accounts for variation in public trust across societies, individuals, and aspects of data governance.

title: Disparity in Police Disciplinary Outcomes: The Mediating Effect of Complaint Disposition for Organizational Outgroups
abstract: In response to demands for greater police accountability, many departments have adopted policies designed to better regulate the use of force and to make it easier to investigate and punish officers accused of wrongdoing. While not widespread, there is some evidence that these changes have increased disciplinary actions. However, it remains uncertain whether police discipline has been applied equitably across racial and gender groups within departments. Drawing on multiple bodies of scholarship, we develop the expectation that, because of their status as members of organizational outgroups, Black, Hispanic and female officers are likely to be disciplined at higher rates. Importantly, we also argue that racial, ethnic and gender differences in disciplinary outcomes are at least partially mediated by the way in which police departments treat complaints against these officers. We test these hypotheses in data from Chicago's Civilian Office of Police Accountability (COPA) from 1971 through 2018. Analyses of over 249,000 allegations indicate that female and Black officers and officers face a higher likelihood of reprimand and suspension compared to White male officers. Differences across these groups are entirely explained, however, by the greater likelihood that complaints against these officers are deemed sufficiently supported by evidence to warrant disciplinary action. We conclude by discussing the broader implications for understanding employee discipline and the potential impact of recent efforts to enhance police accountability.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Negotiating Presence: The Dynamics of Passive Representation Among Ultra‐Orthodox Women in Public Organizations
abstract: ABSTRACT Studies in representative bureaucracy have focused on whether passive representation translates into active representation. We shift this analytical lens by conceptualizing passive representation not as a static demographic condition or a preliminary stage, but as a dynamic organizational process. Drawing on 15 in‐depth interviews and a focus group with 14 ultra‐Orthodox women serving in mid‐ and senior‐level public positions in Israel, we examine how passive representation is enacted, negotiated, and gradually institutionalized in male‐dominated settings. Findings show how women's underrepresentation structures their entry and advancement through informal expectations and gendered networks, and how women “negotiate presence” by building legitimacy through heightened professionalism, creative networking in the face of gender segregation, and strategic engagement with supportive leaders. Through mentoring and gate‐opening practices, our participants created ripple effects that increased access for others over time. We argue that passive representation is a relational and evolving mechanism shaped by role interpretations and organizational constraints, reshaping access and participation even without formal policy changes.

title: The accuracy of survey measures on political activity on Facebook. Evidence from a data donation study
abstract: Self-reported survey measures of social media use are commonly used across disciplines, yet the validity of findings in this area depends heavily on the accuracy of these reports. In political communication research, measurement error in reported online political behavior can distort estimates of media effects and lead to misleading conclusions about online political engagement. To address this concern, our study leveraged donated digital trace data from 758 Hungarian Facebook users and compared it with responses to standard survey questions provided by the same individuals. In addition, in a pre-registered experiment, we varied the ordering of the survey items. Our findings reveal moderate correlations between self-reported and actual digital behavior. General items showed closer alignment with observed behavior than self-reports of specific political activities. Participants typically underestimated their general Facebook activities and overestimated their political engagement on Facebook. Importantly, some of this discrepancy may stem not from respondents’ inaccuracy but from difficulties in classifying digital actions as politically relevant. Survey measures were more reliable in the general-specific questionnaire design and among individuals with high political interest. We discuss potential avenues for improving survey-based measures and emphasize the need for further research to address the methodological challenges associated with the use of digital trace data.

title: Deriving and validating a new modified two-dimensional surrogate safety measure to investigate driving risk across different passenger vehicle types
Understanding the resistance to trauma-informed care: The emotional, relational and ideological challenges of shifting power dynamics in child and youth residential care
abstract: BACKGROUND: Trauma-informed care (TIC) is a relational approach emphasizing safety, attunement, and collaboration. In child and youth residential care, this orientation sits in tension with longstanding compliance-oriented approaches that rely on rigid systems of incentives and consequences to guide behaviour. OBJECTIVE: This study examines how residential care staff experience the challenges of shifting power dynamics during the transition from compliance-oriented approaches toward relational practice during TIC implementation. PARTICIPANTS AND SETTING: The study was conducted in a large urban child and youth residential care agency in Québec, Canada. Participants included staff across roles and organizational levels. METHODS: Using a constructivist grounded theory design, data were generated through 17 in-depth interviews with staff, 45 h of participant observation of trainings, clinical support sessions, and leadership meetings, and analysis of institutional and implementation documents. RESULTS: Analysis produced five interrelated theoretical categories characterizing the challenges experienced during TIC implementation: (1) perceptions of TIC as "too permissive," (2) destabilization associated with relinquishing punishment without concrete alternatives, (3) the emotional and relational challenge of "looking inward" through self-regulation and accountability, (4) an unspoken taboo around naming power, control, and compliance, and (5) a gap between intellectual buy-in and embodied practice under pressure. CONCLUSIONS: Ideological resistance to TIC implementation emerged through concerns that its relational approach was overly permissive. Letting go of compliance-oriented approaches without clear enough relational alternatives often left staff feeling unsafe and helpless. Meaningful TIC implementation requires confronting punitive and childist belief systems, supporting deep self-reflection, and investing in experiential learning, supervision, and organizational conditions that sustain relational practice.

title: Clusters of out-of-home care trajectories and precarious school-to-work transitions: A Norwegian national register study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Trajectories through child protection services involving out-of-home care (OHC) are diverse, yet studies of OHC and school-to-work transitions often overlook this heterogeneity. METHODS: Using monthly records for three complete Norwegian birth cohorts (1994-1996; N = 172,638), we identified five OHC trajectory clusters among individuals with OHC before age 18 (N = 4789). These clusters were based on placement timing, duration and type. Individuals without OHC were included as a non-OHC group. We examined how cluster membership, together with care instability, is associated with precarious school-to-work transitions using linear regression models. RESULTS: The adolescent residential care cluster has higher school-to-work precarity scores than the kinship care (b = -0.14, p < .001), foster care from teenage years (b = -0.04, p < .001), foster care from young age (b = -0.14, p < .001) and non-OHC (b = -0.31, p < .001) clusters. This pattern appears despite the adolescent residential care cluster having the least turbulent OHC trajectories among the OHC groups, suggesting that low turbulence does not necessarily indicate sustained or protective support. CONCLUSION: OHC experiences should not be treated as a simple "in care" versus "not in care" dichotomy, but as heterogeneous patterns. Quantitative child welfare research should pay greater attention to the timing, duration, type and stability of care.

title: The Interplay of Partners’ Dyadic Empathic Abilities and Their Associations with Sexual Satisfaction and Desire in Young Adult Couples
abstract: Past studies highlight the significant associations between dyadic empathy and a range of relationship outcomes, with recent research suggesting that higher levels of dyadic empathy are linked to greater sexual satisfaction and desire. However, studies focusing on couples rather than individuals remain scarce, and the interaction between both partners' dyadic empathic abilities in association with sexual outcomes has yet to be explored. This study used a dyadic design with an inclusive sample of 190 young adult couples to investigate (1) both partners' dyadic empathy and (2) their interaction in association with sexual satisfaction and dyadic sexual desire. Dyadic empathy, sexual satisfaction and dyadic sexual desire were assessed via self-report questionnaires. Results indicated that individuals' higher levels of dyadic empathy were associated with their own greater sexual satisfaction and dyadic sexual desire, as well as with their partner's greater sexual satisfaction. However, dyadic empathy was not significantly associated with partners' dyadic sexual desire. No significant interaction effects were found between partners' dyadic empathy. Sensitivity analyses using the perspective-taking subscale yielded a comparable pattern of findings for sexual satisfaction, but not for dyadic sexual desire.

title: Study Protocol Packages and Threats to Validity
abstract: ). Media effects scholars are quite cognizant of various research protocol threats to validity, thinking extensively about their selection of measures, methods, and data analysis tactics. They may pay less attention to how the protocol package aspects of their studies could pose validity threats, however. Using a recent study's recruitment and informed consent documents as illustration, this letter describes a specific and serious protocol package-based validity threat in media effects research. We encourage our fellow sexuality scholars, those interested in media effects and beyond, to think as much about potential protocol package validity threats as they do other aspects of their research designs.

title: Impact of Repeated Negative Affective Social Media Content on Acceptability of the IUD
abstract: Access to safe and effective contraception is important for the advancement of public health and feminist goals. Unfortunately, social media harbors negative content about contraceptives, specifically the intrauterine device (IUD). Viewing this content repeatedly may deter people from considering IUDs. Value-centered decision-making about contraceptives requires that people are not unduly pressured or biased by external sources. Social media may bias people by overrepresenting negative experiences and reducing acceptability of IUDs. This study examined whether exposure to negative IUD content influenced acceptability of the IUD and evaluated if this effect was mediated by two psychological pathways – the affect heuristic and/or availability heuristic. In an online experimental study, participants (N = 206, MAge=18.9 SD = 2.02) were randomized to view a negative IUD social media exposure or a control condition. Participants self-reported IUD acceptability, dread about the IUD, and likelihood of a negative IUD experience. A two-way ANOVA revealed that acceptability of IUDs among participants exposed to negative content was significantly lower than participants who did not view content. The relationship between social media exposure and lower acceptability of IUDs was serially mediated by the availability heuristic (i.e. perceived likelihood of a negative IUD experience) and the affect heuristic (i.e. feelings of dread about the IUD). Our findings suggest that IUD content may have a harmful impact on acceptability of IUDs, which could have downstream impacts on contraceptive decision-making. This study provided support for two mechanisms: the availability heuristic and the affect heuristic. Future interventions should leverage these mechanisms to mitigate the impact of negative IUD content.

title: Norms and Sanctions for Talking About Sex: Women’s Sexual Communication with Friends
abstract: Sexual communication with close friends plays a role in how women interpret and navigate their sexual experiences across the lifespan. However, women often must contend with conflicting scripts that simultaneously encourage and discourage sexual exploration and satisfaction, even when communicating with close friends. Sexual communication norms between friends dictate what topics are acceptable and how often they can be discussed. While most social norms research focuses on sexual behaviors, little has explored communication norms, particularly amongst women. This study provides an in-depth exploration of women’s sexual communication norms, including how often they talk to friends about sex, how much they want to talk about sex, and whether they think this kind of communication should be normalized. We also explored the social sanctions that motivate these norms and the underlying rationales for those sanctions. A quantitative survey of 608 women age 20–77 was conducted in the U.S. Results suggest that sex is discussed relatively infrequently amongst women, though most want this communication to be more frequent and normalized. Across all sex-related topics, women reported wanting to talk more to their friends about them than they currently do (t(607) = -34.99, p < .001. However, participants anticipated an average of three social sanctions for bringing up sex-related topics to their friends, and believed these sanctions are justified because sex-talk can be immoral, disgusting, and taboo.

Multiscale fractal-LLM synergy for secure synchrophasor data authentication in smart grids
abstract: Synchrophasor Data (SD), which captures the states and dynamics of transmission and distribution power networks, is recorded by dispersed Phasor Measurement Units (PMUs) that are connected through advanced communication infrastructures in cyber-physical systems. While the source information of SD is critical for PMU-based applications, it remains susceptible to data integrity attacks. Reliable SD source authentication must be performed efficiently before any SD analytics to ensure application integrity. Existing machine learning authentication methods are focused on sparse SD across vast regions and fail to represent realistic network conditions. This study presents a data-driven SD source authentication of dense PMUs at intra-state locations without requiring detailed power network topology, parameters, or costly upgrades to PMU hardware and data infrastructure. It offers a practical data-driven approach through multiscale fractal - Large Language Models (LLMs) synergy for secure SD authentication. Specifically, Multiscale Vector Visibility Height Correlation Analysis (MVVHCA) is developed to extract long-term fractal correlations from SD with multiple attributes simultaneously and pinpoint scales exhibiting peak multifractality. Then, high-fidelity synthetic SD is reconstructed through Adaptive Multifractal Interpolation (AMFI). These synthetic SD are further processed by LLMs to achieve robust, real-time source authentication. Validation on extensive real-world SD from multiple intra-state locations confirms superior accuracy and computational efficiency, which establishes a scalable solution for secure operation of renewable-dominated smart grids.

title: Joint production, externalities, and terrace conservation strategies
Rethinking land readjustment: Fit-for-purpose rules for joint use in real estate development
abstract: Urban development frequently requires land assembly, cross-parcel coordination, and allocation of costs and benefits created by zoning plans. In Norway, property-formation tasks typically rely on cadastral procedures that depend on voluntary agreement and may involve multiple fragmented, sequential, and time-consuming approvals. This article examines whether organizational instruments under the Land Consolidation Act – rules on joint use, orders for joint measures, and governance arrangements – can function as a less invasive and more efficient complement to physical reallotment in urban land readjustment. Using a structured review of Norwegian zoning plans and Land Consolidation Court decisions, supplemented with targeted literature, we identify (i) coordination problems these instruments can address, (ii) their legal effects and constraints, and (iii) practical conditions for implementation, including loss-prevention rules and transition to later physical property formation. We conclude that organizational instruments are best suited for early-phase cooperation and shared functions (e.g., access, infrastructure, common areas), reducing transaction costs and holdout risks when physical reallotment is premature. We discuss implications for ‘fit-for-purpose’ land readjustment and outline how comparable rule-based joint-use solutions may be adapted to resource-constrained contexts, provided that legal clarity and registration mechanisms are addressed. In Norwegian land consolidation law traditional physical readjustment includes measures such as land exchange and the reduction of fragmentation of holdings. Organizational instruments, by contrast, operate closer to the actual coordination problems faced in urban development. As such, they represent a more fit-for-purpose response to the challenges of fragmented ownership and cross-boundary planning in transformation areas.

Pressure-aware multi-modal CO2 transport planning for industrial decarbonization: A case study of Germany's steel sector to 2050
abstract: Multi-modal CO 2 transport networks involve coupled decisions on operating pressure, mode-switching equipment, and infrastructure deployment timing, yet existing optimization studies typically treat the associated compression, liquefaction, and heat exchange as post-processing assumptions. This study develops a pressure-aware mixed-integer linear programming framework for multi-modal CO 2 transport planning that couples mode selection with pressure-state-dependent conditioning, allowing pressure regimes and mode transitions to be optimized jointly. The framework integrates phased deployment across three time horizons (2030, 2040, 2050) under three decarbonization pathways, carbon pricing for uncaptured emissions, and selective reuse of existing pipelines within a single optimization. Seven mode-pressure variants are considered, with mode-transition costs derived from a 49-transition simulation matrix. The framework is applied to twelve major German steel emitters connected to the Northern Lights offshore storage site via three candidate ports. The cost-optimal network shifts from truck-and-rail logistics in the early, low-volume stage to a dense-phase pipeline backbone as captured volumes grow. Unit transport costs remain within 15–18 €/tCO 2 across the scenarios. The marginal cost of expanding transport and conditioning capacity stabilizes at 13–14 €/tCO 2 from 2040 onward. These figures indicate that transport is not the binding economic constraint on scaling up capture ambition, rather than that CCUS as a whole is inexpensive. Existing pipeline reuse is found to be capacity- and stage-dependent: sufficiently large reused assets can reduce new-build requirements. The framework offers a transferable approach for cleaner industrial logistics design, supporting the transition to low-carbon hard-to-abate sectors in Europe and beyond.

title: Decision-making for enhancing thermal resilience: Identifying and prioritising intervention domains across social, economic, ecological, and technological systems
Global perspectives on the curricular integration of nature-based solutions in hydrology and water resources management education
abstract: Nature-based Solutions (NbS) are strongly advocated in international environmental discourse and policy agendas for climate risk management. However, a critical knowledge gap remains regarding the extent to which NbS concepts are systematically integrated into higher education curricula, despite the role of universities as institutional settings for developing and disseminating knowledge relevant to NbS. In this study, we examined the degree of curricular integration of NbS within university study programs in water resources management (WRM) and hydrology at the undergraduate, master's, and doctoral levels across 25 countries in 8 geographic regions. Data were collected through a structured survey, and curricula analysis was conducted, in which the proportion of NbS content within each course was categorized into Major (core focus), Moderate (partial coverage), Minor (peripheral inclusion), or NA (no explicit content). Our findings reveal significant regional and disciplinary contrasts. Countries with research-active disciplines, such as engineering and environmental science, and those with formal NbS policy frameworks, such as in the EU, show earlier or more extensive NbS curricular integration. Contrary to the interdisciplinary nature of NbS, we find that NbS are predominantly, yet sporadically, embedded in civil and environmental engineering and natural sciences, with minimal contributions from other disciplines, such as social sciences. Moreover, NbS concept remains insufficiently represented at the undergraduate level as 45.9% of the courses contain Minor content and 33.9% have no explicit NbS content, which represents a missed opportunity for NbS exposure during foundational professional study and training. More substantive NbS content appears in master's and doctoral programs, suggesting that NbS remains a specialized, research-oriented topic rather than foundational curriculum content. Faculty-led NbS teaching initiatives, identified through the survey, though encouraging, reveal a misalignment between high NbS research activity and their low curricular integration, where 31–41% of lecturers in courses with NA and Minor NbS integration do publish NbS-related research. Without explicit NbS framing in WRM and hydrology curricula, study programs may remain confined to specific disciplinary silos, potentially limiting students' overall engagement with NbS concepts. These findings collectively suggest that advancing comprehensive NbS integration in higher education may require deliberate and coordinated curricular reform across institutional levels, highlighting the importance of a whole-institution approach that systematically integrates NbS into curriculum, governance structures, and campus infrastructure.

title: A decision-support framework for structuring and assessing photovoltaic panel recycling costs in emerging economies
abstract: The rapid expansion of solar energy systems has intensified concerns about the sustainable management of photovoltaic panels at the end of its life cycle, particularly recycling and resource recovery. Despite the growing volume of end-of-life solar equipment, significant uncertainties persist regarding recycling costs, especially in emerging economies, where structured economic assessment approaches remain limited. This study proposes a structured decision-support framework to support the assessment and management of recycling costs associated with end-of-life photovoltaic panels. A Systematic Literature Review was conducted to identify cost components related to photovoltaic recycling, which were then structured using the Function Analysis System Technique. Expert evaluation was used to validate cost relevance and structure. The Fuzzy Delphi method and Mean Rank Position were applied to reach consensus on cost relevance, while the Stepwise Weight Assessment Ratio Analysis method was used to assign weights to cost categories. The resulting framework consolidates consensual cost components into weighted functional clusters, providing a structured basis for economic assessment and supporting decision-making in photovoltaic panel recycling initiatives. The proposed framework contributes to resource conservation and circular economy strategies by supporting managers, investors, and policymakers in structuring and comparing the cost dimensions associated with photovoltaic panel recycling in emerging economies.

title: Towards cleaner rare earth metal production: Techno-economic and life cycle assessment of direct Nd2O3 pyroelectroreduction in low-temperature chloride-based molten salt
Toward circular biochar systems from waste-derived precursors: multi-analytical and multivariate insights into adsorption and heterogeneous Fenton-like oxidation performance
abstract: Understanding how waste-derived resources can be transformed into functional materials is essential for advancing circular economy strategies and sustainable water treatment technologies. In this work, a combined multi-analytical and multivariate framework is developed to elucidate how waste-derived precursor type, pyrolysis temperature, and iron functionalization collectively control adsorption and heterogeneous Fenton-like oxidation in biochar-based systems. Biochars were produced from 4 waste-derived precursors: spent coffee grounds, olive pomace, olive pomace stones, and sewage sludge, at three pyrolysis temperatures (450, 550, and 650 °C), generating 12 pristine materials and, after iron functionalization, a total of 24 materials. This design enables a systematic evaluation of waste-to-resource pathways and the decoupling of compositional and structural effects. Advanced characterization was combined with I-optimal response surface methodology (RSM) and principal component analysis (PCA) to provide complementary information: RSM was used to optimize material and process variables, whereas PCA was applied to interpret structure-property-performance relationships and identify the main descriptors controlling adsorption and heterogeneous Fenton-like oxidation. Equilibrium adsorption data were better described by the Freundlich model (R 2 ≥ 0.97), indicating that surface heterogeneity was a dominant factor, while Langmuir-derived Qmax values were used only as comparative capacity indicators. Lignocellulosic biochars were governed by surface area and aromaticity, whereas sewage-sludge-derived biochars showed enhanced affinity due to their mineral-rich matrices and oxygenated functionalities. Iron functionalization significantly improved performance, with Fe-SSBC450 showing the highest Langmuir-derived adsorption capacity (Qmax = 6.57 mg g −1 ) and oxidation efficiency (∼76% phenol removal). Oxidation proceeded via • OH-driven mechanisms following pseudo-second-order kinetics. This work demonstrates how waste-derived precursors can be valorised into high-value materials for environmental remediation, supporting circular economy strategies through resource-efficient water purification.

title: Annual energy use and economic performance of rice-based cropping systems: A three-year field study in Southwest China
Supply chain carbon penalties of U.S. carbon capture deployment: An EEIO-based assessment of net abatement performance
abstract: Carbon capture and storage (CCS) is increasingly viewed as an essential option for decarbonizing emissions-intensive sectors, yet its net abatement value depends not only on captured emissions at host facilities but also on the economy-wide effects induced by deployment spending. Existing studies rarely integrate output propagation, supply-chain emissions added, emissions removed, and net performance indicators within a single U.S.-wide high-resolution framework. This study addresses that gap by developing an environmentally extended input-output model to quantify the economy-wide production impacts, supply chain carbon penalties, and net performance of CCS deployment in the United States. Annualized capital and operating expenditures for CCS were represented as an exogenous final-demand shock and mapped into the 402-sector USEEIO v2.5 framework, while emissions were evaluated using sector-specific capture fractions. For the modeled 90% capture scenario in electricity, lime and gypsum products, cement, and iron and steel, gross CO 2 removal reached 1.14 Gt, supply-chain activity added 0.08 Gt CO 2 , and net abatement remained substantial at 1.06 Gt CO 2 . The corresponding emission penalty ratio was around 67 kg CO 2 added per ton removed, and the net abatement cost was 73 $/tCO 2 . Scenario analysis showed that a 20% reduction in total CCS cost lowered the emission penalty ratio by 19% and the net abatement cost by 20%, whereas a 90% reduction in electricity-sector CO 2 intensity lowered the penalty ratio by 59% while producing only a marginal reduction in net abatement cost. These results indicate that CCS can deliver substantial net abatement, with cost reductions primarily improving economic performance and electricity-sector decarbonization providing greater leverage for reducing the upstream carbon penalty. Because the analysis uses a static national EEIO structure, it does not resolve regional heterogeneity, facility-level technological differences, or endogenous changes in economic and production relationships over time.

title: System-level techno-economic analysis of hydrogen-fuelled genset internal combustion engines with exhaust-driven power recovery
abstract: Hydrogen-fuelled internal combustion engines (H 2 -ICEs) are increasingly considered as transitional low-carbon power technologies, yet their deployment is limited by reduced efficiency and high electricity costs under open-cycle operation. This study presents a unified thermodynamic and techno-economic comparison of gasoline, open-cycle hydrogen, and waste-heat-recovery-integrated H 2 -ICE generator systems using an ASPEN-based process simulation framework. At the highest stable equivalence ratios examined (φ = 1.045 for gasoline and φ = 0.857 for hydrogen), the open-cycle H 2 -ICE exhibits a 17.5 % lower brake thermal efficiency than gasoline, at 33.4 % versus 40.5 %. To mitigate this penalty, an exhaust-mounted electric turbogenerator (ETG) coupled with a proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyser is integrated to recover exhaust energy and enable in-situ hydrogen regeneration. When system performance is evaluated based on the combined engine brake and recovered electrical output, the integrated H 2 -ICE with waste heat recovery achieves apparent extended system-level energy utilisation factors of 54.4 % using ASPEN simulations and 52.3 % based on theoretical analysis. Techno-economic analysis under defined operating conditions of 5 h day −1 and 365 days year −1 shows that open-cycle hydrogen increases the levelised cost of electricity by approximately 34 % for grey hydrogen and more than 400 % for green hydrogen relative to gasoline, whereas waste heat recovery reduces the grey hydrogen LCOE to 0.727 MYR kWh −1 . This corresponds to reductions of 39.4 % relative to open-cycle hydrogen and 18.6 % relative to gasoline. Overall, the results demonstrate that the viability of hydrogen ICEs is governed by system-level energy recovery and integration rather than standalone engine efficiency, highlighting the thermodynamic potential of waste-heat-recovery-integrated H 2 -ICEs as a transitional low-carbon stationary power concept under favourable integration and component cost assumptions.
