Scientific Isolation? The Consequences of Trump's China Initiative on Chinese Research
abstract: ABSTRACT The 2018 China Initiative by the Trump administration complicated procedures and reduced funding for U.S.‐China research collaborations. Using Scopus data, we analyze its impact on Chinese research. We find that it significantly lowered the quality of both publications and co‐authors of Chinese researchers with prior U.S. collaborations compared to those with prior European collaborations, and reduced yearly citations for affected researchers by 6%. The effect was stronger for high‐productivity Chinese researchers in U.S.‐dominated fields. While China is at the forefront of the scientific frontier, it still depends more on the U.S. than the reverse.

title: Discussion of “Local Shocks and Regional Dynamics in an Aging Economy”—The Downward Elasticity of Regional Capital
abstract: ABSTRACT The paper shows that population aging can reduce the welfare cost to individuals of a persistent negative local shock, because slower out‐migration restrains forward‐looking capital disinvestment and the retained capital cushions the wages of those who stay. I consider asymmetric capital adjustment: under irreversibility, disinvestment is less elastic than installation. I extend the paper's capital block to allow for this asymmetry and show that the extension can be tractably incorporated into standard dynamic hat algebra solution algorithms, including the one employed in the paper. I then illustrate the importance of asymmetric capital adjustment through a simple one‐region example.

title: The macroeconomic effects of a greener technology mix
Trading electrons: Predicting DART spread spikes in ISO electricity markets
abstract: We study the problem of forecasting and optimally trading day-ahead versus real-time (DART) price spreads in U.S. wholesale electricity markets. Building on the framework of Galarneau-Vincent et al., we extend spike prediction from a single zone to a multi-zone setting and treat both positive and negative DART spikes within a unified statistical model. To translate directional signals into economically meaningful positions, we develop a structural and market-consistent price impact model based on day-ahead bid stacks. This yields closed-form expressions for the optimal vector of zonal INC/DEC quantities, capturing asymmetric buy/sell impacts and cross-zone congestion effects. When applied to NYISO, the resulting impact-aware strategy significantly improves the risk-return profile relative to unit-size trading and highlights substantial heterogeneity across markets and seasons.

title: Corporate Share Repurchase Policies and Labor Share
abstract: This study examines whether corporate share repurchases are responsible for the decline in labor share among U.S. firms since the 1980s. Using census data and various empirical approaches, we find no evidence suggesting that increases in share repurchases contribute to reductions in labor share. We find no correlation between share repurchases and labor share declines, and the firms most engaged in repurchases do not decrease labor share. Using exogenous variation linked to EPS announcements and taxation policies, we further validate these findings, indicating that policies aimed at improving labor share by discouraging share buybacks are unlikely to meet their objectives.

Bridging the Divide Between Agricultural Economics and the Sustainability Sciences
abstract: ABSTRACT This article is based on several decades of experience engaging in interdisciplinary research and teaching involving agronomists, climate scientists, ecologists, hydrologists and geographers, focused on ensuring the long run sustainability of local and global food systems. Through a series of examples of this research, the paper will underscore several key points. The first is that keeping the economics as simple as possible leaves greater room for interdisciplinary collaboration. The more complex the economic models, the higher the barrier to effective collaboration. Basic economic messages on the role of markets in mediating the impacts of policies, along with producer and consumer responses to changing incentives are invaluable to sustainability analyses and can lend important new insights. This doesn’t mean that the ensuing economic analysis is not sophisticated. Indeed, as will be demonstrated, sophisticated analysis is critically important. But this analysis is at the ‘extensive margin’ of economic science—applying established methods to new application domains. A second point is that economists must work at the same spatial resolution as our science collaborators. For food, land and water sustainability challenges, this is typically the grid cell—geospatial units identified by latitude and longitude coordinates. Economists have been slow on the uptake of the geospatial data revolution. For me personally, this has meant moving, over the last two decades, from national scale general equilibrium modelling to gridded partial equilibrium modelling. Ultimately, these two frameworks can be combined, as I will demonstrate in this paper. Many sustainability analyses must start at the granular level where one can leverage the full expertise of the biophysical scientists. This may take many economists out of their comfort zone. However, our tools can be adapted and brought to bear at fine scale. In this context, the paper highlights the value of the Global‐to‐Local‐to‐Global approach to sustainability analysis. The third key point made in this paper is that economics offers a great organising framework for interdisciplinary projects. Too often we let the biophysical scientists frame the discussion prior to our involvement. This leads to frustration on the part of economists who are relegated to a secondary role in the project. However, if we lead the writing of the proposal and frame the overall discussion in economic terms, this gives rise to a very different dynamic which can facilitate coherent and meaningful economic analyses. Further, when economics is not used in the sustainability sciences, policy prescriptions are often limited at best, and misleading at worst. Finally, I have some suggestions for the teaching of interdisciplinary skills at the graduate level. Here, a well‐constructed course can benefit both the students as well as the instructor, fostering fruitful collaborations on grant applications, as well as generating new ideas for research in the sustainability sciences.

title: A Hundred Years of the Agricultural Economics Society
abstract: ABSTRACT The centenary of the UK‐based Agricultural Economics Society (AES) is an obvious opportunity to provide an updated summary institutional history of its development and achievements. Knowledge of equivalent associations in the US influenced the foundation of the AES in 1926. After a faltering start, the Society's main activities have been organising residential and one‐day conferences and publishing the Journal of Agricultural Economics . The last‐mentioned began in 1928 as a conference proceedings. Great growth in AES membership occurred in the 25 years after the Second World War, reflecting recognition of the importance of agricultural economics in that era. With the subsequent erosion of the subject's base in British universities, especially around the turn of the millennium, the twenty‐first‐century AES pursued an outward‐looking strategy. It started co‐producing the outreach periodical EuroChoices with the European Association of Agricultural Economists, and holding annual conferences outside Britain. Nowadays AES membership is much more international than in the past but less occupationally diverse, with around three‐quarters of current members drawn from academia. When deemed necessary the Society has occasionally made representations on behalf of the profession, in particular influencing specific aspects of how UK research assessment exercises operate. Numbers of members and annual conference delegates are currently buoyant, and the Executive Committee has launched a £100,000 centenary fund to support postgraduate research students. The AES, then, is well positioned for the opportunities and challenges ahead at the start of its second century.

Does LaTeX enhance perceptions of research quality in economics?
abstract: We conducted two online survey experiments examining how writing style influences economists’ perceptions of research quality. Participants were randomly assigned to evaluate manuscript cover pages that varied by document editor (Microsoft Word versus LaTeX) and the presence of a spelling or grammar error. In the original experiment, conducted among U.S. economists, spelling and grammar errors significantly reduced perceived research quality, whereas document editor had little effect. In a follow-up experiment, conducted among an international sample of economists, LaTeX use was substantially more common, and manuscripts prepared in LaTeX were generally evaluated more favorably than those prepared in Microsoft Word. Taken together, our findings suggest that careful proofreading and preparing manuscripts in LaTeX are prudent best practices. Depending on the reader, both may improve perceptions of research quality while carrying little or no downside risk.

title: Approximately efficient resource allocation: A theoretical and experimental evaluation
Beyond circularity: Topological and temporal limits of the circular economy
abstract: The circular economy has established itself as a dominant sustainability paradigm, yet the formal properties of its foundational metaphor, the circle, remain unexamined. This paper identifies two analytically distinct constraints embedded in the dominant circular imaginary. The first is topological: when the operative metaphor functions as a single closed loop, it reproduces the cycle graph, a one-dimensional structure with zero redundancy and minimal resilience. The second is temporal: the assessment apparatus associated with circularity operates within quantitative, sequential time (chronos) and renders qualitative, heterogeneous temporalities (kairos) structurally invisible. The claim defended here is specific. Sustainability paradigms generally pose time as a problem left open; the circular economy's founding metaphor figures time as resolved (return, cycle, regeneration) while its apparatus operationalizes only chronos. This blindness is not general ignorance but performative contradiction. Empirical evidence from three continents (African solar projects, Mexican circular assessment, Peruvian extraction) substantiates the diagnosis. We propose a polyrhythmic completion structured as a wheel, with Doughnut Economics as the rim, regeneration as the hub, and ArtefactKairos (institutional devices for temporal composition) as the spokes, operationalized through the Temporal Composition Diagnostic (TCD), a four-step governance protocol. The TCD is applied to a published sugar beet pulp biorefinery assessment that models feedstock as a fixed daily input without addressing the seasonal harvest sustaining it, then calibrated ex ante against the Antamina mining region in Peru. In both settings it reveals what standard assessment cannot detect and specifies the institutional clauses it would generate.

Trade diversification and food price volatility
abstract: Abstract Recent shortages and price volatility have exposed vulnerabilities in international agri-food value chains. This paper develops a new framework for measuring trade diversification based on Hill numbers, which capture both the extensive and intensive margin of trade connections. Using HS6-level bilateral data for 188 countries from 2000 to 2022, I first document global patterns of diversification and concentration across agri-food sectors. The descriptive evidence shows that most countries trade with many partners in principle, yet effectively rely on only a few, especially for grains and oilseeds. I then estimate the effect of import and export diversification on within-year food price volatility using a shift–share instrumental-variable design that exploits exogenous foreign sector-level shocks weighted by lagged bilateral trade exposure. The empirical results show that more balanced and diversified import portfolios are strongly associated with lower food price volatility, whereas export diversification plays a more limited role. Policies encouraging diversification can reduce food price volatility but involve trade-offs between efficiency from international specialization and resilience of the input–output network.

Firm turnover under asymmetric information: Tanzania's agro‐dealer sector
abstract: Abstract We study firm turnover (i.e., entry and exit) and its consumer implications in a market characterized by asymmetric information. Using a three‐round census of agro‐dealers in Tanzania's Morogoro Region, we document annual firm entry and exit rates of 33% and 17%, respectively. These rates are more than double those observed for non‐agricultural micro‐, small‐, and medium‐enterprises in comparable low‐income countries. To analyze how these high rates of entry and exit affect consumers, we develop a theoretical model of firm turnover under asymmetric information and empirically test its predictions for farmers. We find that farmers' market‐level beliefs about agricultural input quality are systematically related to agro‐dealer turnover, with the relationship depending on farmers' prior perceptions of market quality. Farmers report more favorable beliefs about agricultural input quality in markets with recent agro‐dealer exits, consistent with our model when consumers perceive exiting firms as having sold low‐quality products. In contrast, farmers who usually purchased agricultural inputs from the same agro‐dealer expect new market entrants to provide lower‐quality agricultural inputs, suggesting farmers rely on incumbent relationships to manage quality uncertainty in markets with information asymmetries. As a result, agro‐dealer turnover may shape and even attenuate farmers' technology adoption.

Climate Uncertainty and Financial Subordination: Evidence From a Two‐Country Stock‐Flow Consistent Model
abstract: ABSTRACT In the face of climate change, uncertainty is deep, systemic, and does not propagate amid an institutional vacuum, contrary to assumptions often underlying existing macroeconomic climate models. The paper presents a macroeconomic Stock‐Flow Consistent model to examine the impact of climate‐related financial pressures under fundamental uncertainty within a hierarchical international monetary and financial system. It demonstrates how climate uncertainty induces asymmetric cross‐country interactions, highlighting the potential for the climate catastrophe to exacerbate regional economic disparities. These findings call for a more structural approach to a just transition in which financial governance is geared towards global equity and long‐term sustainability.

title: Behavioral New Keynesian Models: Learning versus Cognitive Discounting
abstract: Abstract This paper estimates a New Keynesian model with new and old behavioral elements. Agents in the model exhibit cognitive discounting, or myopia: they discount variables far into the future at higher rates than typically implied in the benchmark model. We investigate the model under different expectational assumptions: rational expectations, subjective expectations with infinite‐horizon learning, and subjective expectations with Euler‐equation learning. Under rational expectations, the model necessitates of large, possibly unrealistically so, degrees of myopia. The same result persists under infinite‐horizon learning, given that agents are still remarkably far‐sighted. But, under Euler‐equation learning, the model can fit the data with only minimal estimated degrees of myopia. The results indicate that the empirical evidence for cognitive discounting may be sensitive to the modeling of expectations, and they highlight learning as a key behavioral feature to understand macro‐economic fluctuations.
journal_name: Journal of Money, Credit and Banking

title: Corporate disclosure, government bailout, and liquidity crisis
Making stablecoins stable(r): can regulation help?
abstract: Abstract Rapid growth of stablecoins has raised concerns about issuer default and spillover risks. To assess these risks, we model a stablecoin issuer facing persistent demand shocks. Absent regulation, the issuer holds little capital and favours interest-bearing but illiquid bonds over cash. This exposes coin-holders to default risk and poses spillovers via bond fire-sales. How can regulation mitigate these risks? Capital and liquidity thresholds can help, especially when introduced as usable buffers. The thresholds can be breached, providing flexibility. However, breaches trigger additional redemptions that discipline the issuer. The thresholds operate through asymmetric channels: the liquidity threshold raises only cash, whereas the capital threshold increases both capital and cash. Both thresholds mitigate default and spillover risks, making them substitutes when either risk is targeted separately but complements when both risks are targeted jointly. We provide a two-way mapping that helps derive capital-liquidity threshold combinations implied by chosen risk targets (and vice-versa).

title: Mixing QE and Interest Rate Policies at the Effective Lower Bound: Micro Evidence from the Euro Area
abstract: Abstract We study the interaction of expansionary rate-based monetary policy and quantitative easing, despite their concurrent implementation, by exploiting heterogeneous banks and the introduction of negative monetary-policy rates in a fragmented euro area. Quantitative easing increases credit supply less when banks’ funding costs do not decrease simultaneously. Using administrative data from Germany, we uncover that among banks selling their securities, central-bank reserves remain disproportionately with high-deposit banks that are constrained due to sticky customer deposits at the zero lower bound. Affected German banks lend relatively less to firms while increasing their interbank exposure in the euro area.

title: Unpacking the Local Pay Gap: New Insights Into CSR and Employee Relations
Reimagining Interdisciplinarity: Sensitization, Reflexivity, and Mobilization Across Landscapes of Practice
abstract: Abstract Interdisciplinary research (IDR) is widely promoted as essential for addressing complex societal challenges, yet its enactment remains fraught. We argue that dominant typological and structural approaches miscast IDR and underplay the practical work through which it unfolds. Drawing on practice theory, we reconceptualize IDR as bundles of practices enacted across landscapes of practice. We theorize three guiding constructs: sensitization, reflexivity, and mobilization that support the coordination of IDR without collapsing its ontological multiplicity through misplaced attempts at epistemological integration. A practice lens clarifies why structural and typological interventions supply conditions that support IDR but do not guarantee outcomes; foregrounds the fragility, temporality, and politics of doing IDR; and reframes evaluation around practices rather than proxy measures such as bibliometrics. We outline implications for organizing and leading IDR and a research agenda linking IDR to wider debates in management and organization studies. Our contribution shifts attention from what IDR is to how it is enacted, sustained, and sometimes unravelled in practice.

title: Stay In Your Own Lane: Navigating the Challenges of Upward Knowledge Sharing in Hierarchical Audit Teams
The Eco-Gender Gap in Boardrooms
How Do Organizations Address Anti‐ DEI Pressure? Problematization and Perspectivization
abstract: ABSTRACT Underneath headlines that decree organizations are increasingly abandoning or rolling back diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives in response to anti‐DEI pressures, we argue that how organizations are doing this warrants further focus. While the strategy literature speaks to tactics for addressing institutional pressures, missing in the study of how organizations address anti‐DEI pressures is consideration of how HRM systems impact and are impacted by such action. Incorporating a strategic human resource management (SHRM) view, we offer three approaches—all of which are substantiated with evidence from contemporary organizations—that range in the extent to which organizations resist or embrace anti‐DEI pressures. The common thread linking these approaches is that each one moves beyond an oversimplified emphasis on “alignment.” We do not advocate misalignment per se but underscore how the nuances embedded in each approach reflect the intentionality of organizations and how they consider contingencies (i.e., external alignment) and configurations (i.e., internal alignment) in proactively adapting HRM systems in response to anti‐DEI pressures. In advancing these views, we develop an agenda to drive future empirical research addressing the intersection of DEI backlash and HRM.

title: Feel Free to Chat About Your Kids? Exploring the Effects of Workplace Parenting Conversations
abstract: Workplace conversations are essential for collaboration, knowledge sharing, and relationship building. While much of the literature has focused on work-related discussions, recent shifts toward the blurring of professional and personal boundaries suggest that employees may increasingly converse about aspects of their nonwork lives. One such topic of conversation—parenting—presents a unique and understudied type of workplace exchange given the central role of the parental identity for working parents and the opportunity for them to highlight this important identity through dialogue. In the current set of studies, we introduce workplace parenting conversations as dialogical, in-depth exchanges about parenting-related topics between coworkers who are parents. Drawing from identity management and boundary management theories, we propose that these conversations offer instrumental, affective, and relational benefits that positively impact behaviors across work and parenting role domains. Using a mixed-methods triangulation approach, we first explore the content and processes of workplace parenting conversations through qualitative interviews (Study 1A), followed by an experience sampling study testing our model, complete with behavioral outcomes at work and home (Study 1B). We then explore the underlying micro-mechanisms connecting workplace parenting conversations to the mechanisms in our model through additional interviews (Study 2A) and a field experiment (Study 2B). Our findings contribute to the literature on workplace conversations by identifying an overlooked yet impactful form of workplace dialogue, exploring its primarily positive effects on employees’ behaviors in both work and home contexts, and uncovering unique micro-mechanisms associated with this specific type of conversation.

title: Beyond installation: How pre-adoption advertising drives post-adoption retail app usage
Selecting the Best, yet Following the Crowd: Coevolution of Project‑Based Collaborative Networks and Digitalization Behavior
A strong sociotechnical perspective on digitalisation of and by projects: theoretically pluralistic, technologically agnostic and beyond techno-optimism
Technological and geopolitical disruptions shaping processes and organization design: implications for purchasing and supply management
abstract: Purpose New emerging technologies, such as generative artificial intelligence (AI), and changing geopolitical realities provoke the question of whether operations and supply chain management (OSCM) processes, as well as the way they are organized, need to change. Taking the exemplary context of purchasing and supply management (PSM), what might have traditionally been effective and efficient ways to manage and organize PSM processes might be less so in times of AI utilization and autonomous buying and the current geopolitical situation. Design/methodology/approach This is a perspectives paper. We take a conceptual approach and build on research on PSM processes, the contingency approach to purchasing and supply organizations (PSOs), information processing theory (IPT), organizational buying behavior (OBB) and complement this with illustrative business examples. Findings The findings highlight a variety of impacts that technological and geopolitical disruptions have on PSM processes and organization. Technological advances may facilitate increased automation and analytical capability, eliminate biases and facilitate pooling of more information and, in general, higher information processing capacity for decision-making, but they also increase the complexity of managing supply chains. Geopolitical tensions, on the other hand, increase, for example, the need to manage various and changing tariffs and trade policies, increasing both uncertainty and complexity. Moreover, the empirical illustrations highlight that the effects of geopolitical disruptions on organizational structures seem more immediate than the effects of technological disruptions. Research limitations/implications This perspectives paper seeks to spark future PSM research. Beyond that, the five future research avenues are meant to inspire future research in other functions such as operations, logistics, supply chain management, IT, R&D and marketing. Practical implications The findings underline the strategic importance of PSM for handling an increasingly complex and uncertain business environment by addressing the why, what and how of such a transformation: First, identifying strategic value and strengthening cross-functional collaboration. Second, identifying top AI use cases and adjusting PSM processes and organization accordingly. Third, investing in (digital) transformation capacity and skills (e.g. COEs) contingent upon initial purchasing maturity. Fundamental process redesigns might be required in light of new technologies and geopolitical disruptions, which would then imply the need for (micro-level) PSO redesign, such as defining new job profiles (specialization), as well as adapted cross-functional collaboration patterns (participation) and standard operating procedures (standardization). Social implications The ongoing high-pace developments in technologies as well as major changes in geopolitical realities create new challenges for both on-the-job training and higher education. This perspectives paper highlights five areas for research, education, and practice for the exemplary function of PSM to help researchers, educators, students and practitioners cope with these challenges and to develop competences and solutions for the future. Originality/value This perspectives paper highlights the importance of a conversation on the impact of technological and geopolitical changes for the management of PSM processes and organizational considerations. It moreover highlights the future research opportunities on the potential interaction of technological and geopolitical disruptions.
journal_name: International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management

title: Ecosystem Visioning: An Attention-Based View
International Market Entry Strategy of Digital Platform Firms Evidence from International Ride-Sharing Firms
Entrepreneurial ecosystems, economic complexity, and venture-oriented entrepreneurship in German regions
abstract: Abstract This paper examines how regional economic complexity is associated with entrepreneurial outcomes in German labor market regions. Drawing on entrepreneurial ecosystem research, we conceptualize economic complexity as one structural dimension of the regional capability base and distinguish between industrial, technological, and occupational complexity. We relate these dimensions to the regional share of high-growth firms, gazelles, venture-capital-backed firms, and venture capital volume per capita, while also considering broader regional performance indicators. Using panel models with region and year fixed effects, we find that the relationship between complexity and entrepreneurial outcomes is selective and heterogeneous across dimensions and outcomes. Industrial and technological complexity are more consistently associated with high-growth firms and broader regional growth indicators, whereas occupational complexity appears more relevant for gazelles. Venture-capital-related outcomes also display positive associations with regional complexity, with industrial complexity showing the most robust relationship. These findings contribute to entrepreneurial ecosystem research by showing that regional capability structures are related to growth-oriented and venture-oriented entrepreneurship in distinct ways across different dimensions of complexity. More broadly, the paper demonstrates how economic complexity can be incorporated into the analysis of entrepreneurial ecosystems without treating it as a comprehensive measure of ecosystem quality.

title: Colonial accounting and postcolonial resistance: Aboriginal Stolen Wages in Australia
abstract: This paper advances critical accounting scholarship by exposing the constitutive role of accounting in producing and reproducing the racialised power structures of British settler colonialism in Australia. Australia remains the only ex-British settler colony without formal recognition of, or treaty with, its Indigenous population and Aboriginal Australians continue to experience inter-generational trauma underlined by extreme poverty, poor physical and mental health, and shorter life expectancy. We argue that colonial and postcolonial accounting systems have perpetuated racial biases and legitimised colonial institutions including racist protectionist legislation enabling a system of institutionalised peonage in Australia. Drawing on Bhabha's theorisation of hybridity and the ‘third space’ we conceptualise the Stolen Wages Case , a class action brought by Aboriginal pastoral workers in Queensland, as a site where colonised subjects strategically appropriate the epistemic tools of the State to contest the subjectivities imposed upon them. The case's recognition of oral testimony, its acknowledgement of Aboriginal epistemologies, and its calculation of the ‘reasonable value’ of stolen labour serve to rupture the ‘great Australian silence’ of Aboriginal labour exploitation. Our theoretical contribution lies in demonstrating how accounting functions as a colonial technology that fixes racial hierarchies while simultaneously providing openings for counter-hegemonic resistance. By adopting a hybrid epistemology, we emphasize the potential for collaborative resistance and recognition of historical injustices within a discursive ‘third space’. The successful resolution of the Stolen Wages Case exemplifies the emancipatory potential of legal and accounting mechanisms in addressing colonial legacies. This research contributes to understanding the role of accounting in sustaining colonial oppression and offers insights into pathways for postcolonial accountability and reconciliation in Australia and beyond.

title: Family ownership, performance below aspiration levels and signaling strategies in emerging markets
abstract: Advertising and CSR constitute the two key signaling strategies for family firms in emerging markets to attract new stakeholders and investors and to retain existing ones. However, the preference of family owners for these strategies may shift based on firm performance. We combine Signaling Theory with the Behavioral Theory of the Firm to examine how family ownership influences these strategies and whether these preferences shift when firms perform below aspiration levels. On a sample of Indian firms over the 2006–2019 period, we find that family ownership is positively related to signaling through both advertising and CSR investments. However, when the performance of the firm falls below aspiration levels, family owners invest more in CSR and less in advertising. These findings contribute to literature on family firm signaling and the shifting preferences of family owners during performance fluctuations, in emerging markets.

title: When AI Remembers: Investigating the Dual Role of Long‐Term Memory in Chatbots
abstract: ABSTRACT This research investigates the dual role of long‐term memory (LTM) in AI chatbots and its impact on customer outcomes. Drawing on Mind Perception Theory and Privacy Calculus Theory, we conceptualize LTM as a continuity‐based design capability that may be interpreted as a functional service feature, a privacy‐relevant cue, or a basis for anthropomorphic inference. Across three controlled scenario‐based online experiments in e‐commerce customer service, we manipulated the presence of LTM and, in Study 3, the provision of user data control within a memory‐enabled condition. Results show that LTM significantly increased satisfaction and continuance intention, while its effect on word‐of‐mouth (WoM) intention was primarily indirect. Specifically, LTM improved outcomes through enhanced competence, although these benefits were partially offset by perceived anthropomorphism and privacy concerns. In Study 2, baseline perception of privacy empowerment was insufficient to mitigate privacy concerns associated with LTM; however, within a memory‐enabled condition, introducing an explicit user data‐control mechanism in Study 3 increased perceived privacy empowerment, which in turn reduced privacy concerns and improved outcomes via serial mediation. These findings show how explicit user data control can help manage privacy concerns within memory‐enabled chatbot representations and provide guidance for designing memory‐enabled chatbots with robust user‐control mechanisms.

title: Moral responsibilisation in destination management: The strategic framing of civic practices by DMOs
abstract: This paper examines moral responsibilisation as an emerging destination governance mechanism through which destination management organisations (DMOs) and local stakeholders mobilise visitors to support sustainability goals. Drawing on an intrinsic qualitative case study of the Danish DMO, Wonderful Copenhagen , we develop a practice theory-based model showing that responsibilisation extends beyond narrative persuasion to include the organisational and material reframing of civic conduct. Analysis of interviews, participant observation, documents, and netnography identifies four interrelated stages: interpellation, involvement, intervention, and institutionalisation. Together, these stages connect inspirational messaging with participatory experiences, reward schemes, and decentralised service design. The findings also reveal tensions around the relevance, inclusivity, and feasibility of emerging civic practices. Resistance to responsible subject positions stems from stakeholders’ differing interpretations, negotiations, and disengagement from DMO-prescribed roles. The study advances the understanding of responsibilisation as a practice-based mode of governance and offers insights that may inform destination managers in varied tourism contexts.

title: Impacts of CSR Disclosure on Corporate Financial Performance: A Text Mining Approach
From Information Tool to Meaning Mediator: Understanding Consumer Acceptance of GenAI Review Summaries
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence review summaries (GenAI-RS) are increasingly being embedded in online travel platforms to help consumers process large volumes of reviews, yet the mechanisms explaining their acceptance remain underdeveloped. This study identifies the antecedents of consumers’ acceptance of GenAI-RS and examines how these antecedents shape behavioral intention by using a mixed-method design. Drawing on UTAUT2 and posthumanist and actor–network perspectives, qualitative analysis of semi-structured interviews and online user-generated content identifies two GenAI-RS-specific antecedents: perceived fairness and perceived responsibility uncertainty. A pilot study and the main survey validate the measurement model and test the proposed relationships. Results show that conventional acceptance factors, perceived human-likeness, privacy risk, use-related anxiety, perceived fairness, and responsibility uncertainty significantly shape behavioral intention. This study demonstrates that GenAI-RS acceptance is driven not only by instrumental evaluation but also by normative concerns, advancing acceptance theory and guiding platforms toward fairer, more accountable AI summary design.

title: Those Who Need Help Most, Receive It Least: How Observers React to Perceived (Lack of) Actions by Targets Following Workplace Mistreatment
What Next for Equality, Diversity and Inclusion? Moral Responsibility and Ethical Practice in EDI
abstract: Abstract This review essay provides a reading of Maddy Janssens and Chris Steyaert’s On Practising Diversity . The essay begins by noting the surprising lack of discussion in our field at the intersection of diversity and ethics. This is becoming especially problematic as practices and philosophies associated diversity are questioned by leaders in large corporations and by politicians in office and aspirants. The essay and the reading of the book conclude with observations on the nature of resistance to enforced sameness and the closing of diverse spaces, pointing towards an imminent and urgent research agenda.

title: Moral Deskilling in the Age of AI: How Algorithmic Decision-Making Reshapes Moral Capacities in Organizational Work
The Governance Role of Customer Listing Status: Evidence from Supplier Tax Avoidance
Organization-Level Inclusion: Evidence of Positive Effects for Both LGBT and Non-LGBT Employees
abstract: Abstract This work examines organization-level inclusion signals and their subsequent effects on a broad range of employees. Answering the call for more research on concealable stigmatized identities, we consider the effect of such organization-level inclusion initiatives for sexual and gender minorities (lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender employees) while also considering their reverberating effect on cisgendered, heterosexual (non-LGBT) employees. In a compiled archival data study ( N = 849), a preregistered, time-lagged observational study ( N = 1,165), and a preregistered, randomized experiment ( N = 398), we show that organization-level inclusion efforts lead to more positive perceptions of the organization’s psychological climate for sexual and gender minorities, closing the psychological safety gap between non-LGBT and LGBT employees. Notably, intentional inclusion efforts also positively affect the psychological safety of non-LGBT employees, which challenges theoretical assertions that targeted inclusion policies can harm majority groups, or that organizational inclusion is zero-sum. In turn, these signals shape positive behavioral intentions for all employees, leading non-LGBT employees to engage in more organizational ally work and leading LGBT employees to be more likely to disclose their identities. Unexpectedly, inclusion signals also made non-LGBT employees less likely to conceal sensitive aspects of their own identities (e.g., religion, parental status). In sum, we show that inclusion signaling both increases psychological safety broadly, and reduces disparities between target and non-target employees. This finding suggests that organization-level inclusion initiatives may have wider-reaching benefits than previously assumed.

title: Dynamic platform strategies in an interconnected ecosystem: Navigating standards and complements in the emerging smart home ecosystem
abstract: Whereas prior platform research has mostly assumed standardized interfaces that are platform-specific, we examine how platform strategies based on third-party standards have become prevalent in a nascent ecosystem. Based on a longitudinal analysis of 97 smart home platforms, we analyze the value creation and capture benefits of four platform modes defined by two dimensions: the source of complements (first- or third-party complements) and the standardized interfaces used to connect these complements (first- or third-party standards). Our analysis demonstrates a trend from closed strategies (only first-party complements based on first-party standards) towards strategies that (also) rely on third-party standards. We find that startups and diversifying entrants make different strategic choices at entry and that firms increasingly combine platform modes over time to leverage their distinct value creation and capture benefits. Our findings contribute insights into the ecosystem conditions and pre-entry capabilities of firms under which strategies relying on third-party standards become viable and how this contributes to the proliferation of standards, platforms, and strategies in an ecosystem. We also theorize the time-dependent strategic choices of entrants navigating a nascent ecosystem and the complex complementary and competitive relations that emerge in an ecosystem with interconnected platforms as a result.

title: Investor Orientation and Commitment in Outcomes‐Based Public Service Contracts
abstract: ABSTRACT Outcomes‐based contracts (OBCs) organize public service delivery around measurable results, yet little is known about how different investors engage with these instruments. This article examines how investor orientation (social, financial, or dual‐purpose) shapes investor commitment in OBCs worldwide. Drawing on a global dataset of 338 contracts, we combine descriptive analyses, regression models, and qualitative interviews to investigate how investor orientation relates to investment scale. We hypothesize that OBCs involving socially oriented investors are associated with higher levels of investment than those involving financially or dual‐purpose investors. Consistent with this prediction, socially oriented investors consistently commit larger amounts, whereas financially oriented and dual‐purpose investors typically participate with smaller contributions. These patterns challenge a central premise of OBCs: that such instruments would mobilize significant mainstream private capital for public services. Interview evidence points to reputational risks, limited familiarity with local conditions, and outcome measurement complexity as key deterrents.

title: A Public Values Framework for AI Governance: Evidence From US Federal AI Policymaking
abstract: ABSTRACT Governments at all levels are grappling with AI's implications for public administration. Because federal actions often establish the principles guiding wider governance efforts, this study asks how US federal AI policies reflect—or fail to reflect—core public values. Drawing on a dataset of US federal AI policies from 2020 to 2023, we systematically analyze the risks, harms, and governance strategies employed across government‐issued and enacted policy documents. Specifically, we analyze 120 discrete policy sections or subsections of federal laws and regulations, utilizing the parsing approach of the AI Governance and Regulatory Archive (AGORA), all of which regulate the operation of the government itself rather than private sector behavior. We develop a theoretical and empirical crosswalk linking AI‐related risks and harms to prominent public values. Results indicate that while values such as individual rights, the common good, and accountability are regularly invoked, additional guidance around public values like citizen engagement, workplace standards, and responsiveness may be necessary to prevent public value failure. The study further categorizes governance strategies in AI policy documents into regulatory, service‐based, and informational instruments, and finds that regulatory policies are most likely to engage with public values.

title: Responsible Algorithmization in the Public Sector: A “Natural Perspective” Based on Ethnographic Research in Regulation, Policing, and Healthcare
abstract: ABSTRACT Responsible algorithmization refers to the use of algorithms in the public sector while safeguarding public values. Approaches to responsible algorithmization suggested by the EU, OECD, and others depart from a rational perspective and highlight formal structures and procedures. This paper complements this perspective by adding a “natural perspective,” which emphasizes sense‐making and actual practices. This natural perspective is used for a set of ethnographic studies of algorithmization in three domains in the Netherlands: regulation, policing, and healthcare. Our findings show that algorithmization of government organizations is an emergent, political, open, and fragmented process, rather than, as assumed by rational approaches to responsible algorithmization, pre‐structured, neutral, closed, and simple. This means that rational approaches fall short of providing a comprehensive basis for establishing responsible algorithmization. We conclude that not only passive responsibility but also active responsibility for algorithmization in the public sector needs to be addressed to safeguard public values.

title: Advantages of a Two-Stage Randomized Trial Design to Evaluate Antimicrobial Treatment Strategies: a Simulation Study
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Antimicrobial prescribing policies affect not only treated patients but also their contacts. Two-stage randomized (2SR) designs can be used to estimate these spillover effects, yet this study design has not been widely applied to evaluate antimicrobial strategies. Methods We developed a stochastic agent-based model that simulates a hospital ward with two competing bacterial strains (drug-A-susceptible and drug-A-resistant). We used the simulation to emulate a 2SR trial: six hospital ward clusters were randomized 1:1 to either a 90/10 (90% Drug A, 10% Drug B, drug B was assumed to have no known resistance) or 50/50 treatment allocation strategy; individuals within clusters were then randomized to Drug A or Drug B following the assigned cluster-level allocation strategy. We estimated direct, indirect, total, and overall causal effects on incident infection and mortality. Sensitivity analyses varied the treatment effect, transmission rate, mortality structure, and number of clusters. Results The direct effect of drug choice showed that Drug A recipients had higher mortality (due to non-concordant treatment of resistant infections). This effect varied over time as the ward’s strain ecology diverged between strategies. There was also an indirect effect for Drug A recipients—reflecting spillover from higher resistant-strain prevalence under 90/10—but it was approximately null for Drug B recipients, whose broad-spectrum coverage insulated them from changes in the ward strain distribution. The overall effect—the policy-level comparison—showed that the 50/50 strategy reduced total mortality, but this net benefit concealed a redistribution: resistant-strain deaths decreased while susceptible-strain deaths increased, a consequence captured by the overall effect but invisible to the direct effect. These findings were qualitatively consistent across all sensitivity scenarios. Conclusions We demonstrate that antimicrobial prescribing produces spillover effects not captured by conventional individually randomized trials. These effects can substantially alter treatment outcomes in a population. We propose that the 2SR design, grounded in a formal causal framework for interference, is better suited for evaluating population-level effects of antimicrobial strategies—whether implemented as a randomized trial or emulated with observational data.

title: Effects of a parenting intervention on child maltreatment among Filipino families: Testing mechanisms of change
abstract: BACKGROUND: The Masayang Pamilya para sa Batang Pilipino (MaPa) program is an evidence-based, culturally adapted parenting program designed to reduce child maltreatment in Filipino families. In a randomized controlled trial, families who received MaPa had significant reductions in child maltreatment compared to control families, both at post-intervention and at one-year follow up. However, the mechanisms by which the reduction in child maltreatment is sustained has yet to be established. OBJECTIVE: This study investigated overreactive parenting and positive parenting as potential mediators of the sustained effects of MaPa on reducing child maltreatment. PARTICIPANTS: Parents (N = 120) of children aged two to six were randomly allocated to either the MaPa program or treatment as usual (TAU). All parents were recruited from a community setting and were enrolled in the government's conditional cash transfer program. METHODS: A latent-variable parallel mediation model was tested using parent-report data measured at baseline, immediate post-intervention, and at one-year follow-up. Measures were included on overreactive parenting, positive parenting, and child abuse. RESULTS: Those who received MaPa exhibited reduced overreactive parenting post-intervention compared to TAU, which in turn marginally mediated the sustained effects of MaPa on child maltreatment occurrence at follow-up. Positive parenting, however, did not mediate the effects of MaPa on risk of child maltreatment. CONCLUSIONS: Results suggest that MaPa effectively reduces overreactive parenting, which in turn may be among the mechanisms that reduces child maltreatment in families with young children. Findings provide evidence that reducing overreactive parenting may be an effective pathway towards reducing violence against children.

title: Building food security from the periphery: a study of adaptation and social innovation in the Natuna border region, Indonesia
Impacts of farm electrification on irrigation costs and food crop yields in India’s smallholder agriculture
abstract: Abstract Irrigation costs constitute a substantial share of crop production costs, which often hamper cash-strapped smallholders from applying sufficient water to achieve better crop yields. In Bihar, one of India’s major agrarian states characterized by smallholder-dominated cereal-based cropping system, a mega government-led intervention is transforming irrigation system by replacing costly diesel-powered irrigation pumps with electric ones. We evaluated the farm-level impacts of electrification on energy costs for irrigation, water management, and crop yields of the two principal food crops of the region, i.e., rice and wheat. Using survey data from 600 farmers, we applied propensity score-based Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting (IPTW) to estimate causal impacts. Irrigation electrification reduced irrigation costs by three-fourths for rice and two-thirds for wheat. Irrigation cost reductions for wheat exhibited spatial heterogeneity, with larger benefits in areas where groundwater levels were deeper than 4.4 m. Lower irrigation costs led to increased irrigation intensity for both crops, with more pronounced effects for rice. Rice yields increased by 8% (382 kg ha −1 ) on average, with higher yield gains (> 500 kg ha −1 ) in areas with groundwater levels above 3.6 m. Wheat yields increased more uniformly across the state, by 6% (203 kg ha −1 ). These findings provide quantifiable evidence on the linkages between irrigation costs and agricultural productivity for key staple in smallholder systems, highlighting the moderating role of groundwater conditions within the context of the study area.

title: Harnessing digital capabilities and human capital to strengthen food security under climate stress: evidence from a global dynamic panel
The effect of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy on sexual self-esteem in women with breast cancer after mastectomy: a randomized controlled trial
Absenteeism and Presenteeism in Times of Change: The Role of Stress and Job Satisfaction
abstract: This study investigates sickness absenteeism and sickness presenteeism in the context of organizational development (OD) changes in the police force, focusing on health-related and motivational pathways. Using panel data from 407 employees from 36 Danish police units (1,021 observations), we analyze attendance patterns before the change, immediately after, and 1 year later. Findings reveal that sickness absenteeism is primarily influenced by the type of OD change rather than by job satisfaction or stress, while sickness presenteeism decreases with higher job satisfaction independent of the change type. Notably, employees experiencing an OD change aimed at supporting a long-term vision exhibit reduced sickness absence in the change period. OD changes focused on distributed leadership and enhancing employee motivation did not have the same effect on sickness absenteeism. These results underscore the importance of considering both motivational and health-related dynamics, as well as the type of change, in understanding attendance during OD change.

title: Optimizing rooftop–façade ratio for enhancing stability of building-integrated photovoltaic system in the Asia-Pacific region
abstract: Solar energy is a promising renewable energy source for achieving net-zero carbon emissions because of its low cost and ease of installation, including in buildings. However, the variability of solar energy is currently the main issue affecting the reliability of its implementation and integration into power grid systems. Understanding how solar power generation behaves when installed in a building with a monitoring system is important. Highly spatiotemporal information is required to visualize the detailed behavior of generated solar power. This study integrated a high-temporal geostationary satellite-derived product with 10 min observations and building-height information to obtain high-spatiotemporal solar power observations for a geospatial-based analysis in the Asia-Pacific region. Compared with the existing PV site, this integration showed a coefficient of determination (R 2 ) of 0.791 for 10 min observations and 0.917 for daily average observations. Rooftop and façade solar power observations were then used to calculate the optimal rooftop-to-façade ratio for building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) to achieve greater stability and lower fluctuations than rooftop-only systems. This study used 3 years of observation (2022–2024) and was conducted across 55 cities in the Asia-Pacific region, covering diverse climatic conditions. This study used a minimally constrained optimization algorithm, with stability index (SI) as the main objective function, to determine the optimal ratio. Optimizing the rooftop-façade ratio can increase daily stability by approximately 5%–30% and decrease daily fluctuation by approximately 15%–30%, with the greatest gains in tropical regions. The proposed framework is generic and can be applied to other cities worldwide where geostationary satellite and urban 3D building data are available, providing a scalable tool for assessing and planning urban BIPV. This approach provides a robust tool for urban BIPV assessment and planning, supporting the large-scale deployment of stable solar energy to achieve net-zero carbon emissions and mitigate climate change.

title: High-efficiency full-spectrum solar utilization via a novel continuous spectral splitting concentrator: design, optical validation, and system-level performance assessment
abstract: Spectral Beam Splitting (SBS) is a promising technology to precisely manage the solar spectrum and cascaded utilization of solar energy. However, conventional discrete SBS techniques experience an exponential rise in optical loss with successive splitting, thereby constraining the maximum number of feasible divisions. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a Novel Continuous Spectral Splitting Concentrator (CSSC) based on a refractive prism array. The CSSC enables an approximate spatial separation of spectral splitting and light concentration along orthogonal directions, generating a continuous “rainbow-like” spectrum with improved spectral resolution. A comprehensive optical-electrical model was developed and validated against experimental results, showing a Root Mean Square Deviation of 8.2% in energy flux distribution. Through a comprehensive parametric study, we identified the trade-offs between the spectral splitting coefficient and optical efficiency, determining an optimal prism apical angle limit of 21.5°. The optimized CSSC achieves an optical efficiency of 85.2% in the present configuration. The system achieved a high spectral resolution with a Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) of approximately 110 nm. A coupled optical-electrical case study indicates that integrating the proposed CSSC with a laterally arranged InGaP/GaAs/Ge cell array could achieve a photovoltaic efficiency of 37.0% under 400× concentration. These results suggest that the CSSC can serve as a promising optical platform for spectrum-selective solar-energy utilization.

title: From border carbon penalties to domestic action: can domestic carbon pricing provide a fairer solution to carbon leakage?
abstract: Amid the rapid reconfiguration of the global climate governance regime, border carbon adjustments (BCAs) are reshaping the international allocation of mitigation costs through trade and extraterritorial policy effects. Carbon charges based on embodied-emission estimates affect international competitiveness and may impose additional adjustment pressures on developing economies. Using a recursively updated multi-regional computable general equilibrium model based on the GTAP-E database, combined with input–output accounting to derive bilateral, sector-specific ad valorem trade shocks, this study evaluates the economic, environmental, and welfare effects of alternative carbon-pricing regimes, including unilateral border adjustments, coordinated domestic pricing, and cost-equity-based differentiated pricing. The results show that border-only measures achieve modest global emissions reductions while redistributing trade and welfare effects across economies, without uniformly benefiting all implementing countries. Uniform domestic pricing achieves the largest emissions reduction but also the greatest welfare loss, whereas differentiated pricing retains a substantial share of mitigation with lower welfare costs. China's domestic pricing response strengthens its mitigation relative to reliance on foreign border measures alone, although its global effects remain limited. These findings inform the comparative design of carbon-pricing policies and China's carbon-footprint governance.

title: Strategic pathways for decarbonization: a data-driven typology to strengthen climate policy
Renewable energy droughts under high variable renewables penetration: meteorological drivers, system impacts, and planning uses
An Atmospheric Perspective on Emerging Water Microdroplet Chemistry
abstract: Abstract Microdroplets, as tiny liquid particles, are ubiquitous in Earth’s atmosphere. They serve as dynamic microreactors that drive atmospheric processes, with profound implications for air quality, climate regulation, and atmospheric chemical cycles. Despite its importance, microdroplet-driven chemistry remains inadequately represented in global climate and air quality models. This perspective synthesizes emerging evidence on how microdroplet interface-enhanced multiphase chemistry modifies atmospheric processes including amplifying atmospheric oxidation capacity and accelerating the transformation of key reactive species. Advances in aerosol and microdroplet chemistry highlight the central role of the microdroplet interface in initiating accelerated kinetics and in enabling unprecedented chemical pathways distinct from those in macroscopic bulk solutions. We outline the current knowledge gaps and future directions for advancing the research in microdroplet chemistry from an atmospheric perspective. The concerted coordination among microdroplet chemistry and atmospheric communities across field, laboratory, and modeling has significant implications for understanding the critical role of microdroplet interface-driven chemistry in the atmosphere and climate change.

title: Exposomic Assessment of Endocrine-Disrupting Chemicals Using Hair: A Cross-Matrix Comparison with Serum and Urine by LC-HRMS and Metabolite Profiling
abstract: Abstract Endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) are increasingly implicated in chronic diseases, yet their biomonitoring in human studies still relies mainly on urine and serum, which capture only short-term exposure to these fast-elimination compounds. Here, we evaluated hair as a complementary and long-term biomonitoring matrix for EDC mixtures by integrating it into an LC-HRMS exposomics workflow together with paired serum and urine samples. We developed and validated a method targeting 44 endocrine disruptors from five chemical families (benzophenones, phthalates, parabens, bisphenols, and organophosphate esters), combining quantitative analysis with suspect screening and semi-quantification of phase II metabolites. Applied to samples from 20 postmenopausal women, the hair-based approach provided the broadest coverage and highest concentrations (31/44 compounds), up to about three orders of magnitude higher than in urine or serum, consistent with distinct accumulation mechanisms and temporal integration windows. In hair, EDCs were present in unconjugated form (>99%), whereas urine was dominated by conjugated metabolites and serum showed limited detection. Overall, these findings demonstrate that integrating hair into multimatrix exposomics designs substantially expands both the chemical and temporal resolution of human exposure assessment.

title: Industrial-Scale Production of Photocatalytic Hydrogen in China: Life Cycle Environmental and Economic Assessment in Comparison with Other Solar and Conventional Technologies
abstract: Abstract This study evaluates for the first time the sustainability of photocatalytic hydrogen production in China utilizing a 26-faced polyhedron SrTiO3/Rh/Co/Cr photocatalyst. Life cycle assessment and costing are used to estimate the impacts and levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH). These are compared via multicriteria decision analysis with alternative solar-driven hydrogen technologies (water electrolysis, photoelectrochemical, and thermochemical), as well as with conventional methods (steam methane reforming and coal gasification). The outcomes are used to identify optimal regional configurations in different provinces that minimize both the impacts and production costs. Photocatalytic hydrogen substantially outperforms conventional methods, reducing most impacts by 21–93%, including climate change (67–93%). However, several impacts are significantly higher, increasing from 48% to 20 times. Economically, photocatalytic hydrogen is competitive with conventional methods (1.58–2.42 k$/t H2 vs 1.18–2.38 k$/t H2). Enhancing photocatalyst stability, optimizing solar-to-hydrogen efficiency, integrating renewable electricity, and valorizing oxygen as a coproduct can further improve environmental performance and cost-effectiveness. In comparison with the other solar and conventional methods, photocatalytic hydrogen is the most sustainable option, along with the perovskite/silicon photoelectrochemical alternative. The findings provide critical guidance for scaling up solar-driven hydrogen production and inform policy, research, and regional deployment strategies.

title: Joint Effects of Water Quality Degradation and Non-Native Fish Invasion on Estuarine Biodiversity and Ecosystem Stability
abstract: Abstract Water quality degradation and biological invasions represent major drivers of global ecosystem degradation, yet their interactive effects remain poorly understood, especially in anthropogenically disturbed estuarine ecosystems. Here, we employed environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding to characterize multi-trophic biological communities in a subtropical estuary and to assess how water-quality degradation influences the invasion success of non-native fishes. The results show, firstly, the relative sequence abundance of non-native fish, rather than their species richness, emerged as the primary factor negatively associated with native fish diversity. Based on the observational dataset, we identified a statistical breakpoint, and the transition from low to high invasion pressure corresponds to a unimodal (hump-shaped) diversity pattern. Secondly, non-native fish primarily compete for food resources, thereby constraining the ecological niches of native species. Thirdly, a strong interactive effect exists between water quality degradation and non-native fish invasion. Water quality degradation acts not merely as a direct environmental stressor, but also indirectly weakens native communities. Collectively, these findings provide new insights into how declines in water quality interact with biological invasions and highlight the need for integrated invasion management strategies that simultaneously improve water quality and mitigate the impacts of invasive species in estuarine ecosystems.

title: PM2.5 Constituents and Cardiopulmonary Dysfunctions in Older Adults: A Multiomics Approach Unveiling Molecular Pathways
abstract: Abstract The cardiopulmonary risks of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) are linked to its constituents, yet key constituents and underlying molecular pathways driving cardiopulmonary dysfunctions in older adults remain elusive. In a longitudinal panel study of 313 measurements, we assessed associations between PM2.5 constituents and cardiopulmonary functions and explored mediation effects by DNA methylation and gene transcription using personal monitoring data. We combined a linear mixed-effects model with three machine-learning methods to identify key PM2.5 constituents, and employed mediation analysis and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis to explore potential epigenetic and transcriptional mediators and biological pathways. Our findings revealed that chloride ion (Cl–), nickel (Ni), barium, and selenium were the key constituents of PM2.5 inducing cardiopulmonary dysfunction. Interquartile range (IQR) increases in Cl– and Ni were associated with a 3.48% (95% CI: 1.50%, 5.46%) increase in diastolic blood pressure and a 0.09% (95% CI: 0.05%, 0.12%) decrease in FEV1/FVC, respectively. Mediation analysis identified 212 cytosine-phosphate-guanine (CpG) sites that regulated both cardiovascular and pulmonary dysfunctions, and 7 genes mediating more than two distinct constituent-function associations. Neurotransmission, metabolism, and cardiovascular function-related pathways were primarily enriched, among which 22 CpG sites (e.g., cg07115148, cg26409134, and cg26613778) were identified as key epigenetic mediators. Expression quantitative trait methylation analysis revealed that these CpG sites were associated with 14 protein-coding genes including CERS6 and LRCH3. Our findings suggest that short-term exposure to PM2.5 constituents triggers cardiopulmonary dysfunctions via DNA methylation-gene transcription axes and related disruption of neurotransmission, metabolism, and cardiovascular signaling pathways.

title: Rethinking In-Cloud Aqueous-Phase Nitrogen Chemistry: High-Molecular-Weight Carbonyls as Major Counterparts to Low-Molecular-Weight Dicarbonyls
abstract: Abstract Aqueous-phase reactions between carbonyls and reactive nitrogen species (e.g., ammonia/amine) are critical for forming secondary nitrogen-containing organic compounds (NOCs) and brown carbon (BrC). However, current atmospheric chemical paradigms center almost exclusively on low-molecular-weight carbonyls such as glyoxal, leaving the role of high-molecular-weight carbonyls (HMWCs, with 4 ≤ C ≤ 30) unexplored. Here, we utilize advanced nontargeted molecular fingerprinting (PFBHA derivatization and FT-ICR MS) to unveil an unexpected and highly diverse pool of 1,242 unique carbonyl formulas in cloud water. These HMWCs, predominantly distributed in the C8–C20 range, exhibit a disproportionately high signal intensity (up to ∼35%) despite representing only a small fraction (5.4–13.9%) of the total signal diversity. Using a mechanistic “precursor-product pair” framework, we demonstrate that these HMWCs contribute to nearly one-third of the total NOC diversity (including various light-absorbing N-heterocycles) via Maillard-like reactions. This contribution is strikingly comparable to that of well-studied low-molecular-weight dicarbonyls, i.e., glyoxal and methylglyoxal. We further show that this HMWC-driven pathway covaries with precursor availability and cloud water pH. These findings suggest that incorporating HMWC-mediated NOC formation into future atmospheric models may improve the representation of secondary BrC formation and its associated climate effects.

title: Non-Target Analytical Workflow for Gas-Phase Atmospheric Chemicals Collected on XAD Resin and Application to Passive Samplers
abstract: Abstract The atmospheric gas phase is underrepresented in non-target screening of environmental organic chemicals, partly due to limited evidence on sorbent suitability. Here, we developed a workflow for non-target analysis (NTA) of styrene-divinylbenzene copolymeric (XAD) resin-based air samples that involves both gas (GC) and liquid chromatography (LC) high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS). More than 60 000 features were detected in passive air samplers (PAS) deployed over 4–48 weeks. Of ∼34 000 features retained after blank filtration, ∼14 000 (41%) showed an increasing signal with deployment time, suggesting that they represent substances with volatility and degradability sufficiently low for accumulation on XAD without substantial re-evaporation or degradation during the prolonged sampling period. Such linear uptake is a prerequisite for comparing PAS-derived signals across deployments and chemical classes. Chemical identification by reference standards (level 1) and spectral library matching (level 2) initially identified/annotated 116 compounds, many of which were bioactive and/or brown carbon species. Combining advanced downstream computational workflows of feature-based molecular networking (FBMN) and in silico prediction (Network Annotation Propagation/MetFrag) allowed for the structural annotation (level 3) of >8300 LC-HRMS features, including several compounds of natural and anthropogenic origin which were not previously reported in the atmospheric gas phase. Several long-chain fatty acids showed rapid early increases implausible with atmospheric origins and are likely to originate from microbial growth on the resin. Overall, our results demonstrated that XAD is a sorbent compatible with comprehensive NTA and suitable for time-integrated passive sampling of a diverse range of gas-phase organic chemicals from the atmosphere.

Remote sensing and artificial intelligence integration for seabed seagrass distribution and probabilistic seagrass biomass carbon potential
abstract: The Seto Inland Sea (SIS), Japan's largest semi-enclosed coastal sea, hosts seagrass meadows that form an important and quantifiable reservoir of biomass-based carbon. Reliable mapping of these meadows is therefore essential for ecosystem assessment and coastal management. This study integrates a multiband depth-invariant bottom index (BI) derived from Sentinel-2 imagery with machine learning and deep learning classifiers to map seabed seagrass distribution and estimate the probabilistic seagrass biomass carbon potential of the inner SIS between 2019 and 2025. Sentinel-2 imagery was processed in Google Earth Engine, and Bands 2 (blue), 3 (green), and 4 (red) were combined into three BI configurations ( 𝐵 ⁢ 𝐼 2 − 3 , 𝐵 ⁢ 𝐼 3 − 4 , and 𝐵 ⁢ 𝐼 2 − 4 ). Of nine classifiers tested, Random Forest (RF) performed best, reaching 92.31% accuracy and 𝜅 = 0.81 under a single stratified split. More conservative validation across 50 repeated random splits gave 87.4 ± 9.5% accuracy and 𝜅 = 0.686 ± 0.225, while spatial leave-one-site-out (LOSO) validation gave 77.4% accuracy and 𝜅 = 0.50, indicating reduced transferability to unsurveyed sites. Among the three band-pair configurations, 𝐵 ⁢ 𝐼 2 − 3 was the dominant predictor (variable importance = 0.93). Building on this classification, seagrass biomass carbon potential was estimated by combining satellite-derived seagrass probabilities with field-based biomass distributions through Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation. The resulting estimate reflects standing seagrass biomass carbon only, excluding sediment organic carbon, burial, decomposition, and lateral carbon export, and should be read as a biomass carbon potential rather than a total blue carbon stock. Monthly carbon potential followed a clear seasonal cycle, rising from winter into spring and peaking in May–June. Together, these results show that combining a multiband BI with artificial intelligence (AI)-based classification enables site-specific seagrass mapping and biomass-based carbon assessment in optically complex coastal waters, while underscoring the need for spatially independent validation before extrapolating beyond surveyed sites.

title: Impact of circumsolar irradiance and aerosol optical depth on CAMS surface solar irradiance estimates
abstract: The global horizontal irradiance is a main variable in the integration of solar energy systems in electricity grids, and in climate and weather studies. The physical model McClear is the clear-sky module for the all-sky irradiance retrievals from the CAMS Radiation Service. Validations of McClear against high-quality in situ measurements reveal very accurate global horizontal irradiance estimates with negligible bias. Albeit still good, the beam and diffuse irradiance components exhibit biases generally opposing each other. These biases are mainly attributed to the aerosol optical depth used as input to McClear, and the forward scattered circumsolar irradiance surrounding the solar disc which is not modelled by McClear but intercepted within the solid angle aperture of radiometers measuring beam irradiance (and blocked by those measuring diffuse irradiance). This study performs a global scale validation of a desert-based circumsolar correction, and evaluates the influence of this circumsolar correction and the aerosol optical depth on the beam and diffuse irradiance estimates from McClear. Circumsolar corrected retrievals are enhanced globally, especially for the diffuse component of McClear, with the standard deviation of deviations improving from 26.3 to 24.4%, the bias from 19.0 to 13.1%, and the correlation remaining constant at 0.837. Comparing ground measured and CAMS modelled aerosol optical depth, improvements are expected with further developments to the CAMS aerosol model.

Probabilistic health risk assessment and source-specific risk analysis of potentially toxic elements in metropolitan surface soils using PMF, geo-detector, and KDE-based Monte Carlo simulation
abstract: Metropolitan soils are increasingly affected by multiple anthropogenic inputs, resulting in complex patterns of potentially toxic element (PTE) accumulation. However, the mechanisms linking pollution sources, spatial heterogeneity, and the resulting ecological and human health risks remain insufficiently understood. To clarify PTE contamination characteristics and associated risks, 1122 topsoil samples were obtained across the studied metropolitan region in southwestern China. The results revealed that all PTEs, except As and Cd, exceeded their local background values. Spatially, Hg, Pb, Cu, and Zn exhibited localized enrichment hotspots in the east-central urbanized areas. Combined APCS-MLR and PMF receptor models identified five potential sources, including natural background (25.54%), atmospheric deposition (15.13%), agricultural activities (18.64%), industrial manufacturing and urban emissions (19.14%), and mixed traffic–industrial sources (21.55%). PMF provided better model fit and spatial separation than APCS-MLR under the study conditions. Geo-detector analysis revealed that soil type and land use were the dominant factors controlling PTE spatial heterogeneity, with nonlinear interactions further enhancing their explanatory power. According to the potential ecological risk index, low to moderate ecological risk levels were identified in 83.07% of the samples. Hg and Cd were the major contributors to ecological risk, whereas atmospheric deposition represented the highest source-specific ecological risk contribution. Deterministic health risk assessment indicated higher risks for children, with 7.93% of samples exceeding the acceptable non-carcinogenic risk threshold. Carcinogenic risks were acceptable for both population groups. As was the dominant contributor to both carcinogenic and non-carcinogenic risks, and soil ingestion represented the major exposure route. KDE-optimized Monte Carlo simulation further showed that 9.47% of children may experience unacceptable non-carcinogenic risk, while accounting for the empirical distribution and uncertainty of exposure-related variables. Although the health risk assessment was based on total PTE concentrations without considering metal bioavailability, the proposed framework still provides a scientific basis for source-specific pollution control and risk-prioritized soil management in rapidly urbanizing metropolitan regions.

Sabotage as Industrial Policy
abstract: Abstract We characterise sabotage, exemplified by recent US policies concerning China’s semiconductor industry, as trade policy. For some (but not all) goods, completely destroying foreigners’ productivity increases domestic real income by shifting the location of production and improving the terms of trade. The gross benefit of sabotage can be summarised by a few sufficient statistics: trade and demand elasticities and import and production shares. The cost of sabotage is determined by countries’ relative unit labour costs for the sabotaged goods. We find important non-monotonicities: for semiconductors, partially sabotaging foreign production would lower US real income, while comprehensive sabotage would raise it.

Pushing the Boundaries: Studies on Consumers and Food Demand in the Journal of Agricultural Economics
abstract: ABSTRACT We summarize the development of consumer economics and food demand in the Journal of Agricultural Economics over the past 100 years. Even from an early stage, the role of marketing agricultural products in a thriving agricultural sector was recognized within the works published in the Journal. Early papers focused on the demand for specific commodities and consumer trends more generally. Over time, analyses became more advanced, diving into the development of theory and methods for the estimation of demand systems. While this trend has continued, other topics have come to the forefront, such as consumer demand for food quality and safety, consumer acceptance of novel technologies, the demand for sustainable food products, and the role of nutrition and health in consumer studies. Methods were developed concurrently to address the new challenges that the agricultural sector faced, from secondary data analysis to primary data collection and experimental methods.
