title: Time-Duration Asymmetries in Consumer Decision-Making
abstract: Abstract Consumers routinely make decisions about short time periods, such as waiting for a table or deciding whether to pay for faster delivery. Such periods are often expressed by either a duration or a clock time (e.g., if it is 6:00 PM now, “Your table will be ready in 30 minutes” vs. “Your table will be ready at 6:30 PM”). Eight experiments (N = 16,604) show that these logically equivalent frames change how long a period feels, with downstream consequences for consumer decisions. Relatively short time periods feel longer when framed by duration rather than by start and end time (i.e., clock times or calendar dates), but this pattern reverses as periods get longer. We refer to this phenomenon as time-duration asymmetry: framing an interval by its start and end time versus its duration changes how long it feels, with the direction of the effect depending on the interval’s length. We propose that this occurs because duration frames evoke compressive scalar representations shaped by diminishing sensitivity, whereas start-end frames situate time within structured categorical systems that attenuate compression. This research offers a unified framework for understanding how subtle differences in temporal framing shape perceptions of time and subsequent decisions.

title: Balancing coherence and resonance through linguistic framing: A longitudinal study of German biotechnology ventures' responses to the Covid‐19 pandemic
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Research suggests that ventures benefit from framing to gain audience support, yet how they utilize framing when exogenous shocks redirect attention remains unclear. Drawing on a longitudinal multiple‐case study of six biotechnology ventures following the COVID‐19 pandemic, we show how ventures balance coherence and resonance through framing pathways. Persevering ventures, committed to pre‐shock opportunities, maintained a “Blockbuster” framing, highlighting business viability to engage commercial investors. Flexible ventures, in contrast, adopted an “Emergency” framing, signaling responsiveness to societal threats to attract public investors, before transitioning to a “Preparedness” framing, emphasizing long‐term potential. Across both pathways, ventures anchored framings in a scientific perspective, signaling expertise and rigor. We theorize how ventures balance coherence and resonance through an anchoring frame that provides continuity and complementing frames that enable adaptation to shifting audience expectations. Managerial Summary Our study of six biotechnology ventures shows how high‐technology entrepreneurs communicate with investors during industry shocks, such as pandemics. We identify two distinct pathways. Ventures that pivot toward shock‐related opportunities benefit from adopting an “Emergency” framing, positioning themselves as addressing urgent societal threats to attract public investors. To sustain investor support over time, they subsequently shift to a “Preparedness” framing, highlighting their solutions' long‐term potential. Conversely, ventures that maintain their original strategies gain traction by consistently employing a “Blockbuster” framing, emphasizing their business case to attract commercial investors. Across both pathways, ventures reinforce credibility by anchoring their framings in scientific expertise, rigor, and the ability to address unmet medical needs. Pivoting ventures also leverage new applications to identify and capitalize on additional shock‐related opportunities.

title: EXPRESS: EV Charging Availability and Grocery Store Performance
abstract: Grocery retailers are well-positioned to help address the shortage of EV charging infrastructure but seek insight on the implications for store performance. They lack clarity on the revenue impact of EV charging availability on their parking lots, the underlying mechanisms, and the conditions under which the effect is more pronounced. Drawing on a dataset of over 300 stores of a leading German grocery chain and utilizing a staggered Difference-in-Differences quasi-experimental design, the authors show that EV charging availability increases revenues by 3.4%. Market expansion alone cannot fully explain the effect as the authors find significant evidence for market stealing. They further find that the increase is due to more transactions, not to changes in basket size. The largest increase materializes during off-peak weekend hours. They identify several attitudinal (perceived impulsiveness, storability) and behavioral (penetration, purchase frequency) category characteristics that explain where the revenue increase comes from and provide insights into the role of various store (surface-to-parking ratio, management type) and market (e.g., local competition, apartment-to-house ratio, neighborhood wealth) characteristics. Guidance for store managers interested in increasing the benefits of having EV charging on their premises and chain managers supervising the roll-out throughout their store network is provided.

title: EXPRESS: When Consumers Prefer Point Versus Range Estimates of Product Performance
abstract: Product performance claims play an important role in shaping consumers’ purchase decisions. Through six preregistered studies, including one field study, the authors demonstrate that consumers’ preferences for point versus range performance estimates in common comparative purchase settings depend on whether their attention is directed toward the content of the claim or the manner of its presentation. At baseline, consumers focus on what information is communicated and prefer point over range estimates because point estimates convey greater certainty about the expected performance outcome. When consumers’ persuasion knowledge is activated, however, their attention shifts toward how information is communicated. In this mode, the format of the claim, rather than the stated performance figures, becomes relatively more informative: range estimates signal brand transparency by acknowledging the natural variability of real-world performance, enhancing perceived trustworthiness and reversing consumer preference. These effects are attenuated when products are evaluated in isolation rather than compared side by side. Collectively, these findings inform both theory and practice by revealing when and why consumers prefer point versus range estimates of product performance.

title: The Alignment Paradox: A Theory of AI ‐Driven Misalignment in HR Systems
abstract: ABSTRACT The core principle in strategic human resource management (SHRM) holds that organizations gain competitive advantage from HR systems with practices that work well together (horizontal alignment) and that support overall strategy (vertical alignment). This paper develops a theory explaining how artificial intelligence integration, a tool intended to improve alignment, can unintentionally cause alignment breakdown. Drawing on SHRM theory and the process‐based model of HRM system strength, we build four propositions. We argue that AI's operational requirements weaken horizontal alignment by creating logic conflicts within HR systems, cause employee skill development to drift from strategic needs, cause employees to default to metric‐aligned behaviors, and diminish workforce value as a competitive resource. We synthesize these dynamics in a framework of four organizational states, Strategic Synergy, Contested Alignment, Strategic Fragmentation, and Algorithmic Capture that characterize firms at different stages of AI‐driven misalignment. This paper contributes a process‐based theory explaining organizational risks of AI adoption in management systems.

title: The Virtual Pivot: Adaptive Investor Relations in the Face of Disruption
abstract: ABSTRACT The capacity of firms to communicate effectively with investors during periods of disruption is a critical but understudied dimension of corporate adaptability. The COVID‐19 pandemic offers a rare empirical setting to observe such adaptability: It eliminated in‐person investor events almost overnight, forcing firms to either withdraw from investor engagement or pivot to virtual formats amid extreme uncertainty. Using hand‐collected data on investor relations (IR) events from 2019 to 2024, we examine who adapted to virtual IR, when they adapted, and the capital market consequences of that adaptation. We find that firms with higher digital readiness and more gender‐diverse boards were early and sustained adopters of virtual IR, that the informational benefits of virtual formats are concentrated in periods of heightened uncertainty, and that visibility benefits persist as conditions normalize. The findings imply that disclosure adaptability during a crisis hinges on organizational and digital capabilities built ex ante and suggest that virtual and in‐person formats serve distinct functions as conditions stabilize. Our study has practical implications: CEOs, CFOs, and IR teams may benefit from maintaining virtual IR as a crisis‐ready capability that broadens investor reach and preserves communication during disruption, while continuing to draw on in‐person engagement for richer interactions, credibility assessment, and deeper discussions.

title: Algorithmic identity regulation in the platform-based gig work of Indian food delivery workers
abstract: How do algorithmic systems regulate worker identities by defining who they are expected to become? Identity regulation research has largely focused on how organizational discourse shapes worker identities. Yet, in platform labour, control is increasingly enacted through algorithmic systems that allocate tasks, monitor performance, and assign reputational scores in real time. Drawing on interviews with delivery partners and platform managers, supplemented by multi-source data, we examine how such systems shape the identities workers are encouraged to adopt or avoid, and how they engage with these processes. We make two key contributions. First, we theorize algorithmic identity regulation as a computational, sociomaterial, and affective form of normative control, whereby digital infrastructures continuously evaluate, rank, and allocate work, recalibrating workers’ identities through ongoing cycles of recognition, visibility, and devaluation. Second, we show how algorithmic identity regulation reshapes dignity at work by rendering recognition continuous, depersonalized, and datafied, making workers’ sense of worth increasingly contingent on algorithmic evaluation. In doing so, we show that algorithmic control not only manages work but shapes how workers define their value, worth, and place in the labour process.

title: Correction to ‟Unlocking Social Media Success: How Prosumers Drive Brand Engagement through Authentic Conversations with Consumers”
Evaluating Firm Quadruple Bottom Line (QBL) Performance: Development and Validation of a Brief Scale
abstract: ABSTRACT The quadruple bottom line (QBL) has emerged as a critical framework for assessing corporate performance beyond economic, social, and environmental metrics. Although previous models have proposed additional dimensions such as governance, growing attention is now being directed toward the cultural dimension as a fundamental component of holistic corporate sustainability. However, despite its increasing relevance, no psychometrically validated instrument has been available to measure the QBL. This study develops and validates a brief 15‐item QBL scale that integrates all four dimensions of corporate sustainability, including the new cultural pillar. A rigorous mixed‐methods approach was adopted, involving expert panel validation and focus groups to develop the brief scale, followed by quantitative testing to confirm validity and reliability with a sample of 205 general managers from small and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs) in the Spanish bioeconomy forest sector. Exploratory factor analysis conducted with SPSS 29, along with confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling using AMOS 29, revealed strong reliability and validity at both the first‐order (individual dimensions) and second‐order (overall QBL) levels. These results demonstrate that cultural performance can be integrated into a multidimensional sustainability framework, enhancing the explanatory power of sustainability assessments beyond triple bottom line models and promoting a shift toward viewing sustainability as an interconnected construct rather than as separate domains. The resulting QBL scale constitutes an initial effort to provide a theoretically grounded and psychometrically sound instrument for holistic sustainability assessment by newly integrating the cultural dimension, whereas its empirical validation has been confined to Spanish bioeconomy SMEs.

title: Proactive Despite Tensions? The Role of Paradox Mindset in Organizational Change Towards the Circular Economy
abstract: ABSTRACT As organizations respond to calls for sustainability, many invest in organizational change towards a circular economy (OCCE), which often depends on employee proactivity. However, OCCE is fraught with tensions that can either limit or foster proactive efforts. This raises critical questions: When and why do employees remain proactive for circularity in light of such tensions? Building on paradox theory, we investigate the moderating role of a paradox mindset in mitigating the potentially adverse effects of two central OCCE tensions: intertemporal and intergroup. Further, based on approach‐avoidance and cognitive dissonance theory, we examine the mediating roles of intertemporal cognitive processing and intergroup perspective taking. Using survey data from 199 employees, our results suggest that experienced tensions can positively influence employee proactivity, with exploratory evidence indicating a J‐shaped, curvilinear relationship. We contribute to the emerging micro‐foundational understanding of OCCE, highlight paradox mindsets in attenuating negative effects of tensions, and demonstrate the importance of tension levels in influencing employee proactivity.

title: Stakeholder Alignment Around Technological Pathways in Early‐Stage Sustainability Transitions: A Study of Stakeholder‐Perceived Stakes in Aviation Decarbonization
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines how stakeholder groups become aligned or remain misaligned around alternative technological pathways during early‐stage sustainability transitions. We develop the concept of stakeholder‐perceived stakes, capturing how stakeholder groups evaluate technological pathways through perceived drivers and holdbacks, and how these evaluations shape coordination dynamics. Drawing on an exploratory qualitative study of aviation decarbonization in Sweden, we analyze interviews with five stakeholder groups concerning three pathways: sustainable aviation fuels, electrification, and hydrogen‐powered aviation. While stakeholders share the goal of decarbonizing aviation, they differ in their evaluations of pathway‐specific opportunities and constraints. These differences generate patterns of alignment and misalignment that influence coordination and shape whether technological pathways consolidate, coexist, or remain fragmented. The paper contributes to sustainability transition and stakeholder research by explaining how stakeholder‐perceived stakes shape stakeholder alignment, coordination dynamics, and pathway development under conditions of technological plurality.

title: From ‘Responsible’ to ‘Sustainable’: A Contingent Analysis of Responsible Entrepreneurship and Product Innovation Performance in an Emerging Economy
abstract: ABSTRACT While debate on responsible entrepreneurial activities for sustainable development is burgeoning, studies examining whether small and medium‐sized firms (SMEs) can benefit from responsible entrepreneurship remain underexplored. In this study, we draw on stakeholder theory to fill this literature gap by investigating the effect of responsible entrepreneurship on product innovation performance. We also consider the contingent roles of stakeholder relationship capability and environmental information sharing in this relationship. Our results from analysing survey data from 172 firms in Nigeria (an emerging economy) demonstrate that responsible entrepreneurship has a positive relationship with product innovation performance. In addition, we uncover that stakeholder relationship capability amplifies the product innovation performance benefits of responsible entrepreneurship. Furthermore, our results reveal that environmental information sharing strengthens the moderating effect of stakeholder relationship capability on the link between responsible entrepreneurship and product innovation performance. Importantly, these results support our contingent stakeholder perspective on responsible entrepreneurship and offer rich, nuanced insights for utilising responsible entrepreneurship in emerging market firms.

title: ESG Practices and Corporate Efficiency in Global Manufacturing Multinational Firms: The Conditional Role of Board Size
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices influence sustainability efficiency and profitability efficiency in global manufacturing multinational firms and explores whether board size moderates these relationships. Using a sample of 71 firms from 2017 to 2021, including the COVID‐19 period, this study employs a dynamic network data envelopment analysis model to evaluate two stages of organizational value creation: sustainability efficiency and profitability efficiency. The findings reveal that ESG dimensions exert differentiated effects across these stages. Social practices are negatively associated with both sustainability efficiency and profitability efficiency, suggesting potential short‐term resource trade‐offs associated with social initiatives. By contrast, governance practices significantly enhance profitability efficiency, suggesting that governance‐related ESG practices support the conversion of organizational resources into financial outcomes. Most board size interaction effects are statistically insignificant, indicating that board size does not systematically condition ESG efficiency relationships. The moderating effect of board size is confined to the governance profitability relationship, where larger boards weaken the positive association. By distinguishing between sustainability efficiency and profitability efficiency, this study provides a deeper understanding of how ESG practices influence organizational value creation. The findings offer important implications for managers and policymakers seeking to balance sustainability objectives, governance effectiveness, and long‐term organizational performance.

title: Risk Exposure and Institutional Pressure: Drivers of Environmental Disclosure in Sub‐Saharan Africa
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates how objective environmental and institutional pressures drive corporate environmental disclosure in sub‐Saharan Africa, independent of firms' self‐reported claims. Using 2390 firm‐year observations (2012–2021) from six countries, we proxy for carbon intensity and occupational safety risk using sector‐level benchmarks from the International Energy Agency, the International Labour Organisation and for regulatory stringency using the World Bank's policy index. Findings indicate that firms in high‐risk sectors disclose significantly more, and stronger national regulations further increase transparency, even under weak enforcement. These results refine legitimacy and institutional theories by demonstrating that disclosure responds to measurable risk exposure rather than merely symbolic reporting. We find that grounding analysis in observable risk exposures strengthens environmental accountability in emerging markets. The findings support risk‐proportionate disclosure mandates: stringent, verified reporting for high‐impact sectors and streamlined requirements for low‐risk firms, enhancing relevance without overburdening institutions.

title: Resource entitlements and the trust paradox in cross-sector partnerships: Micro-foundations and cross-cultural dynamics of AI adoption in SMEs
abstract: We examine how cross-sector partnerships influence SMEs' adoption of frontier AI technologies for sustainable value creation. We extend the Technology Acceptance Model through a business network perspective to investigate the roles of perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived risk, and trust in partnership-mediated technology adoption. We collected data through structured questionnaires from 488 SME managers across Türkiye and the UK to account for cultural-institutional and contextual effects alongside micro-foundations of cross-sector partnerships. We find that cross-sector partnerships create value by enhancing the perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use of technology. However, in line with a growing literature on the dark side of trust in frontier technologies and B2B relationships, our findings reveal a significant trust paradox: high trust within cross-sector partnerships is significantly associated with lower AI adoption intentions. This suggests that SMEs may resist the adoption of disruptive resources like AI to preserve existing partnerships and stable resource entitlements. Furthermore, we find that while higher risk perception is directly associated with managers' pursuit of value through AI, this intention appears to be offset by complex mediation mechanisms and the inertia associated with the trust paradox. Cross-country comparison suggests that while partner preferences vary by context, the trust paradox appears to be a fundamental micro-foundation of cross-sector partnerships in the context of disruptive technologies, transcending cultural-institutional factors. We contribute to the network perspective on cross-sector partnerships by identifying trust's dual role as both a facilitator of stability and a barrier to technology-driven sustainable value creation.

title: Worlds beyond scale: Social entrepreneurship and the pluralisation of social value
abstract: This article critically examines the epistemic and normative foundations of scaling social value in social entrepreneurship. Over the past two decades, scaling has become a dominant ideal, routinely equated with success, effectiveness, and legitimacy. We argue that this monocultural fixation on growth narrows what can be seen, valued, and supported as ‘social’, obscuring the relational, contextual, and plural character of social value creation. Drawing on critical and decolonial scholarship, we show how prevailing scaling logics generate counterproductive outcomes by privileging replication and expansion whilst rendering alternative forms of social value creation invisible or illegitimate. In response, we advance the ecology of trans-scales as an alternative epistemological orientation that reconceptualises scaling as a relational and dialogical process, rather than a unidirectional, necessary trajectory of growth. We identify four elements that sustain this epistemic turn in social entrepreneurship: trans-scalar linkages, epistemic humility, politics of mutual intelligibility, and plural evaluation of scale effects. Together, these elements reframe scaling as a process of connection, translation, and negotiation across scales, offering a pathway beyond the monoculture of scale in social entrepreneurship research and practice.

title: Cultural storytelling, felt accountability and the microfoundations of activist commitment
abstract: Purpose This paper examines how storytelling practices operate as microfoundational mechanisms that shape and sustain felt accountability. Focusing on the Repeal the 8th campaign in Ireland, the study explores how narrative practices organise moral, emotional and political commitments, and how these are formed, internalised and made durable through culturally embedded storytelling practices that constitute the microfoundations of felt accountability. Design/methodology/approach Conversational interviews with Repeal activists are drawn on and analysed through a feminist narrative approach oriented towards understanding how felt accountability is narrated and experienced in practice. The analysis is informed by using Declan Kiberd's (1995, 2017) postcolonial literary work on radical traditionalism enabling a culturally situated reading of activist narratives within longer Irish storytelling traditions. Findings The cultural storytelling tropes of confession, silence, absence and spectral presence, domestic intimacy, subversive wit and unresolved loss are identified to have acted as microfoundational mechanisms of accountability that bound activists to Repeal, one-another and the cause of reproductive justice. Through intimate conversations, shared confessions and bearing witness to personal narratives of reproductive experiences and injustices, the reactivation of these storytelling tropes constituted the moral and political bonds that sustained and reaffirmed activists' sense of felt accountability to Repeal under emotionally taxing and abusive conditions. Originality/value The paper contributes to the accountability literature by examining how felt accountability is culturally mediated and sustained through microfoundational narrative practices and inherited storytelling traditions. In this sense, the paper highlights how microfoundational mechanisms of storytelling, drawing on culturally resonant storytelling tropes, actively constitute activist accountability, offering – more broadly – a novel account of how felt accountability is shaped, internalised and maintained. In doing so, the paper illustrates how storytelling acts as a cultural infrastructure and a moral and political practice through which accountability is enacted, felt and made durable.

title: Revealing hidden inequalities: leaked files, shadow accounts and racialised border control
abstract: Purpose This paper investigates how leaked documents can function as tools of shadow accounting to expose and challenge the racialised inequalities embedded in Australia's offshore detention regime – inequalities that further marginalise asylum-seekers already displaced by conflict, persecution and hardship in their countries of origin or transit. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on a Critical Dialogic Accounting and Accountability (CDAA) framework, we analyse the “Nauru Files” – over 2,000 leaked incident reports from Australia's offshore detention centre on Nauru (2013–2015). We interpret these documents as counter-hegemonic artefacts that offer rare insight into the systemic racial injustices and institutionalised forms of violence embedded within border control practices. Through reflexive, theory-informed analysis, we construct a shadow account as a form of CDAA praxis to interrogate how harm, racialisation and resistance are documented, minimised or erased within official reporting practices. Findings The analysis demonstrates how the Nauru Files present counter-hegemonic opportunities to produce shadow accounts to illuminate hidden and racialised forms of suffering and control. These leaked records document repeated instances of abuse, neglect and institutionalised harm, highlighting the compounded inequalities faced by asylum-seekers who, having fled conflict and persecution, are subjected to further dehumanisation within offshore detention. We argue that such leaks and the shadow accounts constructed from them help expose these injustices and can contribute to broader mobilisation among actors, including asylum-seekers, activists, journalists and scholars, to resist and contest the border-industrial complex. Research limitations/implications By situating leaked documents within CDAA praxis, this study expands accounting's capacity to engage with global racialised inequalities. The paper highlights how accounting practices can expose state-sanctioned violence and amplify the calls for justice from those denied the opportunity to live free from persecution in host countries like Australia. Originality/value This study is among the first to explicitly centre race and forced displacement within shadow accounting and CDAA research. It positions leaked documents as potent counter-accounting mechanisms that surface otherwise silenced experiences and challenge the legitimacy of oppressive systems, offering an innovative contribution to the literature on accounting for migration and inequalities.

title: From co-production to value co-creation: NGOs as catalysts of cyclical public value in rural China

Evaluating Robust Tests for Longitudinal Invariance Testing
abstract: Testing parameter constraints in CFA under non-normality is routinely done with robust chi-square difference tests, yet the finite-sample behavior of the available procedures remains unsettled. Pavlov et al. (Citation2020) identified the Mplus mean- and variance-adjusted test DMLMV as the most accurate established procedure in a two-model longitudinal CFA design. Here, we extend their study in three ways: we add penalized eigenvalue (PE) methods; we vary three estimation choices that Pavlov et al. held fixed—Satorra’s (2000) direct estimator of UD, the unbiased estimator of Γ, and the reweighted least-squares (RLS) base statistic; and we broaden the distributional conditions. While the performance of DMLMV was acceptable in the smaller model (p=10), it was too liberal in the larger model (p=30). Our results suggest that PE and the scaled-and-shifted (SS) test, combined with the 2000 method, deserve priority in longitudinal invariance testing. In our simulations, size-adjusted power was very similar across all procedures. In terms of Type I error control, we recommend RLS-based PE with the unbiased Γ estimator, and the RLS-based SS test, as the preferred procedures.
